Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs as profits jump ahead of looming bank tax; French bond yields hit fresh 24-year high – business live
events.summary: Barclays says it is cutting 5,000 jobs Barclays also said it is cutting 5,000 jobs, amounting to about 5% of its workforce, our banking correspondent Kalyeena Makortoff reports . Its chief financial officer, Anna Cross , told journalists on a call that 1,000 of the job cuts have already been implemented, with another 4,000 to go before the end of the year. The news was buried in this morning’s presentation, where the UK bank revealed higher profits of £2.3bn for the July to September period, up 12% on last year. It is handing a further £500m back to shareholders. C. S. Venkatakrishnan , the chief executive, said that the bank’s cost to income ratio has improved from 63% to 62% in the last three months. The Barclays share price is up slightly this morning, but has lost about a quarter of its value in the past three months. 3m ago Barclays bosses say job cuts driven by AI advances 34m ago Barclays says it is cutting 5,000 jobs 1h ago Barclays' bumper profits show need for bank windfall tax at budget, TUC says 1h ago Introduction: Barclays profits jump ahead of looming bank tax; French bond yields hit fresh 24-year high Barclays bosses say job cuts driven by AI advances The 5,000 job cuts are part of a wider cost cutting drive that Barclays bosses said has been driven by advances in artificial intelligence. The majority (60%) affect support roles. The job cuts will mean getting rid of about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff. The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross , told reporters that it was part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5000 full time employees, around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including theory developers. AI makes our people more productive. When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to AI, chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes. That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future. The Barclays results come after reports on Monday that the Bank of England was examining whether Barclays traders had misrepresented illiquid private credit loans by using derivatives. Barclays shares have fallen by 20% over the last three months, also pressured by the prospect of higher bank taxes in the upcoming budget. Richard Hunter at interactive investor said: Indeed, the UK banks have an additional hurdle to overcome in the form of the imminent budget. The sector has underperformed so far this year on a number of concerns, one of which is the bank surcharge. One market estimate suggests that the bank surcharge will be returned to 8% from the current 3% which in turn would reduce earnings by a possible 6%, although whatever the outcome some of the uncertainty which has been overhanging the banks would be removed. On balance, these concerns have blemished the investor confidence which was clearly in evidence at the interim results, even though the longer-term picture remains solid and where Barclays has maintained its guidance for this year and next. Prospects for its three largest units, the Investment Bank, Barclays UK and Barclays US Consumer Bank are the main drivers and it may yet emerge that this quarter’s slightly uninspiring update is a blip rather than establishing a weaker trend. Despite the quarterly share price weakness and the heightened expectations which have resulted in a weaker opening price today, the direction of travel remains intact, with the shares having posted a gain of 15% over the last year, as compared to a hike of 13% for the wider FTSE100. Over the last two years, the price is ahead by 74% and there seems little doubt that the group’s financial strength, alongside its geographical and business diversity are factors which keeps the stock in demand among investors, such that the market consensus of the shares as a buy should remain untroubled. Richard Hunter, head of markets at the trading platform interactive investor, said the Barclays results are a bit “a mixed bag which is unlikely to blow away the clouds which have been hovering over the sector”. In the investment bank, which accounts for 42% of group revenues, the recent US experience of the large names was echoed, he noted. Equity income rose by 47%, but Fixed Income, Currencies and Commodities (FICC) was 19% lower, leading to an overall 4% gain. Investment banking fees and advisory rose by 13%, with other highlights coming from Barclays UK Corporate. A cautious impairment provision of £500m was 20% lower than the previous year, with defaults remaining stable and far from ringing any alarm bells. More broadly, the group reiterated its financial muscle with a further £500m share buyback, in addition to the £1bn announced at the interim results.

events.title: Meta faces Australian lawsuit over alleged social media harm to children
events.summary: Class action could be first in Australia to blame social media for harming its users. Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers. The lawsuit, filed by MinterEllison in the Australian Federal Court, seeks to recover compensation for current and former users of Facebook and Instagram who claim they were exposed to harmful content or developed an addiction to social media as a result of using those platforms, the law firm said in a statement released on Thursday. list 1 of 3 Australia’s proposed ‘opt out’ law targets Big Tech algorithms list 2 of 3 Australia seeks big tech support for internet safety, AI regulation list 3 of 3 Mexico to force Meta, TikTok, and X to better protect minors on platform “This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia. Those questions will now be considered through the Federal Court process,” MinterEllison Partner William Nolan said in the statement. The class action suit was filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were below the age of 18. In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information that could reveal their identities and the statement of claim. “We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously,” a Meta spokesperson said. Litigation Lending Services said it was funding the class action for Australian families who “would have no practical means of pursuing these claims against a global technology giant”. The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech after a world-first ban on social media for children below 16 in 2025, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds. Meta agreed in August to pay $18bn to settle with nearly all US states to resolve claims that it designed social media to addict children.

Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa apologised on Wednesday for the latest error, which occurred despite officials’ pledges to implement steps to prevent mistakes, including playing the correct national anthems. list 1 of 4 How a comedy of errors ‘ruined everything’ for athletes at the Asian Games list 2 of 4 Asian Games: South Korea volleyball team latest to be taken to wrong venue list 3 of 4 Taiwan’s gender-row boxer Lin Yu-ting wins Asian Games gold list 4 of 4 No handshakes and a delayed ceremony as India beat Pakistan at Asian Games “These things happened during the Asian Games, so, of course, the operations were reviewed and examined based on the lessons learned. The fact that it happened again is really just unacceptable,” the mayor said at a news conference. The Asian Para Games is taking place in the central Japanese hub city through Saturday, featuring about 4,000 athletes and officials in 18 sports. On Monday, a Taiwanese athlete won a men’s para taekwondo competition, but the Iranian anthem was played in its entirety, according to Nagoya officials at the mayor’s news conference. Officials realised their mistake after the ceremony, they said. The Iranian anthem was played again that day during a women’s para taekwondo ceremony as a Mongolian competitor was receiving the gold medal, according to the city. The incorrect music was stopped after the Mongolian delegation pointed out the error. Organisers then played the Mongolian anthem after the music was provided by the delegation, Nagoya officials said. Separately on Monday, officials broadcast the South Korean anthem for about five seconds instead of the Chinese one before a sitting volleyball match between China and Iran. “It is unacceptable, or rather, it’s painful. I am very sorry about it,” the mayor said, adding that he felt the tournament was otherwise progressing smoothly. The Asian Games, which concluded in early October, faced heavy criticism for shortcomings ranging from inadequate accommodations for athletes to the playing of wrong national anthems. On September 18, organisers played North Korea’s national anthem for the South Korean hockey team.

events.title: Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography
events.summary: At the recent SPIE Photomask Technology + Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography conference, an expert panel discussed the growing importance of edge placement error (EPE). I had the pleasure of joining moderator Jed Rankin of IBM and fellow panelists Hans Stiepan of Carl Zeiss SMT, Ezequiel Vidal-Russell of Micron Technology, Jo Finders of ASML, Il-Yong Jang of Tekscend, and Vivek Balasubramanian of Applied Materials. Together, we brought perspectives spanning OPC and EDA, mask technology, lithography systems, materials, and metrology. One point quickly became clear: EPE is no longer a narrow lithography metric. It is becoming a system-level measure of how well our industry can translate design intent into a manufacturable, high-yielding device. The mask, scanner, resist, etch process, metrology, OPC, and downstream integration all contribute. Each discipline can optimize its own part, but a collection of local optima does not automatically produce the best device—even if everyone arrives with an excellent slide explaining why their part is already optimized. EPE has become a system problem As pitch scaling becomes more difficult, tighter control of placement, variability, and pattern fidelity becomes one of the main paths to continued scaling. The challenge is that EPE is an unbounded budget. Mask three-dimensional effects, absorber profile, sidewall angle, critical-dimension uniformity, registration, scanner behavior, resist variability, etch, stochastic effects, process-induced stress, and even wafer or die bonding can all move an edge or change its electrical consequence. Yet the audience survey delivered a wonderfully familiar verdict: OPC was viewed both as a major source of EPE and as the leading place from which future EPE reduction would come. In other words, OPC was cast as both the villain and the superhero. Jed leaned into the joke, asking what Ezequiel and I would need from the rest of the industry to carry that superhero burden. By the final poll, confidence in OPC had risen to 58 percent—prompting the prediction that I might appear next time in tights. I am happy to accept the confidence; the cape may be negotiable. The EDA challenge: Stop treating residual error as one big bucket Today, many effects that are difficult to isolate are absorbed into empirical corrections, rule tables, or an “etch” term. This is pragmatic and often necessary in production, where repeatability, runtime, yield, and schedule outweigh a perfect explanation. Ezequiel captured the dilemma well: after seeing the poll, he was not sure whether the OPC community should feel encouraged or concerned. The audience clearly expected OPC to take care of every systematic and correctable effect—and, where possible, reduce sensitivity to the uncorrectable ones too. That is an impressive job description for any superhero. But even OPC needs good physics, good data, and a process window; it cannot leap an inaccurate model in a single bound. As tolerances shrink, the effects we sweep into the correction bucket become large relative to the remaining process window. EDA must therefore represent the real manufacturing system more completely: not an idealized mask with uniform properties, but pattern-dependent mask profiles, realistic metrology behavior, scanner effects, process variability, and the interactions among them. Not more data, better data More data alone is not the answer. We need data that is physically meaningful, sufficiently repeatable for manufacturing, and connected to the patterns that matter on the wafer. A single SEM image contains far more information than one extracted CD. Contours, profiles, roughness, placement, local geometry, and pattern context can all inform better models. At the same time, no fab can measure everything. OPC and process models should help identify the patterns with the highest wafer sensitivity, rank the hotspots, and translate that sensitivity into mask and wafer metrology requirements. This closes a critical loop: modeling guides measurement, measurement improves modeling, and both focus resources on yield-relevant problems. AI must be paired with physics and validation I believe artificial intelligence will deliver one of the largest future gains in EPE reduction. Machine learning can capture residual systematic behavior that is difficult to model directly, while agentic systems can coordinate optimization across traditionally separate domains. But semiconductor manufacturing cannot rely on an unexplained black box. A model that reports zero EPE without showing why it is trustworthy is not production-ready. The path forward is explainable AI anchored by rigorous simulation, validated against appropriate metrology, bounded by known physics, and monitored for the conditions in which it can safely be applied. Agentic systems should solve defined engineering problems Agentic AI should not be turned loose across the ecosystem with the assumption that it will discover a global optimum on its own. Adoption will begin with well-defined problems: reducing global CDU, selecting robust mask geometries, optimizing source and mask together, prioritizing metrology, or connecting pattern variation to electrical impact. For each problem, we must define the objective, the data required, the knobs the system may turn, the physical constraints, and the validation criteria. Confidence will grow locally, and successful agents can then be connected into broader workflows. EDA must connect EPE to power, performance, area, cost, and yield Our customers do not sell EPE; they sell products defined by power, performance, area, cost, and yield. Some EPE limits are hard geometric boundaries: exceed them and a structure shorts, opens, or fails. Other errors occupy a gray zone where their importance depends on device behavior. EDA has an opportunity to bridge that gap by bringing electrical simulation, stochastic analysis, lithography, mask optimization, process modeling, and design technology co-optimization into a common decision flow. The goal is not simply the smallest geometric error everywhere. It is the right allocation of process margin where it creates the greatest product value. Fig. 1: Process simulations using stochastic modeling techniques can predict process characteristics that lead to electrical problems with a design before reticles are built. Collaboration is the path from local to global optimization Foundries and IDMs sit at the center of this opportunity because they see the complete manufacturing flow and hold the data that connects mask, scanner, process, device, and yield. EDA providers need deeper partnerships with them, as well as with mask makers, metrology suppliers, and lithography equipment providers. Those partnerships must enable secure, purposeful sharing of data and context—not data collection for its own sake. events.title: PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload
events.summary: For decades, silicon characterization has been built around Process, Voltage, and Temperature, or PVT. We characterize devices across process variation, sweep voltage and frequency, control temperature, generate SHMOO plots, and establish the operating envelope of the silicon. That methodology remains fundamental. But today’s high-performance processors are increasingly systems in their own right. An AI accelerator may contain thousands of compute elements, distributed SRAM, high-speed SerDes, PCIe and Ethernet interfaces, multiple clock and power domains, advanced packaging, firmware, operating systems, compilers and application software. Two devices operating at exactly the same voltage, frequency, and temperature can behave differently depending on what they are being asked to do. This suggests adding another dimension: PVTW: Process × Voltage × Temperature × Workload Frequency can be swept within this characterization space to determine operating margin. The objective is not to replace traditional ATE characterization with System Level Test. It is to combine the electrical precision and control available from ATE with the realistic operating environment available from SLT, while retaining the ability to use either independently. One platform, two capabilities, three modes One way to implement PVTW is through a hybrid characterization architecture integrating ATE resources and SLT capability. There is no reason to recreate resources that already exist in ATE. Existing ATE infrastructure, including older generation platforms, can provide programmable device power supplies, individual rail control and measurement, variable frequency clocks, digital stimulus and capture, ATPG and structural content, parametric measurements, and conventional SHMOO characterization. SLT provides something fundamentally different: the application environment. The processor can boot firmware and an operating system, load drivers and runtime software, and execute deterministic workloads designed to exercise specific parts of the architecture. For an AI processor, those workloads might emphasize compute, SRAM, external memory, PCIe, Ethernet, or chip-to-chip communication. Other workloads could intentionally activate several simultaneously to create realistic system stress. The architecture therefore provides three modes. ATE mode performs conventional electrical, structural, and parametric characterization. SLT mode executes controlled system workloads. Combined mode uses ATE resources to control and measure electrical conditions while the device executes an SLT workload. Combined mode is where PVTW becomes particularly interesting. From conventional SHMOO to workload SHMOO Consider a conventional voltage and frequency SHMOO using ATPG or appropriate functional content. At a controlled temperature, establish the operating boundary. Now boot the processor, establish a deterministic workload, and repeat the sweep. Start with a compute-intensive workload. Repeat with SRAM, external memory, PCIe, and Ethernet-intensive workloads. Finally, create combinations that deliberately generate simultaneous compute, memory, and I/O activity. Suppose an ATPG SHMOO indicates that a device operates correctly down to 0.72 V at a particular frequency, while an SRAM-intensive application begins producing errors at 0.76 V. That 40 mV difference is not simply a disagreement between ATE and SLT. It is characterization information. Something about the workload is consuming margin. Is it SRAM timing? Clock distribution? IR drop? Simultaneous switching noise? A thermal gradient? Power delivery? Or an interaction among several subsystems? Characterization requires control There is an important distinction between testing and characterization. Booting Linux, running an AI workload, and observing whether the processor crashes is useful testing. Characterization requires controlled variables, repeatability, and the ability to deliberately move the operating boundary. Hold workload, temperature, and frequency constant while sweeping a selected voltage rail. Then hold workload, temperature, and voltage constant while sweeping frequency. Change temperature and repeat. The hybrid architecture can go deeper. Hold I/O and memory rails constant while margining the core rail during a compute workload. Then margin a memory-related rail while executing a memory-intensive workload. We can begin creating subsystem-specific workload SHMOOs that connect: Workload → Subsystem → Electrical Margin From workload failure to electrical debug Consider a device that passes Wafer Sort and Final Test but develops errors after a sustained application workload. Cooling reduces the failure rate, while increasing the core voltage does not eliminate the problem. Telemetry indicates that most errors are associated with the same memory interface or byte lane, although the failing addresses move. The device does not necessarily have to leave the characterization platform. SLT mode can expose the system behavior and help isolate the subsystem. The platform can operate in ATE mode to investigate electrical and structural characteristics using programmable power, clock control, ATPG, functional patterns, and parametric measurements. Or both capabilities can operate together. The workload can reproduce the marginal condition while ATE resources manipulate selected rails and clocks. The three modes therefore answer different questions. SLT exposes the behavior. ATE investigates the electrical and structural characteristics. Combined mode characterizes their interaction. This creates a tight engineering loop: Create workload → Observe marginality → Isolate subsystem → Characterize electrically → Modify conditions → Repeat workload → Establish correlation → Determine root cause For me, that is the interesting possibility behind PVTW. SLT no longer needs to be viewed only as a downstream production screen. Combined intelligently with ATE resources, it can become part of a controlled silicon characterization environment. But this leads to another question. If two devices both PASS, are they actually equivalent? That is the subject of Part 2: Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin with PVTW. The post PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Jeff Bezos reportedly added a $69.5 million beach house to his $237 million Miami compound. A broker says that’s how billionaires live now
events.summary: Jeff Bezos may have a beach house to go with his $237 million Miami compound . In September, a Delaware LLC paid $69.5 million for a 17,500-square-foot oceanfront estate at 255 Ocean Boulevard in Golden Beach, an exclusive oceanfront town in Miami-Dade County, a public records search by Fortune found. The buyer was a Delaware LLC, a structure that keeps the person behind the deal out of public view. But agents and other sources in town have pointed to Bezos, according to The Real Deal , and say he’d likely treat the property as a beach house. Public records list the buyer as Meridian Coast LLC. Bezos hasn’t publicly confirmed the deal, and representatives for Bezos didn’t immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Routing purchases through LLCs and trusts has become a more common practice among the ultrawealthy , who increasingly see public attention as a security risk. “The goal is to ensure that, even if someone digs into ownership records, they still cannot easily connect the property back to the principal owner,” Ken DeLeon, founder of Palo Alto, Calif.-based DeLeon Realty, told Fortune earlier this year. The beach house is only about a 30-minute drive from his compound in Indian Creek, also known as “ Billionaire Bunker ,” a 300-acre, man-made strip of land that has attracted the ultrawealthy. But for buyers at Bezos’ level, owning another home near the one they already have isn’t redundant, Mendel Fellig , founder of the Miami Beach-based Mendel Fellig Group at Compass , told Fortune .  “A buyer may already have an incredible waterfront home but also want direct access to a private stretch of beach,” Fellig said. “Golden Beach is one of the few places in Miami that can offer that. The second property becomes an extension of their lifestyle—almost an amenity in itself.” The deal set a record for a single-family home in Golden Beach, according to The Real Deal . The house has seven bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, plus a guest house, a pool and spa, and 100 feet of water frontage. It hit the market in February for $88.5 million, public records reviewed by Fortune show, and was later cut to $79.5 million. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dina Goldentayer (@goldendina) “Acquiring a whole portfolio gives these buyers access to different residential experiences for their lifestyle while securing properties that are increasingly difficult to replicate or replace,” Felling added. To be sure, Devin Kay of Douglas Elliman told Fox Business recognizable names tend to get attached to blockbuster deals when a buyer’s identity is hidden. “The reality is that South Florida’s billionaire buyer pool has expanded considerably,” Kay told Fox Business . “There are international business owners, hedge fund executives, technology founders and multi-generational families quietly acquiring some of the most valuable real estate in the region.” But if Bezos is the buyer, the Golden Beach home would join a portfolio he started building after leaving Seattle for Miami in 2023. He said at the time he wanted to be closer to his parents and to Blue Origin’s operations at Cape Canaveral, but the move has also paid off at tax time. Florida has no state income or capital gains tax, and Bezos saved an estimated $1 billion in 2024 alone, Fortune previously reported , citing a Forbes calculation he would have owed about $954 million in Washington state capital gains tax on his Amazon stock sales that year. Can Miami’s luxury market keep climbing? Part of what drives these purchases is that there’s so little to buy.  Fellig says one of his clients recently bought a home for $30 million and got a $35 million offer to sell it a month later.  “He declined because he couldn’t replace what he had,” Fellig said. “That’s the dynamic in these exclusive neighborhoods—even when someone is willing to pay more, there may be nowhere comparable for the owner to go.” Still, Fellig cautions neighbors against reading too much into a headline sale.  “These transactions tend to raise sellers’ expectations, but expectations and actual market value are two different things,” he said. “A nearby owner may see a headline sale and decide their home is suddenly worth 20 percent more. That doesn’t mean buyers will agree.” Jay Roberts , CEO of Prosper Group and developer of Bugatti Residences Miami, sees demand holding up. He points to buyers leaving higher-tax states and international buyers seeking stability. He told Fortune Miami-Dade’s residential sales above $30 million have already broken the previous annual record. He also credits corporate and institutional investment, including Carnegie Mellon’s planned Miami campus, which Ken Griffin is funding with $2 billion of his record $3 billion gift . “We believe Miami is still in the early stages of a growth cycle that will compound for decades,” Roberts told Fortune . “People will continue to move here—especially those with a high net worth.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Chip Scaling Moves Beyond The Transistor
events.summary: Key Takeaways: The semiconductor industry reached $1 trillion years early, but keeping pace with demand now depends on systems integration as much as transistor scaling. Packaging, photonics, power, and test are converging into one optimization problem, which means improving any one of them can move the bottleneck somewhere else. AI is shifting from the workload the industry serves to a tool it uses, and the open question is how much engineering and manufacturing authority it will be given. When SEMICON West gathered in San Francisco in 2023, the semiconductor industry was forecasting a path to $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2030. Three years later, the industry has already blown past that number. SEMICON West 2026 returned to San Francisco with a sold-out exhibit floor, more than 30,000 attendees, and an industry confronting a different question: How does it keep up with the growth it once aimed for? SEMI’s own projections show how steep that curve has become. In his opening keynote, SEMI President and CEO Ajit Manocha forecast a market of more than $2 trillion by 2030, and potentially $3 trillion by 2035. At the SEMI Market Symposium, the association projected 300mm fab equipment spending of $149 billion this year, rising to $227 billion by 2029, with construction beginning on 20 new 300mm fabs or production lines in 2026 alone. AI infrastructure is driving much of that growth, but electrification, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and industrial automation are adding semiconductor content, as well. What makes the current expansion unusual is the growing complexity of the systems those chips will enable, not the almost insatiable demand for chips. “We’ve started talking about how to re-engineer engineering because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys . “That’s at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?” Across presentations, panels, and discussions on the show floor, several issues kept converging around that problem. Advanced packaging is becoming part of system architecture. Photonics is moving closer to compute, while bringing new manufacturing and test challenges with it. Test, inspection and metrology have to follow more complicated assemblies and manufacturing histories. And AI is moving from something the industry builds to something it uses to design and manufacture. None of these technologies is new, but each is becoming harder to optimize independently, and that may be the clearest indication of what the industry will be working on in the coming years. Scaling becomes a system-level challenge The shift was apparent in conversations ranging from transistor scaling and HBM to advanced packaging, optical interconnects, and cooling, where improving any one of those can move a bottleneck elsewhere. More compute increases pressure on memory bandwidth and power delivery. Moving memory closer reduces data movement but concentrates heat. Disaggregating a large die can improve yield and allow functions to use different process nodes, but it creates more interfaces that have to be connected, powered, cooled, and tested. “Packaging is no longer simply the place where semiconductor innovation ends,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D at Intel Foundry . “Increasingly, it’s the place where system innovation begins.” That makes memory, data movement, power delivery, and thermal management part of the architecture rather than downstream considerations. “The challenge is not to co-optimize one component,” Immaneni said. “It is to co-optimize across the system from end to end between silicon, packaging, and platform.” Nitin Deshpande, Marvell’s vice president of advanced packaging, made a similar point during imec’s pre-show ITF USA program. “The package is really becoming a system where the compute, the memory, the interconnects, the power, the cooling, all of these things come together.” Making those pieces work together is only part of the challenge. Larger, more heterogeneous packages still have to become high-volume products with acceptable yield, reliability, and cost. “We can have very cool concepts, but if we cannot scale these into high volumes, if we cannot have a high-yielding, reliable process with a supply chain that can provide the parts in time, everything that we do cannot be converted into a business,” Deshpande said. Patrick Vandenameele, CEO of imec, noted that AI infrastructure can keep growing by adding accelerators and racks, but adding hardware isn’t scaling in the traditional semiconductor sense. “These data centers are true engineering marvels,” he said. “But at the same time, this is not what we semiconductor people call scaling. It looks a little bit more like multiplication.” That distinction helps explain why so many separate topics at SEMICON West kept leading back to the same place. The industry isn’t abandoning transistor scaling. It’s adding another level above it, where performance depends on how effectively different technologies can be combined into a functional system. Fig. 2: Redefining a system. Source: SEMI AI moves from assistant to operator AI was nearly impossible to avoid at SEMICON West, but the conversation is shifting. Machine learning has been part of design, process control, and defect classification for years, and generative AI added natural-language access to complicated tools and data. Agentic AI goes further, allowing engineers to hand an agent an objective and let it invoke other tools, models, or agents to reach it. “We started from an assistant copilot to generative capability to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome,” said Synopsys’ Ghazi. The appeal of agentic AI becomes clearer when looking at the size of the spaces engineers are being asked to optimize. “The space that we’re optimizing in has exploded,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research . “We’ve now gotten to a place where the parameter set is intractable.” A current Lam etcher, for example, can have a potential recipe space on the order of 10 23 possibilities, which is well beyond what any engineer can explore manually. “That’s really where AI is coming to the rescue,” Fried said. “It’s the ability to get through massive multi-parameter dimensional spaces, massive sets of intertwined sensitivities between a much larger parameter space, and a much larger spec space.” Acting on what AI finds is where the discussion gets more complicated. Flagging an unusual process signature is different from letting an AI system alter a recipe, and predicting equipment degradation is different from stopping production. events.title: How Self-Aligned CFET Technology Could Extend CMOS Scaling Beyond 10 Å
events.summary: As their dimensions continue to shrink, conventional gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors may face growing challenges, such as leakage, mobility, resistance, and manufacturing variability. A proposed self-aligned complementary field-effect transistor (SA-CFET) architecture addresses these constraints by vertically stacking N-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (NMOS) and P-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (PMOS) devices and using self-aligned modules to improve density and manufacturability. What is a CFET? A complementary field-effect transistor (CFET) is a transistor architecture that vertically stacks NMOS and PMOS devices. This configuration can reduce cell area, increase effective channel width, and improve electrostatic control compared with side-by-side device layouts. With SEMulator3D , the Semiverse Solutions team used digital twin process modeling to show that the self-aligned architecture can support static random-access memory (SRAM) and logic cells while delivering a 0.0094 μm² SRAM bit cell, a 52.7% area reduction compared with N3 technology, and at least a 10 nm overlay window across critical contact layers. Why transistor scaling beyond 10 Å is difficult Many experts believe that the currently most-advanced transistor architecture, silicon GAA nanosheets, may begin to have physics and manufacturing issues past the 10 angstrom (Å) node. These challenges include: Source-drain tunneling and increased leakage current as the gate length shrinks Mobility issues, surface scattering, and manufacturing issues as the channel thickness is reduced Contact and parasitic resistance issues as the transistor size decreases Manufacturing variability that may seriously impact yield beyond the 10 Å node With these challenges, it is becoming increasingly difficult to scale down the nanosheet device area or enhance device density by simply shrinking the active area, gate, or metal patterning pitch. Why CFET matters for sub-10Å scaling CFET architecture stacks PMOS and NMOS vertically to achieve significant area reduction, enhanced performance through larger effective channel width, and improved electrostatics. 1,2,3,4 However, CFET architecture faces its own critical integration challenges: metal gate isolation complexity and contact crowding that can cause electrical shorts or open circuits. These issues intensify at smaller dimensions, requiring innovative solutions for scalability. How the self-aligned architecture works To address these challenges, we propose a SA-CFET architecture with three key self-aligned modules: SA-BPR (buried power rail), SA-CT (contacts), and SA-TSV (through-silicon via). These process modules enlarge the edge placement error window and mitigate contact crowding, improving process margin. The architecture uses non-metal gate cut design and middle dielectric isolation (MDI) for work function split. 5 SA-CFET maintains compatibility with N3 specifications (42-nm CPP, 21-nm metal pitch), transforming overlay-sensitive steps into self-aligned processes for better manufacturability. Fig. 1: Key integration loops of the SA-CFET. Design implementation: SRAM and logic cells The SA-CFET design can be used to successfully build 6T SRAM cells and logic standard cells (NOT, NAND, NOR) with no metal gate split required within any single fin, simplifying the process flow. The complete interconnection network, validated through digital twin (process) simulation, demonstrates complex routing capability while maintaining self-aligned benefits. Fig. 2: 3D interconnection network architecture showing SRAM and logic cells (NAND, NOR, NOT) with complex routing validated through digital twin simulation. Performance results SA-CFET achieves a 6T SRAM bit cell area of 0.0094 μm²—a 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology 6 and 19% reduction versus state-of-the-art A7 CFET designs. Process robustness validation shows at least a 10-nm overlay window for all critical contact layers with no open/short failures, confirming robust process margin. Fig. 3: SRAM bit cell area comparison showing 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology. Fig. 4: Overlay window validation confirming robust process margin across critical contact layers. Conclusion This article describes an innovative self-aligned CFET architecture that employs multiple self-aligned processes. Using this architecture, we designed a process sequence for both a 6T SRAM device and for logic standard cells using digital twin (process) modeling. We found the proposed architecture shares similar or even more relaxed design rules compared to current or conventional semiconductor manufacturing. It also provides an area reduction from both existing N3 devices and state-of-the-art CFET architectures. More importantly, it avoids many of the scaling issues found in existing nanosheet architectures, achieving enhanced performance through larger effective channel width and improved electrostatics at smaller nodes. We believe that this work demonstrates a potential architectural solution to support CMOS scaling for transistors at 10 Å and beyond. events.title: In Israel election, Palestinian citizens weigh fear against disillusionment
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? With polls at a knife’s edge, Palestinian citizens of Israel weigh principle against strategic voting in a system stacked against them. How the Palestinian Israeli vote could reshape Israel's election Occupied East Jerusalem – Laila Atamneh, 19, remembers her parents arguing at the dinner table every time Israel would hold an election. Among the rare Palestinian Jerusalemites who are Israeli citizens and eligible to vote, her father would make the case for casting a ballot for an Arab-led electoral list. Her mother, by contrast, always abstained. “She thinks it feeds into the idea that Israel is a democracy and Palestinians have the same rights here – only to get extremely humiliated, and then get one of the worst governments ever, and be surrounded by fascists,” said Atamneh, who hails from the neighbourhood of Beit Hanina. On October 27, the 19-year-old will vote for the first time in Israel’s general election . She sees it as a responsibility to the millions of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip, who will have no say in the next Israeli government but, she believes, bear the brunt of its occupation, ethnic cleansing and genocide. “I feel like I have to be these people’s voice,” said Atamneh. “Not that one person is really capable of that much – but if this gives them one percent hope, then I will do it.” But Atamneh, who speaks Arabic, said she struggles to follow election coverage in Hebrew. “I personally feel excluded from everything, that we’re not even a part of the discussion,” she added. “It feels like none of the parties really address our generation of first-time Palestinian voters.” Her mixed feelings capture the mood among Palestinian citizens of Israel – about a fifth of its population – ahead of the election. Few believe the system will serve them, but many fear another government led by Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, who has overseen Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip since 2023. Whether fear outweighs disillusion may decide a contest in which opinion polls suggest neither Netanyahu’s far-right-led bloc nor the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance will be able to govern without Ra’am and the Joint List, the two Arab-led parties. And if no one can form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, new elections will be called – keeping the current Netanyahu government, the most hard right in Israel’s history, in place until then. For Palestinian citizens of Israel, the animating force of the election is the acceleration of the hard-right assault on Palestinian rights, livelihoods and land in recent years. “This election comes in the context of the genocide and the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and the harsh state policies towards Palestinians in Israel,” said As’ad Ghanem, a political scientist at the University of Haifa. “Palestinian citizens are really afraid. Their leadership is afraid, and this is real.” For Hanan, a 36-year-old Palestinian Christian in a Druze village in the Galilee, it feels like the danger keeps coming closer to her doorstep. Israeli settlers residing in illegal settlements in the West Bank last month tried to build an illegal outpost near Majd al-Krum, a Palestinian community in the Galilee. Then, Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich released an AI-generated campaign video, in which a Palestinian from the West Bank frantically calls his relative in the Galilee to tell him that “the Jews are coming” to “do to you what they did to us”. “Acts like these make me more afraid that the settlers will get worse and try to take more Palestinian land,” said Hanan. “This makes me want to vote more, and want to encourage other people to vote.” On September 23, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Ra’am and the Joint List – an alliance of the Hadash, Balad and Ta’al parties – before the Supreme Court overturned the decisions. However, Balad’s Sami Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy after the court indicated that a majority of justices supported upholding his disqualification. Many Palestinians saw this as confirmation that the system is illegitimate; some said the attempt to disqualify the parties was further reason to mobilise either way. “We feel that we are under attack,” said Thabet Abu Rass, an expert on Arab-Jewish relations. “This is why we will cast our vote in a higher percentage.” Voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel ranged from roughly 45 to 65 percent over the past five elections, reaching about 53 percent in the last polls in 2022. A Palestinian campaign operative cited surveys estimating about 62 percent of Palestinian citizens plan to vote next week; he said the aim is 70 to 75 percent, last reached in 1999, when a 75 percent Palestinian turnout helped PM Ehud Barak beat Netanyahu.

events.title: Stacked-Die Multi-Chip Architectures: The Tradeoff Between Scaling And Power Delivery
events.summary: By Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Nicolas Butzen, and Vishal Javvaji The semiconductor industry has embraced multi-chip and stacked-die architectures as the primary path for continued performance scaling. As monolithic designs become more difficult and costly to advance, chiplets, advanced packaging, and 3D integration enable higher levels of performance, bandwidth, and functional integration for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Yet the success of stacked-die, multi-chip architectures has exposed a growing power delivery challenge. As more compute resources are integrated into a package, there is a sharp uptick in current density and the number of independent voltage domains, placing unprecedented demands on shared power delivery resources. To address these challenges, we discussed in our recent power delivery white paper how Intel Foundry is moving voltage regulation closer to the load. By enabling higher-voltage power distribution, integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) reduce current density in the package, provide higher regulation bandwidth, and reduce reliance on large decoupling capacitor networks. Intel Foundry’s portfolio spans package-integrated magnetic inductors, fully capacitive IVR chiplets, and advanced package integration technologies, providing multiple paths to improve power integrity, efficiency, and scalability. System-level consequences of stacked-die architectures Advanced packaging delivers significant gains in performance, bandwidth, and integration density. However, consistently distributing power through increasingly complex packaging and interconnect structures introduces new challenges in maintaining power integrity across the package. One consequence is voltage droop. As AI workloads generate rapid swings in current demand, the power delivery network must respond instantly. When it cannot, voltage can briefly fall below target levels, potentially impacting performance. To maintain reliability, designers often add voltage guard bands and operating margins. While effective, these safeguards can limit silicon from reaching its optimal efficiency and performance. Multi-chip and stacked-die architectures also intensify the tradeoff between signal density and power delivery. As more compute tiles, memory interfaces, and die-to-die links are added, routing congestion increases, creating additional resistance, tighter voltage margins, and growing power delivery constraints. Moving power delivery closer to the load As current density continues to increase, the industry is moving toward architectures that bring voltage conversion closer to the point of consumption, reducing power delivery losses while improving responsiveness to rapidly changing workloads. Intel Foundry is advancing several complementary technologies designed around this principle. FIVR with CoaxMIL: Intel was an early pioneer of fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVRs), which moves the last voltage conversion stage onto the processor. By shortening the distance between the regulator and the load, FIVR helps reduce distribution losses and improve transient response. To support rising current densities, Intel developed CoaxMIL, a magnetic inductor technology that delivers significantly higher current density than earlier approaches while requiring less area (see Figure 1). For customers building next-generation AI and HPC devices, this translates into improved power conversion efficiency, faster response to workload changes, and more efficient use of valuable package real estate. The result is greater performance potential without proportional increases in power delivery complexity. Fig. 1: CoaxMIL magnetic inductor technology. C2VR: Intel Foundry’s continuous capacitive voltage regulator (C2VR) takes voltage conversion in a different direction. Rather than relying on traditional inductors, C2VR uses high-density capacitor technology to achieve efficient voltage conversion in an extremely compact form factor. Because capacitors are integrated directly onto the voltage regulator chiplet, C2VR can deliver both high efficiency and exceptionally high current density. It can also respond rapidly to sudden current demands, helping minimize voltage droop during the bursty workload transitions common in AI accelerators. For customers, the benefit is improved power integrity, tighter voltage control, and a scalable solution capable of supporting future multi-kiloamp workloads. IVR chiplet architectures: These dedicated power management chiplets allow voltage conversion to be positioned closer to the compute die than traditional motherboard-based regulators. The primary advantage of IVR chiplet architectures is flexibility. Architects can position voltage regulation where it delivers the greatest benefit, whether on the landside, embedded within package layers, or beneath compute dies. This flexibility allows architects to optimize power delivery for specific applications while reducing distribution losses and improving overall efficiency. In advanced stacked-die systems, these architectures also open the door to vertical power delivery schemes that reduce distribution distance and improve power integrity. The future of power delivery As AI systems continue their rapid evolution, power delivery is becoming as critical to performance scaling as transistor and packaging innovation. The next generation of data center architectures will require a portfolio of solutions that move power conversion closer to the load, improve efficiency at extreme current densities, and maintain stable operation under increasingly dynamic workloads. Intel Foundry technologies are important building blocks, helping ensure that future compute platforms can continue scaling performance without being constrained by the power delivery network. This blog is the second in a two-part series on power delivery innovation. Part 1 explores how data center energy trends are affecting chip power delivery. Nicolas Butzen is a principal engineer at Intel. Vishal Javvaji is a process integration manager at Intel Foundry. events.title: Kathy Hochul defies her own party on Trump’s $26 billion school choice bet: ‘I’m not going to leave money on the table’
events.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has opted the state into the Trump administration’s Education Freedom Tax Credit, breaking with the Democratic leaders of both legislative chambers and making New York the 31st state to sign on to the first nationwide federal school choice program. Hochul is only the second Democratic governor to join, after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis. “I’m not going to leave money on the table when it could help our kids,” Hochul said in her Oct. 9 announcement, adding that she had been clear New York would participate “if, and only if, all schools and students, including those in our public schools, could benefit.” The decision came days after Albany’s top Democrats urged her to stay out. “New York should opt out of the federal voucher program and continue investing in the public schools that educate the overwhelming majority of our children,” Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie (D-Bronx) said in a statement . Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins (D-Yonkers) warned that the federal rules “would undercut New York’s ability to establish meaningful guardrails, leaving the state with little control over which schools and expenses qualify or how this funding is used.” The move also lands weeks before Election Day, as Hochul faces Republican nominee Bruce Blakeman, who has criticized her for not opting in sooner. How the tax credit works The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping tax-and-spending law President Trump signed in July 2025, created the credit. ( Fortune has covered what the law changed and its projected $3.4 trillion hit to the national debt .) Starting Jan. 1, 2027, taxpayers can claim a dollar-for-dollar federal credit of up to $1,700 for cash donations to approved scholarship-granting organizations, or SGOs. Under proposed regulations released Oct. 1, married couples filing jointly are treated as separate taxpayers, so they can claim up to $3,400 combined. Because the credit reduces federal tax revenue, it doesn’t draw on state budgets. Governors must opt in each year for students in their state to receive scholarships, though taxpayers anywhere can donate to SGOs in participating states. Who qualifies in New York? Students are eligible if their household income is no more than 300% of their area’s median gross income. That works out to roughly $309,000 in the Bronx and $510,000 in Westchester County , according to the Manhattan Institute’s City Journal, which estimates more than 2.7 million New York students could qualify. Scholarships can cover private and religious school tuition. Public school students can use them for expenses such as tutoring, special education services, books, and technology. The Scholarships for All New Yorkers coalition cites a projection from Education Reform Now that the program could generate $1.5 billion a year for New York students if a third of eligible taxpayers participate. Critics and supporters line up New York State United Teachers, the state’s largest teachers’ union, called it “President Trump’s private-school voucher program” and had pressed Hochul for weeks to reject it. The union argues that income limits topping $500,000 in parts of the state make it more a tax break for the wealthy than an education program. “The governor says this won’t take a dollar from public schools, but it takes federal tax money, which belongs to all of us, and hands it to private schools with no rules about who they must admit or how they account for it,” Beatriz Beckford of MomsRising said . Supporters, including Catholic and Orthodox Jewish school advocates and Democrats for Education Reform, praised the move. The American Legislative Exchange Council, a conservative group of state legislators and private-sector members, cast it as part of a growing bipartisan movement and urged the remaining states to follow. Nationally, Treasury projects that by 2030 more than 11 million taxpayers could donate nearly $26 billion a year through the program. Other forecasts are far lower: the Joint Committee on Taxation estimates a $25.9 billion revenue cost over a full decade. Treasury and the IRS are accepting public comments on the proposed rules through Dec. 1, with a public hearing scheduled for Dec. 15. The remaining states have until Jan. 1, 2027, to decide whether to join. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: What Breaks When Packaging Moves From Wafer To Panel?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Moving advanced packaging from wafer to panel changes more than available area. Processes developed around wafer geometry, handling, and equipment have to be reconsidered at panel scale. Larger panels amplify dimensional change, warpage, and process history, making what happens at one manufacturing step increasingly important to the next. The most economical manufacturing flow may use different substrate formats at different stages rather than carrying one large panel through the entire process. Moving advanced packaging from wafer to panel sounds, at first, like a geometry problem. Large AI and HPC packages are increasingly rectangular, while the 300mm wafer underneath them is still round. As the package size grows, more of that expensive processing ends up around the circle’s edges where nothing useful can be built. A panel gives that area back. It can fit more large packages into the same process cycle, and unlike a wafer, its dimensions don’t impose the same hard limit on the size of a square or rectangular package. For advanced packages that keep getting larger, the economics are difficult to ignore. But the semiconductor packaging sector has spent decades learning how to process wafers, not panels. Equipment, materials, recipes, handling systems, and process controls were all developed around the geometry and mechanical behavior of a round workpiece. “The risk of doing the assembly on the 600mm panel is high, and I don’t think we have all the equipment today to run the process,” said Teck Chong Lee, technical director of advanced fan-out development for HPC applications at ASE , in a recent presentation. “One of the options is, once you complete the interposer in large format in 600, then you divide it into four pieces to run the assembly and the C4 process. This is a much lower-risk approach.” The economics behind that compromise are substantial. In the same study, a 5.5×-reticle-size interposer produced 9 units on a 300mm wafer, compared with 16 on a 300mm panel. A 600mm panel divided into four 300mm pieces produces 64, while processing the full 600mm area intact raises that to 72. In pure utilization, the intact panel produces 8 times as many units as the wafer, a gain well beyond the roughly fivefold difference in raw area, because the rectangular panel wastes almost nothing at its edges. The flow therefore takes the area advantage where it can use it, then gives some of it back before assembly because the manufacturing infrastructure isn’t ready to follow the larger format all the way through. That compromise exposes the larger transition underway. Moving packaging from wafer to panel isn’t simply making the process bigger. It is discovering which parts of the process were dependent on the wafer dimensions all along. The process was built around the wafer The utilization advantage grows as the package does. In one comparison, Intel Foundry used a 510 × 515mm panel and showed that a roughly 4× reticle package would produce about 10 units on a 300mm wafer and approximately 48 on the panel. Eventually the wafer imposes a harder geometric limit, since the largest square that fits on a 300mm wafer is only about 210 × 210mm. “For certain form factors, we believe a wafer is more economical,” said Tarik Ibrahim, senior principal engineer at Intel , in a conference presentation. “However, when you go beyond a certain form factor, you can see quickly that the panel becomes more effective, mainly because you can get more units out of a panel. Because of the way AI is heading and the need for a very large system, panels became an obvious choice for scale.” Fig. 1: Intel’s Tarik Ibrahim discusses substrate scaling for heterogeneous integration. Source: Semiconductor Engineering The economic crossover doesn’t mean the manufacturing process crosses over with it. Much of the equipment and process knowledge used in advanced packaging was developed for a round wafer, and changing the shape and scale of the substrate changes what those processes have to do. Over time, many of those wafer-specific assumptions became invisible because the workpiece underneath them rarely changed. What looked like a requirement of the process was often just a requirement of the wafer. “At wafer level, it’s a single-sided process,” Ibrahim said. “On panel, it’s actually a dual-sided process. Managing the process at that panel scale with the right uniformity and the right Cpk [process capability index] is definitely a challenge.” Part of the challenge is that familiar wafer processes don’t always transfer cleanly to a larger rectangular surface. Spin coating, for example, relies on radial symmetry, so a rectangular substrate produces uneven film thickness toward the corners while most of the dispensed resist is thrown away. In a 600mm panel flow, photoresist is instead deposited by slit or slot-die coating across an active area of roughly 586 × 586mm. Lithography also changes, with maskless direct imaging displacing the conventional wafer stepper in many panel flows. Those differences propagate into the materials and equipment surrounding the process. Fine-line RDL on glass panels is pushing toward new photoresists and application methods, tighter overlay control, and equipment that can maintain temperature and process uniformity across a much larger area. Large hot plates become a development problem of their own. As line and space moves from roughly 5µm toward 2µm and below, processes that historically belonged farther back in the packaging flow begin demanding something closer to front-end precision. The awkward part is that the panel can’t simply inherit the front-end equipment built to provide that precision. Much of that infrastructure assumes a round 300mm wafer, while traditional substrate equipment was designed around different feature sizes and process tolerances. Panel-level packaging is landing somewhere between the two. The result is less a scaled-up wafer flow than a new manufacturing process being assembled from pieces of several older ones. The panel solves an increasingly expensive geometry problem, but it also exposes how many coating, exposure, handling, and uniformity assumptions were tied to the wafer that came before it. Yield decides how big is useful The simplest argument for a larger panel is that more packages fit on it. The real economic question is how many good packages come off. That matters more as the value assembled onto the workpiece rises. A panel carrying logic and HBM can contain tens of thousands of dollars of known-good silicon before some package-level failures become visible. At that point, even a small yield loss can erase the savings created by processing more area at once. “There’s so much money in chips going onto a wafer or panel that a tiny yield hit, and the loss of some of that super-expensive silicon, will just blow all the benefits from a larger scale that you had right out the window,” said Mike Kelly, vice president of chipl

events.title: Foundries And OSATs Increasingly Overlap
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Foundries have been doing backend work for advanced packages. OSATs are now taking that on. This particularly affects 2.5D and panel assembly with new equipment and materials. Hybrid bonding is mostly a foundry activity now but will likely move to OSATs as well. Foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) houses have traditionally had distinct lanes, but the lines are blurring as OSATs acquire select foundry capabilities and foundries return some of the jobs they have taken from OSATs. “We’re at this bridging point where the IDMs and the foundries are doing more of what OSATs can do, and the OSATs are also trying to get much closer to what the foundry does at the back end,” said Raghu Nayak, head of sales at Zeiss. OSATs will never compete with foundries on advanced nodes and front-end wafer fabrication. But for backend activities, where dimensions aren’t as demanding, OSATs are acquiring capabilities that replicate what foundries can do. The biggest areas of overlap are 2.5D integration and panel assembly, with hybrid bonding likely to move there as well. The change affects equipment and materials. “We are seeing the migration of lithography-related materials and processes from traditional wafer fabs into advanced packaging environments,” said Poupak Khodabandeh, chief business officer at Brewer Science . “As advanced packaging increasingly relies on fine-pitch redistribution layers (RDLs), OSATs and packaging organizations are using materials and process flows that historically would have been associated with wafer fabrication.” “The industry has traditionally operated in silos across equipment, front-end fabrication, design, packaging, and test,” said Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco . “We need to connect those disciplines so teams can use shared, physics-grounded insight to make faster, better-informed design decisions, while also providing greater manufacturing flexibility — especially at the backend.” It used to be “to each his own” Foundries and OSATs have taken on complementary duties for many years. Foundries fabricate the silicon chip, while OSATs put the chip into a housing and test the final product. A vast array of EDA tools and fab equipment makes what the foundry does possible, while OSATs have worked more with tools that originated in the printed circuit board (PCB) world. Two industry trends are challenging this status quo. The first is the development of advanced packaging. It’s no longer enough to put a chip on a substrate, wire it up, and pour molding compound over it. This doesn’t minimize the effort required to do those basics well, but they’re very different from what advanced packaging requires. “Advanced packaging is becoming more lithography-intensive,” said Khodabandeh. “The industry’s push toward higher interconnect density for AI, HBM, chiplet architectures, and heterogeneous integration is driving the adoption of wafer-fab-style patterning processes within packaging facilities. RDL fabrication is a good example, where increasingly sophisticated lithography is required to create finer features.” Intel Foundry works both sides of the aisle, with foundry and packaging capabilities. “When you do fine pitch bumps, the bump count goes up quite a bit compared to coarse pitch,” said Ravi Mahajan, fellow at Intel Foundry. “So you have to figure out things like embedding [bridge dies such as EMIB]. You have to figure out alignment and equipment precision.” For them, they can attempt these things on either side of the divide. Foundries have been heavily involved in 2.5D packaging, but a second industry trend is making that more difficult — a lack of capacity. Foundries can’t make all the chips their clients want, so they’re prioritizing and allocating. That may mean turning away some business they would otherwise entertain, likely in backend and legacy processes, since foundries will focus on newer-node silicon processes they are uniquely capable of. The OSATs are ready to pick up those processes. These are lower-resolution processes that foundries have historically employed but for which OSATs share capabilities. Legacy-node builds can spill over to assembly houses, especially since advanced packaging requires tooling consistent with those older technologies. Although this overlap largely affects older processes, as constraints continue, even more aggressive technology, which foundries have often packaged (or done the first packaging steps) themselves, may be offloaded. “With further volume restrictions, both legacy-node and leading-edge products are shifting toward OSAT packaging,” said Thomas Uhrmann, director of business development at EV Group. Three primary tasks These market dynamics have driven three primary assembly-related processes from foundry to OSAT: 2.5D packaging, panel packaging, and eventually, hybrid bonding. 2.5D packaging in a manner resembling TSMC’s CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate) involves mounting one die atop another. When the base is an interposer, this is 2.5D. When it’s another active die, it becomes 3D. Typical processes place the top die, already singulated, on a bottom die on a wafer that hasn’t been diced up yet. Once the top die is in place, the bottom wafer can be diced, with the stack-up headed for a package. One fast-growing area that needs this technology is photonics. “Customers are coming to us asking if we can do electrical die to photonics die or wafer attach,” said Gerard John, senior director in Amkor’s Chiplets/FCBGA Business Unit. “We take this module, dice it out, and then attach it to a substrate. That’s a new trend we are seeing, and we can do that.” It may, however, bring some tough new requirements. “This is a big challenge because now you have the optic side of the wafer or die,” added John, and this needs active alignment to attach fibers and test them. Panels, meanwhile, have grown to the 500 mm range per side, but moving to a smaller size actually helped. “Several OSATs had early development lines for panel-level packaging, mainly targeting large panels with 500 mm dimensions,” explained Uhrmann. “TSMC’s decision to move to panel-level packaging with 310 × 310 mm 2 , which is a format closer to classical 300 mm round process tools, has enabled traditional wafer-based equipment manufacturers to scale up for high-performance materials and resolution, rather than PCB equipment manufacturers to scale down.” Meanwhile, some assembly houses are doing hybrid bonding. But for high volume, it largely remains a foundry task, owing to the challenges the process presents. As hybrid bonding loses its novelty and becomes standard, it represents another task that foundries could hand off to OSATs. How are you paying for that? Whereas foundries typically have the equipment for these processes, OSATs have to invest to match those capabilities. events.title: Gen Z and millennials expect to inherit $124 trillion—but retired boomers are ‘spending their kids’ inheritance’ to go on vacation instead
events.summary: Millennial and Gen Z heirs are eagerly anticipating a $124 trillion “ Great Wealth Transfer ” as they inherit their parents’ wealth—however, many are set to be disappointed. That’s because new data says boomers are splashing their cash on vacations instead of setting it aside for future generations. It’s become so common that the trend’s even been given a name: Ski-ing. Meaning, “spending the kids’ inheritance.” New data from Abta, Britain’s largest travel trade association, shows that 82% of over-65s took a holiday in the past 12 months, up five percentage points from two years ago—and the company’s CEO says the spike in older people traveling is specifically down to them spending money that would have been part of their kids’ inheritance. A separate report from retirement provider Standard Life found that one in seven British parents plan to prioritize enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance. Why boomers are ‘ski-ing’: cash rich, mortgage-free and spending it Boomers are living longer than previous generations, and they’re also richer than their parents and grandparents ever were. So instead of pottering around or watching daytime TV, they’re enjoying booked beach vacations and city breaks. As Abta’s CEO Mark Tanzer told The Times , “ that generation is probably fitter than it used to be; your mortgage is paid off, you are starting your pension, you are actually quite cash rich.” And with that abundance of time and money, they’re not even letting the cost of living get in the way of enjoying it.  When asked whether cost-of-living concerns would affect their holiday plans in the next 12 months, almost half of over-65s said it had “no impact.” Unlike younger people, many boomers don’t have to worry about rising rents or food bills. In fact, according to The Institute for Fiscal Studies , their disposable income keeps going up. Having spent a lifetime working for it, many have decided it’s their turn to enjoy every penny—after all, you can’t take it with you.  “I think they have got more disposable income and they want to have experiences,” Tanzer added.  “There may be a bit of them thinking, ‘I just don’t want to leave this to my kids’, but they certainly don’t want to leave it to the taxman. There’s that sense of ‘well, if I don’t spend it, it will just go to inheritance tax’.” American boomers are skipping inheritances too—it’s going to be a shock for their Gen Z and millennial kids  The trend isn’t exclusive to Britain. In 2024, a Northwestern Mutual survey of 4,500 U.S. adults found that just 22% of baby boomers expect to leave an inheritance, and over half are explicitly planning not to. Only 11% said leaving something for the kids is their top financial goal. Some boomers are treating it as a philosophy: dying with zero . They’re going out of their way to enjoy all their wealth while they are still alive and die with $0 in their bank account. “It’s such a shame to see people dying with so much money in a job they’ve worked in that they don’t enjoy, or with people they don’t like,” personal finance coach James Beckett previously told Fortune . “They go on autopilot, accumulating wealth and not thinking about what it’s for.” But it’s going to be a huge shock for the heirs when they open their parents’ wills to find nothing left. More than half of Gen Zers and nearly 60% of millennials said they’re depending on an inheritance to retire comfortably. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
