events.title: The next K-pop? POPS founder Esther Nguyen hopes TikTok can make Southeast Asian music a global phenomenon
events.summary: Esther Nguyen has what may be a stereotypical story for a Vietnamese-American entrepreneur working in Vietnam. Her parents fled the country when Saigon fell in 1975; Nguyen, born in Michigan and raised in the Bay Area, had long felt the pull of her family’s former home. “I knew I wanted to do something in Southeast Asia, and specifically Vietnam,” Nguyen tells Fortune . “I thought about what really resonates with the local culture, and landed on music.”  In 2007, she packed her bags and moved to Ho Chi Minh City with a dream of creating the “ Spotify of Vietnam,” before there was even a digital ecosystem to work in.  The local music industry, she recalls, was a mess. Back then, “no one understood digital rights,” and artists were signing contracts for CDs and DVDs that said nothing about digital distribution. Nguyen responded by starting POPS Worldwide, an entertainment company which produces, licenses, distributes, and monetizes digital content across platforms like YouTube and Facebook. Nineteen years after she arrived in Ho Chi Minh City, she now manages a portfolio of over 45,000 recordings across different genres, with hubs in Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia. In March, Primary Wave—the independent publisher whose catalogs include Prince, Bob Marley, and Britney Spears— invested in the company ; a Tokyo listing is in the works. Now, Nguyen sees an opportunity for Southeast Asian music as social media shakes up the world of pop culture . “Nowadays, people are listening to music from Africa, South Korea or Mexico, and embedding it into their stories and reels—and they like it even if it isn’t in their own language,” she explains. “Our goal is to ensure that Southeast Asian music will also resonate globally.” ‘Song by song, title by title’ Nguyen had a tough hill to climb when she arrived in Vietnam in 2007. Her Vietnamese, she says, was “like a two-year-old’s,” so local artists often laughed her out of the room. “They’d kind of brush me away, and I’d keep coming back, and they’d be like, ‘Well, just go take it. Our content is on the internet anyway.’” Still, she says she relied on her Silicon Valley experience to keep going. “The mentality of ‘keep moving, don’t stop’ and that it’s okay to fail—I think I’ve really embraced that part of Silicon Valley,” she says. POPS’ answer was to educate the market—“song by song, title by title,” as she puts it—slowly assembling one of Vietnam’s largest music repertoires and becoming one of YouTube’s first music partners in the region. Following its foundational years in Vietnam, POPS expanded to other markets in Southeast Asia, entering Thailand in 2016 and Indonesia in 2020. “Vietnam is our home country. Indonesia has close to 300 million people, and Thai consumers have high purchasing power,” Nguyen explains. “You put those three markets together…it’s really a powerhouse for the region.” POPS is part of a growing Vietnamese pop-culture scene. Yeah1, Vietnam’s first listed media company, reported a 60% revenue jump in 2025 thanks to formats like Call Me by Fire, a singing competition that drew crowds as large as 50,000 people a night. Corporate heavyweights are stepping in: Vingroup, No. 26 on the Southeast Asia 500, made culture a “core pillar” of its strategy last year. Even Vietnam’s government is backing the cultural industry. In January, Vietnam’s government passed Resolution 80 , which set a target of growing the cultural economy by 10% a year, until it reaches 7% of GDP by 2030.  Easy to scale, tough to monetize Still, consumers in Southeast Asia’s emerging markets are also highly price-sensitive, which Nguyen admits made it difficult for her to grow the business financially. “Southeast Asia is a place where you need a lot of patience—it’s a difficult place to to scale in terms of monetization, but it’s really easy to scale in terms of numbers,” she says. “I’m still waiting for the two to converge together.” Apart from licensing Southeast Asian content, POPS also helps to bring foreign IPs from markets like the U.S. and Japan to the region . The firm is one of Southeast Asia’s biggest importers of Japanese anime, including series like Doraemon , Naruto , One Piece, and Detective Conan. (In 2022, Japanese broadcasting company TV TOKYO, which airs major titles like Sergeant Keroro and My Guardian Characters , was the lead investor in POPS’ Series D fundraising round .) “The secret to our success is going deep into each market, understanding the cultural nuances, and then layering on cross-border content, whether it be from Korea, U.S., or Japan,” Nguyen explains. POPS is also working toward a Tokyo listing , through the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s Asia Startup Hub program. POPS executives had previously suggested a listing might come in 2027, but Nguyen won’t put a date on it for now. “Japan is not like the U.S., where if you decide this, you can list in six months,” she says. “There’s a lot of requirements for a Japan listing.” Nguyen says the firm is “near breakeven” today, with plans for profitability in 2027 across its markets, though she declined to reveal exact figures. AI, a double-edged sword Generative AI has flooded the market with cheap content— AI-generated microdramas have proliferated on Chinese streaming platforms like iQIYI, while apps like Suno and Google’s Lyria can generate a song from a prompt. Creators, Nguyen says, have to experiment. “It’s about cutting costs,” she says. “AI allows creators to deliver high-quality content in a short period of time, [which is important] because the hunger for content is so prevalent.” Her own focus group is at home—she has four children. “The younger generation is very anti-AI,” she says. “They’ll criticize something as long as they can see or smell AI in it. Instead, they value content not produced with AI, which they deem as more authentic.” Platforms, she notes, are still “rewarding fully authentic, human-made content”—or at least content with a human touch. Yet POPS itself straddles that line. The firm runs AI influencers , and brands have booked them, Nguyen says, “without us having to do anything because they couldn’t tell it was AI.” She calls that “a little unnerving.”  The industry’s way through, she argues, is labeling and enforcement: platforms and artists are locked in “a chicken and egg” discussion over how to flag AI content and train the systems to protect the originals. ‘That’s the K formula’ Social media, Nguyen argues, is giving lesser-known artists a chance to shine outside a music ecosystem that privileges local acts and Western superstars. “Social media has really democratized content,” she says. In 2024, “I Like You the Most,” a song by Thai R&B singer PONCHET, went viral on TikTok, after global creators and influencers adopted its “sped up” version for dance challenges and acoustic covers. events.title: Elon Musk’s dream merger is a nightmare for SpaceX shareholders
events.summary: The blowout news from SpaceX’s Q3 earnings wasn’t the rocket and AI giant’s outstanding performance that far exceeded even the analysts’ elevated expectations, but Elon Musk’s revelation that SpaceX and Tesla are weighing a merger. On the call, held the evening of October 20, Musk declared that his two signature holdings have each named “special committees” composed of independent directors to explore a union. Musk’s statement confirmed Wall Street’s long-held view that the union was highly likely, and now—given that Musk effectively controls both companies and loves the idea (though as a “conflicted party” can’t serve on the committees), the tie-up looks all but inevitable. The prospect of a SpaceX-Tesla combo got rave notices from the research crews covering both companies. In most cases where the acquirer is en route to paying a price amounting to a humongous PE, the acquirer’s stock falls. Not this time. This time, investors applauded both enterprises, sending Tesla up 3.4% the day following Musk’s statement and SpaceX up 7.8%, adding $155 billion in market cap. At first glance, their already tight kinship, and all their many overlapping businesses, suggest that a new SpaceX-Tesla makes sense. SpaceX buys Tesla Megapack batteries and Cybertrucks, Tesla invested $2 billion in xAI, bought by SpaceX in February, and they share ownership of the much-feted chip project Terafab. Not to mention that the deal would clinch Musk’s long-harbored vision of running a single colossus as a kind of Berkshire Hathaway of AI-driven tech. The wizard freed to blend these two great elixirs of innovation? What’s not to like? A close examination of claims made for the deal, especially assumptions on its supposed advantages in bolstering the finances of both companies, points to an extremely risky wager that must perform never-before-seen heroics to reward shareholders. It’s the ultimate, buy the leap of faith, it’s about the vision, not the numbers, never bet against Elon scenario , set against the sobering numbers. Let’s explore four frequently made arguments for what would prove the largest and, so far, probably the most universally praised, merger in the annals of capitalism. SpaceX-Tesla would be accretive to SpaceX shareholders The idea is that while SpaceX profits are just starting to accelerate, adding Tesla’s earnings, generated from its bedrock EV sales, would immediately raise the former’s EPS. In fact, it’s technically true: If the pair combined now, that’s how the math would work. The problem: The addition to SpaceX’s GAAP profits per share would be minuscule, and since SpaceX’s bottom line’s growing and Tesla’s dropping, the deal if done a year or two from now would prove extremely dilutive for the Starlink provider. What stands out when you examine what SpaceX would pay versus what earnings it would get is how shockingly expensive the transaction would be. One big question: How much premium would SpaceX offer over Tesla’s current price? As Rajat Gupta of JPMorgan points out in a report on a likely merger, that number in most tech acquisitions is 30% to 35%. So let’s posit 30%. Right now, Tesla’s market cap is $1.52 trillion; tack on 30%, and SpaceX would be out $1.98 trillion. SpaceX’s valuation stands at $2.14 trillion. We’re looking at almost a merger of equals. SpaceX would need to issue the equivalent of 92% of its current shares outstanding to capture Tesla. Hence, SpaceX’s count would zoom from 13.1 billion to 25 billion shares. SpaceX would be awarding nearly half of its future earnings to Tesla’s selling shareholders, And what’s it getting in return? We don’t know what the robots and self-driving cars will deliver, but we do know that Tesla booked just $3.28 billion in GAAP net profits over the past four quarters. Since SpaceX had a $1.5 billion loss over the past four quarters, the deal would be “accretive” in the sense that buying Tesla would make the combined company slightly profitable. But SpaceX would just go from EPS that’s a minuscule negative to a tiny positive. What’s important is the amount SpaceX is paying for those earnings and puny “accretion.” It would be getting $3.28 billion in profits in exchange for stock worth $1.98 trillion. That’s $600 for every $1 in extra earnings. To make matters worse, Tesla’s profits have been falling while SpaceX’s bottom line is taking off. In Q3, SpaceX reversed the three prior quarters of deficits by registering $4.4 billion in GAAP net profits, enough to lower its 4-quarter loss to that $1.5 billion. In other words, profits are trending the right way, big time. Via a merger, SpaceX would be sacrificing half of those fast-rising earnings to the Tesla shareholders, and getting what’s for now a minimal contribution from Tesla. On the “accretion” argument, it looks like a bad outcome for SpaceX shareholders. But overall, this would be a good deal for SpaceX, right? Even if SpaceX didn’t buy Tesla, its valuation is so gigantic alongside its earnings that only by achieving stupendous growth in revenues and profits can it deliver shareholders an even decent return. In May, David Trainer of New Constructs provided math reckoning that at its current valuation of $2.14 trillion, SpaceX would need to be generating around $300 billion in profits on sales of roughly $1.6 trillion by 2035 to provide a competitive return. That’s a tall order, to put it mildly. The profits number would be almost a quarter more than what Alphabet makes now, on over three times its revenues. The rub: A Tesla acquisition simply gives SpaceX a far steeper hill to climb, one that’s almost twice as steep. If SpaceX shoulders a 30% premium, the combined companies would start life with a market cap of $4.12 trillion. (That’s SpaceX’s current $2.14 trillion plus the $1.98 trillion paid for Tesla.) SpaceX 2.0 would edge Alphabet ($4.0 trillion) and Microsoft ($3.9 trillion) to rank as the third-most-valuable enterprise in America behind only Nvidia ($5.3 trillion). and Apple ($5.0 trillion). By Fortune’ s estimate, SpaceX would need $550 billion in profits and around $3 trillion in revenue to ring the bell by 2035. That $550 billion target is over twice what Alphabet amasses today. Once again, if Tesla were bringing already big and fast-rising profits to the table, the task wouldn’t be nearly as difficult. But it’s just the opposite. The EV-maker’s providing minimal profits that have already declined from $15 billion in 2023, and $5 billion in 2024 to a run rate that two-thirds the figure of just two years ago. events.title: AI power demand underestimated, say 81% of energy executives
events.summary: More than eight in 10 energy industry decision-makers expect artificial intelligence to drive electricity demand beyond current forecasts, raising concerns about whether there is enough global infrastructure to power the rapid expansion of data centres. A global survey commissioned by Adipec , Abu Dhabi's annual energy conference, found that 81 per cent of energy industry insiders believe AI-driven electricity consumption will exceed existing projections, with 32 per cent expecting demand to be significantly higher. Only 3 per cent expect demand to fall below current forecasts, according to Adipec's Global Energy Report 2026, released on Thursday. Those surveyed included executives from energy companies, technology providers, investors and industry suppliers. The findings come as technology companies accelerate investment in energy-intensive data centres, creating opportunities for power producers while putting additional pressure on electricity networks. The International Energy Agency expects data centres to consume about 950 terawatt-hours of electricity by 2030, roughly double the 2025 level, according to figures cited in the report. The growth in data centre power demand has become an increasingly important consideration for energy producers and governments. At Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week in January, Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc , said global electricity requirements from data centres could increase fivefold by 2040. The report's findings build on the “power is knowledge” message that was the theme of discussions at Adipec last year, as The National reported. The relationship between AI and electricity remains a central focus of this year's event, which will take place at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi from November 2 to November 5. Technology companies reign The expansion of AI is also expected to change the balance of influence within the energy industry. About 43 per cent of respondents believe technology and AI companies will gain the most influence over the sector, compared with 15 per cent who selected governments and regulators. Financial institutions were also selected by 15 per cent, followed by international oil companies at 14 per cent and national oil companies at 9 per cent. The findings reflect the increasingly close relationship between AI and energy , as technology companies become major drivers of investment in electricity generation and infrastructure. For oil and gas companies, the shift is creating new commercial opportunities. While gas and liquefied natural gas growth currently ranks as the biggest commercial opportunity for oil and gas insiders, AI-driven efficiency is expected to take the top position over the next decade. About 27 per cent identify AI-driven efficiency as a leading opportunity in 10 years, while 25 per cent cite supplying power for AI and data centres. The report also found that 81 per cent of oil and gas insiders believe adopting AI will become essential to remain profitable over the next decade. The findings are particularly relevant to the UAE, where Abu Dhabi is developing a 5-gigawatt AI campus that will house the Stargate UAE computing cluster, expected to cost more than $30 billion . However, a quarter of energy insiders believe the industry is unprepared for AI-driven electricity demand, with grid delays among the biggest obstacles. At Adipec last year, Dr Al Jaber called for “massive” energy investment to meet growing requirements. The Adipec report, conducted by global strategic communications consultancy Kekst CNC between August and October 2026, surveyed 1,832 energy industry decision-makers across 78 countries and included 17 executive interviews. Its findings reflect industry expectations rather than independently verified demand forecasts.

events.title: Children in care to get £10 a week savings
events.summary: The States of Guernsey said about 40 people in care will be eligible for the scheme. A new government savings scheme will set aside £10 a week for children in care for them to access when they turn 18. Established by the States' Children and Family Community Services and Guernsey Community Savings, it is designed to give young people a financial foundation when becoming an adult. The States said the scheme will apply to children from entry into the care system and 40 will benefit immediately. Associate director of children services Lucy Cook said the savings accounts would support young people by "helping them to access opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach." The States of Guernsey said the transition to independent living for people in care can bring "significant financial pressures, from setting up a home to managing everyday living costs". "Having savings of their own can offer greater choice, security and confidence as they take this important step," it said. The States will pay a one-off fee to allpay, a payment services company, to establish the scheme. The charity Guernsey Community Savings will then open and manage the accounts, and work with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday. At 18 years old, they will have the choice of opening an account with Guernsey Community Savings or transferring their savings to an account of their choice. Cook said children in care deserve the opportunity to "look ahead with confidence and hope for their future". "This initiative is about giving our care-experienced young people a stronger foundation and recognising our commitment to them as corporate parents. "We want every child in care to know that they are valued, supported and encouraged to achieve their full potential." Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Chief executive of Guernsey Community Savings Joe Brown said children from care are "particularly vulnerable to financial exclusion when they reach adulthood". "Giving them the opportunity to build up savings, and the financial security that comes with this, can make a real difference as they take their first steps towards independence." events.title: US universities are failing to protect victims of sexual assault
events.summary: The Cornell case illustrates how university bureaucracies discourage complaints, obstruct accountability and protect institutional reputations. Cornell University’s internal processes for responding to sexual assault reports failed “Jane Doe”. In 2024, the third-year student reported being sexually assaulted by seven men while incapacitated at a fraternity house . Cornell launched an investigation that would last months, but the process failed to deliver the accountability Jane Doe sought. She was left feeling unheard and unsafe, dropping out without completing her degree. No criminal charges were brought against the men she accused. She is now suing Cornell over its handling of her case. None of the administrators involved in those processes have been named. They have yet to face accountability. Her experience reveals the ways in which confidential procedures at universities are intended to make “problems” go away, rather than work towards any form of justice for victims. It also reveals how those in positions of authority – deans, provosts and presidents, alongside Title IX and Affirmative Action officers, and university lawyers – are primarily invested in protecting their institutions. That is the real goal. They are not here to advocate for vulnerable students, staff, or faculty. Every week, students on campuses throughout the United States – overwhelmingly women – are sexually assaulted. A 2025 Cornell University survey found that 35 percent of undergraduate women respondents had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since enrolling. The problem extends well beyond Cornell: a 2025 Michigan State University survey found that approximately one in five undergraduate women had experienced sexual assault since enrolling. Yet most incidents go unreported. A US Department of Justice study found that fewer than 5 percent of completed and attempted rapes were reported to police. Students – and their parents – must understand that the pathways for reporting violations are strategically designed to be difficult to navigate, or outright broken. Although you will hear administrators make all the right noises, they ensure that their publicly-touted systems remain labyrinthine and impossible to access. This army of well-paid administrators – lovely, trustworthy-looking senior faculty and members of staff that welcome you on Parents’ Day and at Alumni functions – answer to the institution, making them unreliable allies of the victim. Those who are victimised are expected to be the responsible party, documenting what happened to them in detail even as the trauma of the experience is ongoing. They are forced to repeat the particularities of the assault multiple times – to campus policemen and various administrators supposedly there to protect the student. As research shows, being forced to repetitively “perform” for various administrators makes one relive the violation and compounds trauma. Educational institutions often weaponise incompetence, blaming it on systems that are purposefully nonfunctional in order to avoid dealing with legitimate, even catastrophic, concerns. On top of this, administrators strategically perform care while caroming anyone who reports harm from one office to another. This seemingly absurd game of musical chairs is aimed at exhausting the victims. As feminist scholar Sara Ahmed argues in her 2021 book Complaint!, this process frames the complainant as the problem and dissipates the threat they pose. It ensures that lessons are imprinted on those who dare to voice dissent and demand accountability. Strategic dysfunction has a purpose: It safeguards the institution and silences victims. The “broken” system encourages victims to keep things in-house, assuring them that institutional processes will be less injurious than reporting a violation to the police. Disciplinary proceedings are kept secret, ostensibly to protect the victims. (Indeed, those traumatised by sexual violence deserve privacy. But these are not the reasons that institutions want to keep things quiet). Wondering why students, staff, or faculty members who have experienced a violation do not immediately get “lawyered up”? As Dr Sonia Cheruvillil, a public health advocate, noted, “Getting a lawyer is rarely what happens in sexual violence cases anywhere. The vast, overwhelming number of sex crimes are not reported to any authority because they are committed by friends, family. Authorities are not safe. University campuses are a microcosm of a larger eco-system of harm that keeps survivors and victims in place, individualizes their experience, and denies them justice.” Students may not be able to go to family for support, because not all families are safe. Some are actively discouraged by their families from making formal complaints. Universities across the US often flaunt their programmes aimed at educating students about sexual assault.

events.title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
events.summary: Published 22 October 2026, 04:48 BST For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on Wednesday A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. What happened after the flaws were exposed? Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said. Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms. The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X. "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said. Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems. E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability. The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz. The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said. "The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.

events.summary: China finished 0.233 points ahead of the Americans, denying them a chance to win an gold eighth consecutive team gold. China have denied the United States an eighth consecutive women’s team title at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships as Qiu Qiyuan sealed a dramatic victory with the final routine. Qiu needed to score more than 12.600 points in the closing floor routine to give her country gold and did just enough with 12.833 on Wednesday. list 1 of 4 Man United captain Fernandes slams Carrick’s tactics after Como hammering list 2 of 4 Declan Rice grabs Arsenal draw at Bayern Munich in Champions League list 3 of 4 Saudi Arabia cancels 2026 ‘Davos in the Desert’ amid Houthi attacks list 4 of 4 Ballon d’Or: Which countries and players have won the most awards? The USA last failed to win gold when they were beaten by Russia at the 2010 championships, but were left to count the cost of several errors on the balance beam in Rotterdam. China, who also led the way in qualifying, finished with 165.764 points, edging out the Americans by 0.233 overall. Japan were a further 1.468 points behind as they completed the podium ahead of fourth-placed France. USA superstar Simone Biles, a 23-time world champion including five times in the team competition, is taking a break from the sport and has not competed since the 2024 Paris Olympics, where she won three gold medals. The reigning champions took a healthy lead at the halfway stage, helped by strong vault and uneven bars routines by Skye Blakely, the only gymnast on the team who was part of the quintet that won their seventh consecutive title in 2023. But 18-year-old Caylor Dulcy stumbled on the beam, scoring just 12.333, as the Americans were outscored by more than four points on the apparatus by their rivals. Zhang Qingying, who topped beam qualifying, in particular made them pay with a sparkling performance that earned her 15.066 points. The Chinese were put under pressure on the floor, but Qiu held her nerve to secure their first women’s team world crown since 2006. The championships continue in the Netherlands on Thursday as Japan’s Daiki Hashimoto defends his men’s all-around title, with a big challenge expected from his compatriot and Olympic champion Shinnosuke Oka. Japan took the men’s team title on Tuesday, pipping Russia and China.

events.title: Singapore security robotics firm Kabam to cease operations on Nov 20
events.summary: Kabam’s product offering comprises AI-powered security robotics and management software, designed to conduct video surveillance and autonomous patrolling. Kabam Robotics, a Singapore security robotics firm, will stop business on Nov 20. It apologised to customers and asked those with open cases to contact it before then. The closure reason was not given. It is unclear how many staff or customers will be affected, though LinkedIn lists 54 employees and the firm has major clients such as Aetos, Certis and Changi Airport Group. Kabam was founded in 2020, later merged with Cognicept Systems, and had more than 150 robots deployed. Its shutdown comes as Singapore pushes to grow its robotics sector through programmes like RoboNexus. SINGAPORE – Home-grown security robotics company Kabam Robotics will cease business operations from Nov 20, an e-mail issued to its customers showed. In the e-mail seen by The Business Times, Kabam’s management said it apologised for any inconvenience caused and thanked customers for their support over the years. “We sincerely appreciate the trust and support you have placed in Kabam over the years. It has been our pleasure to work with you, and we are truly grateful for the opportunity to serve your business,” the company said. It added that customers requiring assistance with existing matters should contact the company before Nov 20. The reasons for the closure were not disclosed. It is unclear how many employees will be affected, or what will happen to the company’s existing customers and robot deployments. Kabam’s LinkedIn page lists 54 employees associated with the company. BT has reached Kabam for comment. The company did not immediately respond. The company counts local security services firms Aetos and Certis among its clients, as well as Changi Airport Group, JTC Corporation, Sats, Amazon Web Services and Mandai Wildlife Group, its website showed. Its product offering comprises artificial intelligence-powered security robotics and management software, designed to conduct video surveillance and autonomous patrolling across indoor and outdoor facilities. The company is a majority-owned subsidiary of Singapore-based precision engineering company Patec Group, which is listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange. It was founded in 2020 as Patec’s robotics venture, before merging with fellow local robotics startup Cognicept Systems in 2022. BT reported in 2023 that more than 150 of Kabam’s robots were deployed globally and in Singapore, including at Jewel, Paya Lebar Quarter Mall and Toa Payoh HDB Hub. The company’s planned closure comes amid Singapore’s considerable efforts to develop its robotics industry. It was among the first six companies supported under RoboNexus, an accelerator programme first piloted by Singapore’s National Robotics Programme in September 2024. The programme was officially launched in March 2025 to support local robotics startups through tailored mentorships, business development support and global market access. Kabam was among two robotics companies that tapped the programme’s research and talent pipelines at the product development stage. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Cookies and weapons: Women in Yemen’s Taiz find ways to help the city’s defence
events.summary: Amid growing threats, a grassroots aid effort has transformed into an initiative to get more ammunition to the front. Taiz, Yemen – As Houthi fighters tighten their siege on the government-held southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz , women who initially organised food deliveries for soldiers defending the city have begun raising money to buy weapons and ammunition. The initiatives have emerged spontaneously since the resumption of fighting in early September in the western countryside of Taiz governorate, between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed armed group. list 1 of 3 Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict? list 2 of 3 Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks list 3 of 3 WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond At first, women volunteers came together to bake cookies for fighters on the front lines. The aim was “to strengthen the relationship between the supportive social base and the members of the national army and pro-government popular resistance forces stationed at the front lines in defence of their besieged city, which is subjected to daily shelling in preparation for an invasion,” said Amira al-Saghir, an activist involved in the campaign. The cookie-making initiative attracted widespread participation among women volunteers, drawing encouragement and support on social media. It coincided with a broader community campaign to supply fighters with food and other basic necessities, as well as weapons, with people contributing from districts and villages across the governorate. In Yemen, a conservative country and the poorest in the Middle East, the vast majority of women do not participate in active fighting in the civil war, which began in 2014 . Instead, these initiatives allow women to take part in what they see as the defence of their city against an invading force, and support for the men who are fighting. After nearly four years of relative calm following a United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022, Houthi forces launched a major ground offensive in western Taiz in early September. The armed group rapidly captured territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic port city of Mocha on September 10 , expanding its presence around Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital shipping route. The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God, subsequently advanced towards other parts of Taiz governorate, taking control of key routes into the provincial capital and effectively surrounding the city. Government forces have since launched counteroffensives, with control of some areas remaining contested. The renewed siege has severely restricted the movement of people and essential supplies into the city, triggering shortages of food, fuel, and medicine. As the fighting intensified, the women’s initiatives expanded. What began with baking cookies and organising food convoys to supply arms kitchens gradually evolved into efforts to buy ammunition for fighters. Women involved in the initiatives told Al Jazeera that they felt they had been “forced” to act because of the risk of their city falling to the Houthis. The change began as more rural districts began falling to the Houthis, leading to some donors making their contributions conditional on part of the money being used to buy ammunition for fighters. Al-Saghir believes the shift was encouraged by information and criticism circulating on social media suggesting that government fighters in Taiz lacked sufficient ammunition to continue defending the city and surrounding front lines. The initiatives soon took off, encouraging more women to get involved. Among them was Huriya Wabel, a humanitarian activist. “After we saw that those [Houthi] militias … are waging a war of extermination against our city, we felt that we had to take a serious stand to support the army, not just with food and clothing, but with weapons as well, especially since a siege has been imposed on Taiz and supplies can no longer reach it easily,” Wabel told Al Jazeera. “We also found many civilians who wanted to participate in the fighting alongside the army in defence of the city, but they did not have weapons,” she added. “So it became incumbent upon us to help by focusing more of our activities on this aspect at this stage.” For Khadija al-Majidi, the move from providing humanitarian supplies to delivering military equipment is a response to the growing threat facing Taiz. “When the enemy reaches the gates of your city and imposes a complete siege on it in preparation for storming it by force, and everyone in it – including you, your children, and members of your family – is threatened with being killed, captured, or displaced … then what do you expect from us?” the activist told Al Jazeera. “Did you expect us to carry flowers for the criminal who came from the farthest reaches of the country to destroy our city and kill us?

events.title: Man United’s Carrick not worried about his job despite ‘unacceptable’ loss
events.summary: ‘I have not given my own position any thought’, Carrick said after United’s 4-1 loss to Como in the Champions League. Michael Carrick has admitted that Manchester United were difficult to watch during an “unacceptable” 4-1 Champions League thrashing by Como , but insists he is not concerned about losing his job as manager. The three-time European champions were outclassed by the Italian debutants at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia on Wednesday, as the embarrassing defeat extended their winless run to seven matches in all competitions. Carrick’s position has come under scrutiny amid United’s slump, which has included their worst start to a league season for 40 years, but he told a news conference that he was not fearing for his position. “I have not given my own position any thought,” Carrick said. The Old Trafford boss insisted that his apology to the travelling fans at the end of the game held no extra significance as pressure builds on his position. “I always go over to the fans regardless,” Carrick said. “It wasn’t a particularly different reason why I went over. I think it’s the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they have gone through and what they have done over a period of a few weeks now. But particularly tonight.” United fell behind within two minutes to a Nico Paz goal, becoming the first English team ever to concede in the opening two minutes of two consecutive major European matches, having gone behind one minute into a 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid last week. Cesc Fabregas’s side romped into a deserved 4-0 lead in northern Italy before substitute Joshua Zirkzee pulled back a stoppage-time consolation and Carrick admitted he was alarmed by the manner in which his team were outplayed. “For us to play in that way, it’s not acceptable,” he said. “It wasn’t a good performance at all. We wanted to build on what we brought and the performance we had at Leeds . “That bit of intensity, that spirit, that aggression, that real willingness to give everything. Tonight was the total opposite performance. I have to say, it was tough to watch.” “There’s a lot going through my mind, watching that,” he continued. “Genuinely, it’s difficult to understand how it can be so different [from the Leeds performance]. “It shouldn’t be like that. We can all play well, we can all have poor performances, but to do it in that manner is really not right at all.” Next up for Carrick’s side is a home Premier League game against Bournemouth on Sunday. “I’m frustrated, more than frustrated, I’m really angry, to be honest,” Carrick said. “You’ve got to move on, you’ve got to deal with what’s next and see what that looks like. At this moment in time, there’s a lot to do before that next game to get the team ready because that was a difficult night for everyone tonight.”

events.title: China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
events.summary: As Beijing prioritises development of the technology, a China-led committee aims to dictate how it is built China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority. The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a technical director with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases. “The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group.

events.title: The world is $365 trillion in debt, and the interest bill is climbing
events.summary: Protests in Europe have highlighted debt squeeze, with France now paying more to borrow than Italy and Greece. Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks, angry at rising living costs, low wages, unaffordable housing and underfunded schools. Protests in France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal have sometimes descended into clashes, looting and fires, although many protests have remained peaceful. France has been at the centre of the unrest. More than 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday , according to the Interior Ministry, amid weeks of student protests over education and living costs. The unrest has turned the spotlight on a fiscal squeeze that governments are struggling to control. Years of heavy borrowing have left many European countries deeply in debt, and that debt is getting more expensive. France’s borrowing costs are the highest since 2002, and the more governments spend on interest, the less they have for the schools, hospitals and pensions that protesters want. In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at how governments borrow, where France ranks among the most indebted countries, and the trillions that governments spend on interest. Governments borrow money much like people do, but instead of going to a bank, they sell bonds. In return, the government pays the buyers interest and promises to repay the full amount on a set date. A 10-year bond is a loan the government pays back after a decade. Its yield – the return investors earn for lending – is the most closely watched measure of how much markets trust a country to manage its debt. The government borrows money – An investor pays €100 for a 10-year bond. The government pays interest – Every year for 10 years, the investor receives a fixed payment. At 2.5 percent, that’s €2.50 a year, or €25 in total. At 5 percent, it’s €5 a year, or €50 in total. The government repays the loan – After 10 years, the investor gets the original €100 back. What happens when borrowing gets more expensive? When bond prices fall, yields rise, making borrowing more expensive. Like a family facing a higher mortgage rate, a government then spends more on interest and has less money for essentials, such as schools, hospitals and roads. Ten-year borrowing costs for major European economies have not been as high as 5 percent since the early 2000s, shortly after the euro was launched. During the eurozone debt crisis of 2010 to 2012, only struggling countries such as Greece, Italy and Spain paid that much or more, and yields above 7 percent pushed Ireland and Portugal into bailouts. France now pays around 5 percent to borrow for 10 years, compared with 3.41 percent for Germany. The widening gap shows investors want a higher return for lending to France. The chart below shows 10-year borrowing costs across the euro area and the UK. France now pays more than Italy and Greece, two of the countries hit hardest by the eurozone debt crisis. Only the UK, which is outside the euro, pays more. The United States has by far the largest government debt, at $41.4 trillion, or 127 percent of its economy, or gross domestic product (GDP). The US benefits from borrowing in dollars, the world’s dominant reserve currency, which supports global demand for its debt. But its borrowing capacity is not unlimited. China follows with $22.5 trillion, or 104 percent of GDP, while Japan owes $8.7 trillion and has the highest debt ratio among major economies, at 199 percent of GDP. The UK’s debt stands at $4.4 trillion, or 102 percent of GDP. France ranks fifth globally, with debt of $4.2 trillion, or 118.5 percent of GDP. That is more than Italy’s $3.7 trillion, although Italy’s debt is larger relative to its economy, at 138 percent. Germany owes $3.5 trillion, just 65 percent of GDP. The IMF projects France’s public debt to rise to 121.8 percent of GDP by 2030, complicating efforts to put the country’s public finances on a sustainable path. The table below ranks countries by government debt. Use the search box to find yours. Global debt, including that of governments, households and companies, rose by $10 trillion in the first half of 2026 to more than $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance (IIF) . That is roughly $44,000 for every person on Earth. Much of the increase came from emerging markets. Paying for that debt is costly. Advanced economies paid more than $3.3 trillion in interest on their government bonds over the past year. That is more than the world spends on defence ($3.1 trillion), artificial intelligence ($2.6 trillion) or clean energy ($2.3 trillion). For the public, rising interest costs mean less money for services such as schools, hospitals and pensions. Governments may have to raise taxes or cut spending to cover the bill. Higher government borrowing costs can also push up interest rates on mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

events.title: ‘Stupid talk’: France rejects Trump’s attempt to blame unrest on migration
events.summary: The US president has turned his attention to France, but his comments appear to have been dismissed by French leader Macron. Paris, France – As France reels from violent clashes during protests, riots and looting, the blame game is on. One argument making waves across the political spectrum – and across the Atlantic – is that migrants and open-border policies are responsible. list 1 of 4 ‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors list 2 of 4 ‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence list 3 of 4 Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’? list 4 of 4 France’s Macron says protesters won’t be allowed to ‘cause chaos’ “If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished,” United States President Donald Trump said at the White House on Monday. “When I look at France, when you look at Italy , when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred – that’s not about school. That’s about people coming into the countries that hate the country.” French President Emmanuel Macron has since slammed “stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders”, but did not name Trump. Speaking during a visit in Qatar, he said there was no evidence of foreign interference behind the riots. Young student protesters in France were unimpressed by Trump’s intervention. Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old student at the Paul Eluard high school near Paris, one of the first to witness protests, called it “stupid talk”. “They can think whatever they like. We’re focusing on the main subject, which is the students’ demands,” Narjissi said. “The far right has to say these kinds of things because they base their politics and political programmes on instilling fear.” Emmanuel Dupuy, president of the Institute for European Perspective and Security Studies, a think tank on diplomacy and political analysis, said Trump’s argument was aimed at American voters. “It’s an artificial argument used as a political tool in the context of midterm elections,” he said. “They are trying to argue that what is happening in France would happen in the US if Democrats get elected.” Trump’s comments came after largely peaceful high school student demonstrations in France descended into chaos over the weekend when rioters attacked city halls and looted stores, marking the most violent unrest in France in years. More than 2,000 people were placed in police custody – the vast majority of them minors – and thousands of businesses were ransacked. Accused of letting the situation spiral, French authorities imposed partial and temporary curfews in certain cities across the country, including in areas of Paris. While concerns over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes and teacher shortages were at the fore, the protest movement quickly catalysed wider discontent over the cost of living and social unease. Italy, Albania and Spain have seen similar demonstrations. French authorities have not linked crime with migration. The state does not share the identities of people arrested and sent to trial. Under constitutional laws aimed at equality, it is illegal to collect data on ethnicity and race. Both far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen and politicians from the centrist bloc, including Macron and Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, have accused hard-left groups of fomenting disorder. The wave of protests seems to have struck a nerve across the European bloc, too. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was now “clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on immigration”, posting on X a video showing buildings burning in France. Without explicitly referring to events in France, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk also weighed in. “Poland will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, nor will it pay for them,” he asserted on X a day after the mass demonstrations and looting in France. “We will be uncompromising on security.” Dupuy said the origin of those who joined the violence was beside the point. “These protesters were high school students; then professional black bloc and looters joined, too – whether they came from a third or fourth generation of former migrants is irrelevant,” he said. “Eventually, this is a problem of integration, not immigration.” Vance attacks ‘Western liberals’ in Europe The US is in campaigning mode as it gears up for key elections in early November that will determine who dominates Congress. events.title: The director behind Yung Lean's viral 'Storm' video says AI imitations on social media made even good work look 'lame'
events.summary: The director of Yung Lean's viral "Storm" video says AI made his work look "lame." Francis Specker/CBS via Getty Images The director behind Yung Lean's "Storm" video said AI copies made him consider quitting filmmaking. Romain Gavras said AI imitations of "Storm" on social media made his work look "lame." The original video, released in April, has amassed more than 40 million views on YouTube. The director behind Swedish rapper Yung Lean's viral "Storm" video says AI almost drove him from filmmaking. In  an interview  with Vulture published on Tuesday, Romain Gavras said he was disheartened by the wave of AI-generated copies of the music video. Gavras directed the video for "Gener8ion," an audiovisual project he runs with French producer Surkin. The video, which has amassed over 40 million views since its release in April, follows Lean as a bully at a boarding school before the boys he has been tormenting break into an elaborate dance sequence around him during a class photo. In September, social media users began using AI to remake the dance scene from "Storm," swapping Lean and the schoolboys for a wide range of new characters, including animals and celebrities. "My daughter sent me the first one I saw," Gavras said. "She was like, 'Look, this dog is doing it.'" It was funny for a while, he said, but the novelty soon wore off as the copies seemed to spread everywhere. "It made me sad for all the people who put in so much work on our video," Gavras said. "A trend like this can make even good work look lame. Part of me wanted to quit filmmaking, move back to Greece, and become an olive farmer." Gavras said he wasn't trying to make any commentary on AI, but when people started calling "Storm" the kind of video AI couldn't pull off, he found himself drawn into the debate. "The tech people were like, 'Oh yeah? AI could never?' Then they started replicating it. So we were forced into this conversation. It's a nightmare," Gavras said. He added that he has turned down a few AI companies that have approached him about licensing the video. "There's an economic model coming that we didn't want to be a part of," he said. However, even as AI-made versions of his work proliferate online, Gavras said the technology can imitate elements of the video but has yet to create anything with the same originality or human spark. "They're missing the swagger of Yung Lean . He looks like a dangerous baby. There's something in the imperfection of humanity, and the interior life of someone who dances or even someone who just smokes a cigarette, that's not quite there yet," he said. Last month, Lean and the dancers performed the choreography at the MTV Video Music Awards. A video of the performance has since racked up nearly 14 million views. Gavras is not the only filmmaker who has weighed in on the impact of AI on creative work. Other major Hollywood directors have raised similar concerns: Guillermo del Toro has said AI could rob future filmmakers of the chance to learn their craft, while Tim Burton has said it strips away the humanity behind art. events.title: Ukraine’s access to Starlink a decision for Elon Musk, Rubio says
events.summary: US secretary of state says White House not to blame for reported speed limits on internet services in Ukraine. United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio says decisions about Ukraine’s access to Starlink are in the hands of its parent company, SpaceX, and CEO Elon Musk, not the White House, in response to claims it was involved in restricting Kyiv’s access to satellite internet services. Rubio’s comments on Wednesday may increase scrutiny of US decision-making to potentially throttle the high-tech system, which allows Kyiv to intercept incoming projectiles and target Russian launchers. list 1 of 3 Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy list 2 of 3 Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine list 3 of 3 US-Ukraine relations sour as Trump, Zelenskyy clash over talks, arms The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered a slowdown of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on for defence against Russian missile attacks. The Journal quoted one person as saying Musk, US President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand and two people as saying Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown. The Reuters news agency has quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter as saying the decision ultimately came from the White House. This version was also confirmed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy but denied by the Trump administration. Zelenskyy adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on the Telegram messaging app on October 14 that SpaceX had imposed a limit of 160 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) on Starshield services. That affected guidance systems for drones that Ukraine uses to intercept Russian drones flying at far greater speeds. “Our defence forces received no prior warning regarding this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence confirmed the resumption of services on October 15. Rubio told reporters during a trip to India on Wednesday that he was not aware if the administration knew about the decision beforehand but said it was “irrelevant”. “The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” he said. Musk had previously said on X that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS (President of the United States).” Trump, asked by reporters on Wednesday whether Musk ordered the slowdown, said he did not know who did it but “I was not involved.” Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Tuesday also portrayed the Starlink cutoff as a commercial matter. “There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” he said. One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX’s Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon. Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield while Zelenskyy has said both services had been disrupted in Ukraine.

events.title: El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
events.summary: President Nayib Bukele says he has initiated military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted in Haiti. El Salvador has initiated a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted by gangs in Haiti, President Nayib Bukele announced in a post on X, without elaborating. Bukele, known for his intense crackdown on gang violence in El Salvador, warned in Wednesday’s statement that a more forceful response was coming if the personnel were not released alive and well. list 1 of 3 Ecuador defends US sinking of vessels as joint anti-drug operation list 2 of 3 ‘Handcuffed and blindfolded’: Is the US targeting Ecuadorian fishermen? list 3 of 3 Trump rallies Latin American allies against drug cartels “Do not take our word for empty threats,” the president wrote, addressing the gangs allegedly responsible for holding the four men. “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.” Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle carrying the men three days earlier, in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country last year. The four men, aviation technicians with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince. Haiti’s government issued a news release on Wednesday evening saying the release of the abducted soldiers was an “absolute priority”. It was not immediately clear if Haitian authorities received any confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive. The government said a meeting was held at the prime minister’s office “to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force”. A spokesperson for the GSF did not immediately respond to a message seeking details The UN-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday’s attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors. More than a million displaced in Haiti No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops, which comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince. El Salvador is among several countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form part of the gang suppression force, with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti. Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years. More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured from January through mid-September this year, and more than 230 have been kidnapped, according to the UN. The area where the armoured vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs, including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitel’Homme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and the US.

events.title: KPMG ban on government work extended after 'serious ethical failings'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ban on KPMG getting government work extended to February after audit leaks scandal Topic: Accounting and Auditing Services KPMG is under the spotlight for "serious ethical failings". ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February. Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into KPMG and found the way the Big Four firm had handled a whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings". KPMG CEO John Sams and chairman Michael Ebeid say they are working on a plan to make "lasting change" and hope to win back the government contract. The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February, following a review that found "serious ethical failings" by its leadership and some of its senior partners. Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into the Big Four firm, following allegations its audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it . In response to Mr Watt's review, which was handed down today, the department said it has agreed with the firm to a further extension to the pause on KPMG bidding for Australian government work until February 28, 2027. During this period, KPMG will provide the department with an implementation plan and the first of its quarterly progress implementation reports. The department also needs to ensure that "KPMG is engaging constructively with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) and the Tax Practitioners Board (TPB) reviews, and is committed to addressing any recommendations that have been made by those organisations". Dr Watt said in his review the way the accounting firm had handled the whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings by some senior members of KPMG" and "significant cultural concerns within KPMG". Dr Watt noted the review was focused on the leadership and culture of the firm "that had been warned on previous occasions about weaknesses in ethical culture, speak-up confidence and accountability, but did not deal with them with the rigour and urgency required". Firms raise doubts about KPMG's integrity In the wake of the KPMG audit leak scandal, executives from Macquarie, Westpac, Optus and Dexus cast doubt on their faith in the auditor. He said since March, KPMG has undergone significant change, with a new chair and a new CEO, and a number of senior personnel having left the firm. Dr Watt said the firm had also commissioned several reviews to understand the root causes of the events. "As was often observed during review interviews, trust takes time to build, and while transparency builds trust, lack of transparency damages it." Dr Watt said his report should not be read as a judgement on every member of KPMG. "Virtually all of KPMG's staff had no involvement in the events that occurred," he said. KPMG CEO John Sams and its chairman Michael Ebeid said they accepted the findings and recommendations of Mr Watt's review. John Sams says the firm is working to revamp its internal culture. ( Supplied ) "The report lays bare our failings and highlights the hard work that we must do to address them," they said in a statement. The firm had appointed Kerry Schott to provide independent oversight and said "while we are making important progress, we know that changing culture takes longer than changing individual roles, structures or controls". "Confidence in KPMG's suitability for Commonwealth work must be earned through evidence of effective, lasting change," the statement said. Call to overhaul code governing bids Dr Watt also recommended the department of finance strengthen the Commonwealth's supplier code of conduct, including tougher sanctions for suppliers breaching their obligations and more reporting pathways for potential unethical behaviour. Whistleblowers need better protection Without whistleblowers, Australians would be kept in the dark about major corporate scandals, but evidence suggests the experience of raising alarm bells can destroy their lives. Several states and territories have also banned KPMG from taking on public sector work pending the outcome of Dr Watt's review, or their own reviews. They are working through their responses to the findings. Greens finance and public service spokesperson Senator Barbara Pocock said a small extension of the freeze on KPMG contracts was not dealing with the issue.

events.title: Woman 'scared to turn heating on' due to oil cost
events.summary: Roslynn Garner-Gatley says she relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water A woman has said she is frightened to put her heating on because the cost of domestic oil has nearly doubled. Roslynn Garner-Gatley, 76, lives in a three-bedroom semi-detached cottage in Yealmpton, south Devon, with no gas supply and relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water. She said her oil tank held 1,000 litres (220 gallons). About six months earlier, she bought 500 litres (110 gallons) for £317 plus VAT but, when she contacted her supplier for a current quote, she was told the same amount would cost £600 plus VAT. Garner-Gatley said: "I did not expect at my age after working for 50 years to be in a situation where I am terrified of putting on the heating because of the price of it." The cost of filling her heating oil tank has nearly doubled Garner-Gatley said she had started going to bed earlier to keep warm while watching television and had recently begun using a hot water bottle and bed socks as evening temperatures dropped. She said instead of keeping hot water on a timer, she only switched it on when she needed it for washing, cooking or bathing before turning it off again. She added that people living in rural areas who depended on oil had "no choice" but to buy it. She said: "After working all my life I didn't expect to be constantly worrying about how to keep warm at my age. It is really quite frightening." Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington. Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector . Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels set for some customers would also be reviewed, they added. Cornwall Council and Devon County Council have money available for households struggling with increasing heating oil costs from their crisis resilience funds, which are provided by the government. Cornwall Council said it had issued payments of £300 to £1,386 households, a total spend of £415,800, which would double after a decision was made to award a further £300 to the same households. The Devon fund, worth about £8.4m a year, is available through district councils, and is targeted at low‑income households facing an "essential cost they cannot afford". Plymouth City Council and Torbay Council also have their own crisis resilience funds. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? events.title: 'I can't afford to heat my home on my pension'
events.summary: Teresa Goubert said the cost of heating had become so expensive that she could not afford to heat her home this winter Some pensioners say they are going to bed early, wearing extra layers and using hot water bottles because they cannot afford to heat their homes this winter. Teresa Goubert, from Guernsey, who uses electric and oil heating, said: "I'm trying to keep it off as long as possible because it's got very expensive and I just can't afford to do it [heat home] on my pension." The States has proposed a 19% increase in the means-tested winter fuel allowance to £50.48 a week. It will be debated in November. Tina Bury, Employment and Social Security President, said: "The fuel allowance is quite a broad brush approach and obviously everyone's needs are different in this area." Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Ms Goubert, who receives the allowance, said: "The first £70 of it is standing charges, so you're only getting sort of £100... just over £100 for your month, which is nothing at the moment." "I'm putting blankets on me and then if I get too cold, I go up to bed, you know, just put more blankets on up there. That's the only solution." Islander Katina Jones, who lives with her husband, said they waited as long as they could before turning the heating on. "Once I make a cup of tea, I use the extra hot water in a hot water bottle to use just to keep us warm." Sheila Cornelius, who lives in an over-55 housing development in the island, said: "It's not very good because I don't believe in being cold so of course all my money, most of it goes on there. "Luckily I've got some nice thick clothes that I can wear instead of having the heating on full, you know, [I] can't afford it." Gareth Wordingham, from Guernsey Electricity, said: "The standing charges this year only went up by 3% so it wasn't a large proportion of the increase itself. "We buy our electricity in international markets, years in advance, so that smooths the price that we pay or our customers' pay. "We have to balance between the smaller customers and also those larger customers who might be equally vulnerable, a family with children, could be equally strapped for money." Nick Crolla, head of marketing for fuel suppliers, Rubis Channel Islands, said: "Since August, we've seen prices increase by up to 30%. "We are really seeing that we're not shielded from the volatile international market. "If customers are concerned about the cost of heating oil, the best thing is to come speak to us, we have payment options to help the customer ease the volatility of the oil prices." Bury, said the committee could respond if heating oil prices increased sharply over winter. "Should we get to the depths of winter and there's a massive spike in costs of oil, for example, we do have the ability to react to that," she added. events.title: 'An £8k service charge left me unable to pay bills'
events.summary: Callum Maddern says he is still straddled with debt after facing a huge increase in his bills A housing association has defended the charges faced by its leaseholders after many complained of huge bill increases to pay for maintenance. Callum Maddern, who lives in Bath, said he had seen his service charge increase six-fold to more than £8,000 per year after Curo said vital work needed doing on his accommodation block. "I didn't have enough money to put the heating on," he said. "I had water on my sink and coffee tables that was freezing. I'd be lying in bed and I could see my breath." Curo, which says it does not make any money from the contributions, said it was "trying to work with residents to prepare them for these bills". Man jailed for 'cruel' attack that killed pensioner Published 16 hours ago Community ownership could restore city landmark Published 17 hours ago Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life Published 19 hours ago When Maddern bought his flat in 2023, the annual service charge was about £1,300 per year. He was told there was £5,000 in what is known as a sinking fund to cover any necessary works. But the following year, he received a bill for £8,000 to go towards fire safety work and new windows. "Originally I thought there was some kind of mistake," he said. But when he queried the charge, Curo confirmed it was accurate. Maddern describes "constant delays" in his attempts to reach out to Curo and negotiate. "They were totally uncaring," he said, adding he was told he could sell his property and pay the fee that way. Maddern said he ended up selling possessions and taking out loans to pay for the work. While he said he knew that as a leaseholder he had a responsibility to contribute towards maintenance costs, he questioned why everything suddenly had to be done in a three-year period. "If new windows are needed, absolutely that must be scheduled in. But to have everything in the space of three years, surely that is not a good approach," he added. Andrew Snee, director of housing and support at Curo, acknowledged the way charges had been communicated could have been better and said he wanted to apologise "if our correspondence has caused any concern or upset". But Snee denied the company could have managed the costs better, describing the situation as a "perfect storm". "The cost of living is increasing, the cost of contracts is increasing, at the same time we've got increased legislation around property safety and fire safety, which has to be a good thing but it does come at a cost," he said. "We are being as honest and transparent as we can to deliver these costs in as caring a way as we can. Keep talking to us." Ken Pearson says Curo have a responsibility to prepare leaseholders for large bills Ken Pearson owns his flat in a different block elsewhere in Bath. He says his sinking fund contributions dropped to £124 per year when Curo took over his building, but then increased dramatically to £1,767 when a new roof was needed. "We were only being prepared for the new roof when it was a matter of urgency because two flats upstairs had leaks," he said. "We should have paid over a longer period." Pearson took Curo to a tribunal over the sinking fund increases and lost his case, but now believes there needs to be a change in the law to ensure that landlords prepare leaseholders better for expected works. "Curo have failed us and need to be held to account," he said. "They have not picked up that there was this financial catastrophe coming along." In response, Snee said: "I think sinking funds have been managed as well as we can in today's world with all of the pressures on costs and contracts." He added: "If you've been building a sinking fund up and decoration has taken place, that would have potentially drawn quite a lot out. "Then if you're looking at a roof replacement in four to five years' time, not only are you looking at paying for that you're also starting from zero." The government is working on a new law that would ban the use of leasehold for most new flats and create a new right for leaseholders to request improvements.
