events.title: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
events.summary: "Purchase to sit" signs are popping up in Starbucks stores around China Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there. A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes. Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee. Starbucks stores around the world have also been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers. In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores , after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow. In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers. Starbucks China is now following suit. Ahead of the official announcement on Wednesday, reports of the new seating policy at China's Starbucks stores had been circulating this week - along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores. Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy. "Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit," "There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented. Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying. Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products. Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks. In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain. Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital. In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours". events.title: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout
events.summary: The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks. Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins. China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens. The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday. Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment. "I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China. Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year. The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand. Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment. China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty. Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC. "For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions. While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities. "It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027. Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

events.title: Sundar Pichai explains how a team of AI agents helps him run the company
events.summary: The Google CEO said he uses AI agents to track Google's model development and internal discussions. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sundar Pichai said he uses AI agents to track Google's model development and internal discussions. The bots summarize updates and monitor how Google's computing resources are used. Pichai said humans still make consequential decisions about resource allocation. Even Google's CEO needs help keeping up with Google. On the Sources podcast released Wednesday, Sundar Pichai  described to host Alex Heath how he delegates some of the information-gathering that comes with running the tech giant. “It could easily take me an hour a day to kind of catch up, what's happened in the last 24 hours, right?" Pichai said. "But now I have agents running which summarize and bring that information to me. I can still go deeper, and I do so often." Pichai said that his AI agents give him a way to "understand the model development arc," figure out how Google's computing resources are being used, and follow threads spread across numerous internal chat groups without having to read through every conversation himself. “Similarly, there are agents with telemetry into our compute usage by product area, efficiency, utilization, and giving me inputs and insights, you know," Pichai added. "I think it's made all of us, you know, be better at what we do." That doesn't mean Pichai has handed over the important calls to AI. He said humans — including himself — remain directly involved in consequential decisions about allocating computing resources. Managing agents is becoming a skill in its own right, giving some workers a new set of headaches, from checking the bots' output to preventing them from duplicating work or straying beyond their assignments. Business Insider previously reported that the need to manage agents is making everyone a boss without higher pay. Delegating to bots doesn't necessarily make work easier, either. A Cisco engineering director who manages more than 10 agents told Business Insider that overseeing them involves more task switching and can make work feel more intense without shortening his days. For the Google CEO, however, continuous work is a plus. "So because your agents, they're running in the cloud, they're running 24/7, they have your context, and so they can pick up things where you left off," Pichai said. "It's a continuum there. By the time it's doing that, you would be applying yourself to the next problem and so on." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
events.summary: In a few days the busiest shopping street in Europe will be closed to traffic. The hope is that an unloved and polluted thoroughfare will turn into somewhere that people actually want to spend time I n February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan , announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in. This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe , attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling. Pedestrianisation is one thing; making Oxford Street somewhere anyone actually wants to spend time is another. For weary Londoners and anxious visitors alike, it is a headache in the form of a high street. Its primary associations are crowds, stress, dirt, noise, the tackiest incarnations of consumer capitalism, and crime. At one point during my research I approached a harried police officer in the throng outside Tottenham Court Road tube station and asked if she thought pedestrianisation would be good for Oxford Street, or make her job harder. Both, she said. This is not to say Oxford Street is an empty, dying high street. At the last count, it receives more than 500,000 visitors every day – equivalent to the population of Edinburgh. It seems reasonable to assume that most of London’s 22 million annual foreign visitors set foot on it at some point. The street generates 5% of the capital’s economic output , and lives in the national imagination the way few others do. “When I was 17, London meant Oxford Street,” sang Everything But the Girl, in their 1988 song of the same name: “It was a little world.” And yet, nobody loves Oxford Street. During the course of writing this article, I haven’t met anyone who will even admit to liking it. On a Sunday evening in September, I did something I had always carefully avoided doing before and cycled its full length. Even at the end of the weekend, it was overwhelming – with teenagers careening on rented ebikes and gaudy pedicabs parked in the middle of the pavement, blaring music. The pavements were thick with people, in part because the road was still thick with traffic. On another occasion, I watched a late-middle-aged woman perch awkwardly outside Ikea on a narrow black electricity box, in the absence of anywhere else to rest. For most Londoners, Oxford Street is a necessary evil, to be visited with surgical precision before fleeing the scene: a site of crime, grime and perhaps some Christmas shopping. “Who,” wondered the FT’s architecture critic in 2020, “lingers any longer than they have to in London’s worst thoroughfare?” The grime itself is no joke. In the 1990s, when Oxford Street was known for its huge record shops such as HMV and Virgin Megastore, I remember returning to my south London home on the tube, blowing my nose and seeing a tissue full of jet-black snot. Its narrow streetway and tall buildings on either side create an “urban canyon”, trapping the heavy diesel fumes emanating from its buses and taxis (private car access has been restricted since 1972). In 2014, it was found to have the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. In the same year, the crime had become so bad that the United Arab Emirates warned its citizens to avoid the area for their own safety. Since then it has become better known for its lawbreaking small businesses, where substantial raids have hauled in counterfeit goods and illegal vapes. This decade has seen the rise of mysterious US candy stores and empty souvenir shops that allegedly thrive thanks to tax evasion . Covid and internet shopping hit Oxford Street hard: vacancy levels soared from 4.5% in 2019 to 16.9% by early 2023, and it was often these businesses that filled the gaps. The current Google Street View images of its shopfronts, taken just two years ago, already look like a postcard from the past. That Oxford Street has been struggling hurts the reputation of London as a whole.

events.title: Waitrose opens first new supermarket in eight years in north London
events.summary: Grocer launches Cricklewood store as part of £1bn investment plan, with Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, to follow next month As part of a £1bn investment plan , Waitrose has chosen Cricklewood in north London as the location for its first supermarket in eight years. The upmarket grocer will open the store on Thursday and another supermarket in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester , next month. It also plans four smaller stores next year, including a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge). In 2024, Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, said it planned to open up to four large supermarkets and 100 convenience stores over five years and would also refurbish a number of outlets introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections. Tina Mitchell, the retail director at Waitrose , said: “Our supermarkets provide the ultimate showcase for everything that sets Waitrose apart – from our unmatched quality and industry-leading welfare standards to the expert service of our partners.” This year the company – led since January by the former Tesco executive Tom Denyard - also plans to refurbish 29 stores. After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems which led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. However, the chain is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, which now has a higher share of the grocery market, under some measures, after opening a number of new food-led outlets. Sales at Waitrose rose 4% in the six months to 1 August. However, its underlying operating profit slid by £7m to £103m as it invested in keeping prices down and improving its loyalty scheme. It was also hit by higher energy costs during the summer heat wave. Waitrose’s parent company, the John Lewis Partnership – which is owned by its staff – reported a £98m pre-tax loss in the half-year to 1 August, as sales fell at the department stores despite heavy investment in updating the outlets. The company has been reducing the number of staff it employs directly as it tries to trim costs. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning On Wednesday, the partnership announced it had signed its first company-wide union recognition deal. The collective agreement with Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, comes ahead of new rights of union access in workplaces that come into force at the end of this month. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said: “Usdaw already has members working within the business and this agreement will strengthen that presence and help us in supporting and representing members across the partnership. We now look forward to growing our membership and influence within the partnership and to working with the partnership’s management on finalising the details of how the agreement will work in practice.”

events.title: Flurry of activity for China’s richest ahead of offshore wealth tax deadline
events.summary: Regulations announced in July levy a tax of 20% on dividends and interest gained from offshore trusts. China has set an Oct 22 deadline for rich citizens to pay a new 20% tax on dividends and interest from offshore trusts. The move comes as Beijing faces a fiscal hole and wants more revenue from wealthy people with money in Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo and other hubs. The rules may also target some foreign nationals or residents if their “main economic interests are derived from China”, and analysts say it aims to keep talent and capital in China. Beijing – China is aiming to claw back some of the colossal riches kept overseas by the country’s millionaires and billionaires, who have until Oct 22 to pay new taxes levied by Beijing aimed at filling a growing fiscal hole. The rapid rise of China’s economy in recent decades has produced legions of super-rich – many of who keep their fortunes in trusts across Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo and other locations. However, regulations announced in July levy a tax of 20% on dividends and interest gained from offshore trusts, with a 90-day “transition period” for initial payments concluding on Oct 22. The law has prompted a flurry of activity in recent weeks for China’s wealthiest individuals and families to sort out their financial affairs, analysts say. It comes at an uncertain time for the Chinese economy, as local governments that once relied on land sales for revenue face cash shortages amid a years-long property crisis. Chinese President Xi Jinping has long promoted a narrative that he has rectified huge problems that beset China and the Communist Party during the tenures of his predecessors, such as graft and the unequal distribution of wealth. Nevertheless, Chinese offshore wealth is reported to amount to hundreds of billions of dollars – money Beijing is eager to leverage. China’s fiscal burden will ensure that the enforcement of new overseas taxes will be sustained, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP. Economic challenges will encourage Beijing to expand its taxation of the wealthy, she said, adding that personal income tax will be “increasingly important” as a source of revenue. In 2025, Hong Kong narrowly surpassed Switzerland to become the world’s top host for foreign or cross-border capital , according to a report by the Boston Consulting Group. The sum of US$2.9 trillion (S$3.7 trillion) held in the Asian financial hub was “driven by mainland China flows and a vigorous stock market”, the report said. “With mainland flows representing over 60% of assets under management, Hong Kong is cementing its role as China’s gateway to global markets,” it added. The new measures have also raised questions, including about whose assets are subject to the one-fifth tax. The July 24 announcement by the State Tax Administration notes that individuals who have acquired foreign nationality or residency but whose “main economic interests are derived from China” could be subject to the rules. This stipulation indicates that “obtaining foreign nationality or overseas residency may not, by itself, remove an individual from China’s worldwide taxation regime”, law firm King and Wood wrote in a statement about the new taxes. Some analysts see parallels with Beijing’s recent campaign to prevent local technology from leaving the country, as economic and geopolitical competition with Washington simmers. “This is not only a tax on wealth. It’s much more than that,” Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Asia-Pacific chief economist at Natixis, told AFP. “It’s a way to keep the talent in China,” she added. The new tax policy is aligned with other recent measures imposed by the Chinese authorities, she said, such as the blocked acquisition earlier in 2026 of AI start-up Manus by US tech giant Meta. Wang of Eurasia Group told AFP that the taxes also serve to keep capital within China’s borders, where they can be accessed for funding to spur “technological innovation”. AFP

events.title: DeepSeek raises US$15 billion in challenge to leading US labs
events.summary: Chinese AI DeepSeek has the ability to compete with US AI models at a fraction of the latter’s costs. DeepSeek raised about 100 billion yuan (S$19.13 billion), one of China’s largest fundraisings, as it aims to compete globally with Anthropic and OpenAI. The round drew major backers including CATL and Tencent, and the startup may be preparing for an IPO, Bloomberg News reported. DeepSeek is spending more on AI data centres and open-source models, while its low-cost releases keep pressuring rivals in China and overseas. The Chinese AI pioneer DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan ( S$19.13 billion ) in its latest fundraising round, one of the country’s largest ever and a sign of the start-up’s ambitions to compete globally with the likes of Anthropic PBC and OpenAI. The Hangzhou-based firm boosted its financing target at least twice as it talked with investors, from 50 billion yuan to 80 billion yuan before reaching the final tally, according to people familiar with the matter. Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings were among the biggest investors in the round, said the people, asking not to be named as the details are not public. DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years. The AI upstart triggered a US$1 trillion ( S$1.28 trillion ) meltdown in global markets in 2025 when it showed the ability to compete with Silicon Valley’s leaders at a fraction of the cost of their models, but it has never had the financial resources of the US frontier labs. The latest fundraising shows that imbalance is beginning to moderate, although it still has far less financial firepower than Anthropic and OpenAI, which have each raised more than US$100 billion. Like rival Moonshot , DeepSeek is preparing for an initial public offering that would be an important milestone for Chinese markets, Bloomberg News has reported. DeepSeek has begun to spend more aggressively to build out AI data centres and to develop more open-source models for use in China and abroad. The firm has regularly rolled out high-performance, low-cost models that put pressure on its domestic competitors and gained customers in the US and other overseas markets. In September, for example, it dropped V4.1 Flash, setting off a drop in the share prices of local rivals MiniMax Group and Z.AI. DeepSeek, Tencent and CATL representatives did not respond to e-mailed requests for comment. More broadly, companies from Alibaba Group Holding to ByteDance have introduced low-cost AI services, typically open-sourced so customers can modify them as needed. One widely shared benchmark chart from Artificial Analysis sketched out what has been called the “DeepSeek death zone”, where competitors will struggle to survive if they cannot beat the firm’s performance or they cannot charge lower prices. events.title: Mum and son offered to repay Alan Jones after being 'berated', trial hears
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mother of complainant was caught in 'web of dependency' with Alan Jones, court hears The mother of Complainant A is giving evidence in the Alan Jones trial on Thursday. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The mother of Complainant A defends staying in contact with Alan Jones after her teenage son told her "something sexual" happened. Complainant A, who is now an adult, is alleging Mr Jones kissed him and put his hands on his bottom when he was a 17-year-old boy. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. The mother of a man who has accused Alan Jones of kissing him when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy has defended keeping in contact with the broadcaster, telling a court she was in a "web of dependency" with him. The woman has been cross-examined on day 50 of Mr Jones's criminal trial, in which Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. Mr Jones is accused of kissing a 17-year-old boy, Complainant A, with his tongue and touching his bottom during a visit to his NSW Southern Highlands property. The woman told the court she offered to repay Mr Jones after feeling "berated". ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The NSW Local Court has heard the boy first contacted Mr Jones when he was 13 years old, asking for help for his struggling single mother, and the pair were in regular email contact while Mr Jones helped the family financially. His mother, who cannot be identified to protect the complainant, has told the court her son wrote her a note about 10 days after the alleged assault, telling her "something sexual" had happened during his visit to Mr Jones's farmstay. The court has heard the boy spoke briefly to police about the alleged assault when they turned up at his school in November of that year, but he did not want to make a complaint. Under questioning from the prosecution, the woman agreed she emailed the broadcaster that same month, seeking advice after her son had "messed up" his university application. She said Mr Jones "offered" to contact the university, and did so, but that "it came to no avail anyway" because her son's application was not accepted. "I continued to contact Mr Jones," the woman told the court. "I was in a web of dependency with Mr Jones… so a crisis would come up, and I would ask for advice." The trial has previously been told Mr Jones gave about $100,000 of his own money towards the building of the complainant and his mother's home, and used his connection to the then-head of the Commonwealth Bank to have their home loan reduced by $600,000. Emails handed up to the court show Mr Jones raised concerns with the mother and son about the "enormous cost" of his assistance. "I recall feeling berated about how much it had cost," the woman told the court. "[Complainant A and I] had a conversation to suggest that we repay money, that we go on a payment plan to pay for some of these things." The pair offered to repay Mr Jones, but he declined, the court heard. "I recall [Complainant A] and I saying to each other, 'well, we've offered… could you take us up on the offer rather than continue to berate us about your generosity?'" the woman said. Under cross-examination, Complainant A's mother was asked whether she intended to give Mr Jones the impression that emails from her son's account were coming solely from him, when in fact they were at times partly drafted by her. The mother agreed she did not specify which emails she had contributed to, but asked why anyone would expect a 14-year-old boy to know his mother's mortgage details without her input. Mr Jones's lawyers also asked why she did not produce the note her son allegedly wrote her in the aftermath of the alleged assault when her son made police statements in 2018 or 2024. The woman said she found the note in 2025, in a drawer of "stuff" in her bedroom which she had not previously searched because it was "full of emotion". Mr Jones's counsel Claire O'Neill also asked the woman whether she had "encouraged" her son to make a complaint to police, despite his reluctance to. "Did you tell him you thought it was a good idea?" Ms O'Neill asked. "I told him that I would support him in whatever he did," the woman responded.

events.title: Trump administration seeks Supreme Court approval to build Big Bend wall
events.summary: US federal judge blocked wall’s construction on Texas-Mexico border amid an ongoing legal battle. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume plans to build a border wall through the Big Bend region of West Texas, as part of its anti-immigration policy to strengthen security on the border with Mexico. The Justice Department filed an emergency request on Wednesday asking the court to lift a federal judge’s injunction in a lower court that has halted construction while a lawsuit against the project, brought by an environmental group and other challengers, plays out. list 1 of 3 Landowners in Texas ask court to stop Trump border wall list 2 of 3 Tree nearly as old as US torn down to expand Mexico border wall list 3 of 3 ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections The Department of Homeland Security plans include vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology in and around Big Bend National Park. Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, and, according to opponents of the project who have sued the administration, accounts for about 1 percent of migrant arrests. The lawsuit , filed by plaintiffs including the Center for Biological Diversity and a Big Bend-area river guide, seeks to preserve the landscape, protect a historic church, and challenge the federal government’s waivers of environmental and historical laws to fast-track the $1.7bn project. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an “area of high illegal entry”, requiring additional barriers to control the border. US District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an injunction in El Paso on October 2 halting work “until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws,” she wrote in her order. In a later opinion, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin. The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone’s injunction. The Supreme Court has not yet responded to this appeal. “Even assuming that the secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction,” the Justice Department wrote. In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife.

events.title: Abu Dhabi Finance Week to make half of 2026 sessions private to drive deals
events.summary: Abu Dhabi Finance Week will hold about half of its sessions behind closed doors this year, as organisers seek to encourage more candid discussions among global financial leaders and generate tangible business outcomes. The event to be held from December 7 to 10 is expected to draw more than 40,000 attendees, including 8,000 senior executives, with financial leaders representing about $70 trillion in assets under management. Chris Hughes, editor-in-chief of ADFW, said private meetings enable senior executives to exchange information more openly than on public stages, potentially influencing investment decisions and corporate strategies. "I find that when they are in the private rooms there's a little bit more openness, a little bit more dialogue," he told ADGM's Global Media Forum on Tuesday. "It's not just monologue, it's dialogue," he added, which is physically represented by attendees and speakers alike being seated face-to-face rather than shoulder-to-shoulder. The shift towards invitation-only discussions, he said, reflects growing demand among executives for meetings that deliver practical outcomes rather than simply provide networking opportunities or public exposure. ADFW recorded 82 memorandums of understanding and partnerships in 2025, according to the organiser, Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM, which was almost double the 44 agreements and announcements in 2024. The agreements involved major financial institutions and businesses including BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, Mubadala, Mastercard and Swiss Re. While the figures demonstrate the event's growing role as a platform for forging partnerships, ADGM has not disclosed how many resulted directly from private meetings or their combined monetary value. From dialogue to deals Private meetings could allow investors, regulators and executives to discuss commercially sensitive issues, identify investment opportunities and advance potential transactions without the scrutiny of a public audience. Mr Hughes referred to a closed-door leadership meeting involving the International Monetary Fund during last year's ADFW, attended by chief executives of major financial institutions. He recalled watching senior executives take handwritten notes throughout the discussions, which suggested that information exchanged in such settings could influence decisions within large organisations that aren't directly seen, but have major implications. "That extra grain of information they didn't usually have, that can change the economy of... a city or town, or company, or country, just by a tiny little 0.1 degree." The growing emphasis on private engagement comes as Abu Dhabi attracts more international financial institutions. Fourteen global financial firms managing more than $5 trillion announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM during the first half of this year, according to figures disclosed by ADGM chairman Ahmed Al Zaabi this week. ADFW is also expected to host more than 80 events and 400 content sessions this year, compared with more than 70 events and 350 sessions in 2025, according to organisers' projections. The preparations come amid regional uncertainty as the Iran war continues to disrupt business activity, energy markets and travel across the Middle East. Saudi Arabia this week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26 to 29 in Riyadh, until 2027, after a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The attacks, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, have raised security concerns among international executives and investors. Asked about contingency plans for ADFW amid the regional tension, Mr Hughes expressed confidence in Abu Dhabi's security and preparations to welcome international delegates in December.

events.title: No direct exposure to Indonesia fires, says Olam Group
events.summary: The company says it manages upstream environmental risks through monitoring, supplier engagement and a responsible sourcing framework. Olam Group said it has no direct exposure to Indonesia’s forest and peatland fires because it does not own or run palm plantations or concessions there. The group said Olam Agri is mainly a trader and now no longer a subsidiary after its sale to a Saudi fund in April 2026. Olam said it sees no material impact, no formal regulatory inquiry, and expects no major operational, financial, legal, regulatory or reputational harm. SINGAPORE – Neither Olam Group nor Olam Agri owns or operates oil palm plantations or concessions in Indonesia, and therefore has no direct operational exposure to recent forest and peatland fires , the agri group said on Oct 21. The group was responding to queries from the Singapore Exchange Regulation on whether its activities may have contributed to transboundary haze in the region. The mainboard-listed group also pointed out that Olam Agri had ceased to be a subsidiary of the group in April 2026 following its sale to a Saudi fund. Although about 70% of Olam Agri’s global palm oil sourcing volume comes from Indonesia, the company operates mainly as an intermediary trader, sourcing from third-party refineries, said Olam Group. Olam Agri does not own or operate oil palm plantations, mills, refineries or other palm oil processing facilities in the country. Responsibility for directly preventing or suppressing fires and managing land rests with upstream landowners and plantation operators, the group said. Nevertheless, Olam Agri manages upstream environmental risks through monitoring, supplier engagement and a responsible sourcing framework. The group said it was not aware of any material impact on Olam Agri’s palm oil sourcing operations arising from the recent fires. The group also said it was not aware of any formal regulatory inquiries, notices or notifications relating to the recent fires. As part of its monitoring process, Olam Group said it had reviewed recent fire alerts, stakeholder reports and media coverage concerning fires in Indonesia. “Mills and corporate groups referenced in external reports have been screened against Olam Agri’s supply chain and relevant suppliers and affiliated groups have been engaged for clarification where appropriate,” the group said. Several cases have since been clarified by the companies concerned, while others remain under internal assessment or are awaiting further information from suppliers and affiliated groups, it added. It does not expect matters relating to the fires to have any material operational, financial, legal, regulatory or reputational impact on the group.

events.title: Sovereign wealth funds' China and Hong Kong investments surge 190% after a bruising slump
events.summary: Sovereign wealth funds are pouring billions of dollars back into China after a sharp investment slump. Investments by sovereign wealth funds into mainland China and Hong Kong surged to $14.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up nearly 190% from the $4.9 billion invested throughout 2025. Sovereign wealth funds are pouring billions of dollars back into mainland China and Hong Kong, reversing a sharp investment slump, with Middle Eastern investors leading the charge. Investments into mainland China and Hong Kong surged to $14.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, surging 190% compared with the funds' investments through the entire 2025, according to data provided to CNBC by Singapore-based consultancy Global SWF. That's in stark contrast to a 54% plunge in 2025 from the prior year as geopolitical tensions and concerns over China's economic outlook weighed on investor sentiment. The resurgence this year has been driven largely by Middle Eastern sovereign investors, with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund alone accounting for $6 billion of the inflows, followed by Abu Dhabi Investment Authority's $2.5 billion, data from Global SWF showed. Abu Dhabi's Mubadala and Qatar Investment Authority have invested $800 million and $600 million, respectively. Together, the four Gulf funds accounted for nearly 70% of sovereign investments into China and Hong Kong during the period, underscoring the growing role of Middle Eastern capital in the region. Renewed interest in China comes as sovereign investors increasingly look beyond geopolitical tensions to capitalize on opportunities in Chinese technology, biotechnology, consumer businesses and advanced manufacturing. "I think China has gone from 'China is not investable’ to ‘is China investable?’ to today, the most common question I get is: ‘are we missing out?'" said Jenny Lee, senior managing partner at investment management firm Granite Asia. Lee said China's established strengths in manufacturing and biotechnology could give it an advantage as AI development increasingly expands beyond frontier models into industry-specific applications, including robotics and drug discovery. China's extensive network of factories and research laboratories provides access to real-world data that could become increasingly valuable in developing these applications, she added. For Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala, Asia in general has become an increasingly important destination as the sovereign investor seeks to diversify its portfolio and deepen exposure to long-term growth opportunities. Andrew Wang, who leads consumer division for private equity at Mubadala, said the firm sees compelling opportunities in China, citing attractive valuations and the country's vast consumer market as the fund continues to expand its presence in Asia. "Valuations are lower than they've been in years. I think this will be a really good vintage for investors in China," Wang told CNBC. He said China was the fund's top priority for consumer investments in Asia, pointing to the potential for household consumption to expand and the growing competitiveness of Chinese brands. Chinese companies were increasingly moving beyond their reputation for producing inexpensive goods toward higher-value products, Wang said, as homegrown brands demonstrate stronger innovation and competitiveness globally. Mubadala announced a minority investment in China's Luckin Coffee in September, as part of a roughly $1 billion deal alongside Centurium Capital. Other big funds have also shown interest this year. Qatar Investment Authority and Norway's sovereign wealth fund participated in Alibaba's $10.2 billion share offering in August, while Singapore's Temasek is identifying opportunities in China, particularly in biotechnology, domestic consumer brands and AI-related hardware. "China continues to be interesting," said Rohit Sipahimalani, Temasek's chief investment officer, at the Milken Summit in Singapore recently. "Biotech in particular [is] a very exciting area out there which we're investing in. Local consumer brands could really be important," he said. Sipahimalani also pointed to China's growing competitiveness across the AI hardware supply chain, predicting that Chinese manufacturers could increasingly challenge established global players. Temasek was among the cornerstone investors in optical-components manufacturer Zhongji Innolight's multibillion-dollar initial public offering in July. Pandu Sjahrir, chief investment officer at Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara, told CNBC that the fund was also looking to expand its cooperation with China beyond its existing partnerships in nickel processing and battery manufacturing, with growing interest in artificial intelligence, robotics, healthcare and energy efficiency. The Indonesian sovereign investor sees opportunities to build on its energy resources to develop AI-related digital infrastructure and downstream industries.

events.title: Frasers Centrepoint Trust posts 2.6% higher second-half DPU to hit new full-year record payout
events.summary: The increases in revenue and net property income were driven by contributions from Northpoint City South Wing as well as higher passing rents across most malls. Frasers Centrepoint Trust reported a record full-year DPU of $0.1235, after second-half DPU rose 2.6% to $0.06214. Distributable income, revenue and net property income also grew. Growth was driven by Northpoint City South Wing, bought in May 2025, and higher rents at most malls. CEO Richard Ng said FY2026 was supported by operating strength, capital recycling and AEI. FCT cut leverage to 38.7% and lowered borrowing costs to 3.2%. It plans more work at Nex and Causeway Point, while Singapore suburban retail stays resilient. SINGAPORE – Frasers Centrepoint Trust (FCT) posted on Oct 22 a distribution per unit (DPU) of $0.06214 for the second half ended Sept 30, up 2.6% from $0.06059 in the previous corresponding period. This brought full-year DPU to $0.1235, a record high. Distributable income for H2 rose 3.3% to $127.2 million, from $123.1 million in the same period the year before . Revenue was up 8.7% at $223 million for the half-year, from $205.2 million before. Net property income rose 11.5% to $160.9 million for the half-year period, from $144.3 million in the same period the year before. The increases in revenue and net property income were driven by contributions from Northpoint City South Wing, which was acquired in May 2025 , as well as higher passing rents across most malls. For the full year, distributable income rose 8.2% year-on-year to $252.2 million. Revenue increased 14.2% year on year to $444.9 million, while net property income grew 15.7% year on year to $321.7 million. Richard Ng, CEO of FCT’s manager, said the trust’s FY2026 performance was underpinned by healthy operating metrics, its capital recycling strategy and asset enhancement initiatives (AEI). He said the $467 million divestment of White Sands created debt headroom for FCT to re-invest part of the proceeds in the joint development of the Bayshore Drive site, providing a new growth driver and potential future acquisition opportunity. The trust also completed enhancement works at Hougang Mall in September. The first phase of AEI at Nex is scheduled for completion by end-2026. Enhancement works at Causeway Point are expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027. Aggregate leverage fell to 38.7% as at Sept 30, from 40.4% as at June 30. Gearing would stand at 36.8% after repaying borrowings with divestment proceeds from White Sands after the close of the financial year. Group short-term borrowings fell to $111 million from $404 million. The average cost of borrowing was 3.1% in Q4 FY2026, with a full-year cost at 3.2% compared with 3.8% in FY2025. The interest coverage ratio improved to 4.37 times as at end-September. The manager expects Singapore’s suburban retail market to remain resilient, where positive demand and supply dynamics underpin organic DPU growth through healthy rental reversions and high committed occupancy. FCT’s retail portfolio recorded committed occupancy of 99.7% as at end-September, while rental reversions averaged 6.6% for FY2026. Shopper traffic and tenants’ sales rose 1.8% and 1.3% year on year, respectively. FCT’s second-half distribution will be paid on Nov 27, after books closure on Oct 30. Units of FCT ended on Oct 21 at 1% or $0.02 higher at $2.06. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Bank of Korea holds rates after President Lee calls for boosting housing supply
events.summary: Inflation has stayed at or above the BOK's 2% target for 13 months. Price growth in Asia's fourth-largest economy came in at 2.9% in September. South Korea's central bank expectedly kept its policy rate steady at 3% on Thursday, after two straight hikes, with analysts pointing that it does not signal a change in policy stance as inflation stays elevated. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the Bank of Korea to hold rates, and the decision comes after President Lee Jae Myung reportedly called for an "all out effort" to boost housing supply. The BOK in its statement said it opted to hold rates as it assesses the effects of the two prior rate hikes, and looks at "developments in both domestic and external risk factors," citing increasing uncertainties around the Middle East conflict and monetary and fiscal policies of major economies. Last week, BOK Governor Shin Hyun Song said at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings that the central bank will keep monetary policy restrictive until it's confident that inflation was heading back to target. "Inflation has really picked up, both from the cost-push and the demand-pull," Shin said. Inflation in Asia's fourth-largest economy came in at 2.9% in September, staying at or above the BOK's 2% target for 13 months. As President Lee pushes for increasing the housing supply, the BOK on Thursday flagged that "housing-related loans continued to increase and the pace of increase in housing prices in Seoul and its surrounding areas accelerated again." The Kospi was trading 1.23% lower, while the won strengthened marginally against the dollar to trade at 1,326.1. Given a strong economy and persistent inflation, a pause does not mean the end of the tightening cycle, according to Gareth Leather, senior Asia economist at Capital Economics. Leather foresees one more hike at BOK's meeting next month. South Korea's growth has been largely supported by exports of semiconductors as demand for chips to power the AI boom continues. Exports in September skyrocketed at a record 83.7% year on year, with semiconductor shipments surging 263% compared to the same period last year. The IMF has projected the country's growth at 3.3% for the whole of 2026. GDP growth for the country came in at 3.8% and 3.7% for the first and second quarters respectively, both times beating expectations. — CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

events.title: Tesla aims to sell Cybercab robotaxis by end of 2026 despite federal probe
events.summary: The gold, two-seater car features butterfly doors and drive themselves without any steering wheel, pedals or mirrors. Tesla plans to sell Cybercab robotaxis by the end of 2026, with vice-president Lars Moravy saying they will be the first fully designed autonomous vehicles for customers. The Cybercab has no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, and Tesla is starting small in Austin before scaling up and expanding the service to Dallas in November. The US safety agency NHTSA is probing whether the Cybercab meets federal rules, and Tesla must respond by Oct 30 as it seeks regulatory approval. SAN FRANCISCO – Tesla is aiming to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of 2026, its engineering chief said on Oct 21, even as the US auto safety agency probes the vehicles that come without manual controls which federal regulations typically require. The gold, two-seaters – that come with butterfly doors and drive themselves without any steering wheel, pedals or mirrors – are one of the key bets CEO Elon Musk has made in his ambition of turning the EV maker into an AI and robotics company. “As Tesla grows, we’ll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercabs will be the first,” Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice-president of vehicle engineering, told analysts after reporting third-quarter results. “We’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026,” he said. “As we start small this year, and we learn... about delivery and ownership and fleet management of autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that.” After years of missed promises by Musk, Tesla started offering paid rides on a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin, Texas, early in September amid a frenzy of fans and social ​media influencers. Just hours later, the ‌National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said it opened an investigation into Cybercabs to assess how Tesla determined the cars comply with federal vehicle-safety regulations. Those regulations, written decades ago for human-driven vehicles, require manual controls and limit commercial deployment of vehicles that are designed without them. Unlike most other countries, where new vehicle models and technology need regulatory clearance ahead of launch, carmakers in the US can deploy them on the public roads by self-certifying ​that they meet federal standards. The agency in September said it was looking into the basis of Tesla’s certification of the Cybercab and the extent to which the company determined that certain standards were not applicable to the vehicle. Tesla has until Oct 30 to respond to the agency. NHTSA has proposed changes to federal safety standards to allow autonomous vehicles that are designed without human controls. Until those changes are complete, existing standards remain in force, ​NHTSA has said. “I think the key thing which we are trying to make sure is that we have all the regulatory approvals where we can start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them,” Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI, ‌said on the call. That aside, “scaling would not be that much of a challenge”, he said, adding that the Cybercab was “one of the easiest products” to scale in terms of manufacturing. The Cybercab is part of Tesla’s robotaxi network that includes autonomous Model Ys, some with human safety monitors. Over time, Tesla intends to make the Cybercab the main driverless vehicle model operating within a larger robotaxi network. Tesla plans to expand the Cybercab service to Dallas in November, Elluswamy said. The vehicle, however, will mainly be Tesla owned and used for its ride-hailing service, Musk said. REUTERS

events.title: Tigray resumes daily life amid fears of wider war
events.summary: Mekelle’s reopening offers little relief as instability and economic hardship persist. Mekelle, Ethiopia- In Mekelle, shops are reopening, and banks are resuming services, but residents remain anxious about what comes next. Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters retook the Tigray regional capital on October 4, as renewed fighting raised fears that the region’s fragile recovery could be derailed once again. Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, is still recovering from the 2020–2022 war between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the region’s dominant political movement. For residents, the return of fighting has brought new uncertainty over jobs, education, security and the future. Daily life resumes, but hardship remains. Businesses and financial services are gradually reopening in Mekelle, but many households are struggling to afford necessities. Delayed salaries have left public employees struggling to cover food, rent and school costs, while years of conflict have depleted family savings. “Things may be reopening, but that does not mean our problems are over. We still have expenses every day, and without our salaries, it is difficult to know how we will manage,” said Gebregziabher, a public servant in Mekelle. The funding crisis has affected the wider public sector. In March, Tigray’s interim administration said it could no longer cover monthly salaries for about 137,000 civil servants because expected federal budget transfers had not arrived. In April, the regional finance bureau reported an 8.5-billion-birr (about $52,000) funding shortfall affecting salary payments and development projects. For many residents, the reopening of businesses offers only a partial return to normality. Without reliable incomes and greater security, everyday expenses remain difficult to manage. For students in Tigray, renewed fighting has revived fears of another interruption to their education. Many already lost valuable study time during the previous war and worry about falling further behind. In Adigrat, Shewit, a grade 10 student, said uncertainty about classes and security had left him worried about his future. “I have already lost so much time because of the war. I am afraid that if our education is disrupted again, I will lose another year and fall further behind,” he said. Some university students have left Tigray for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, to seek transfers to other public universities. The Ministry of Education announced temporary placements at universities elsewhere in the country for students enrolled at institutions in Tigray. More than 5,000 returning students had applied by September 17–18, according to reporting on the ministry’s programme. Abel, a third-year student at Axum University, travelled to Addis Ababa to request a transfer. “I didn’t want to leave, but I also can’t keep putting my education on hold. I came to Addis to see if I can transfer to another university and continue my studies. I just want to finish what I started,” he said. For students who have already lost years to conflict, the uncertainty means more than interrupted classes. It threatens to delay graduation and make an already difficult path to employment even harder. Border communities fear a wider conflict Near the Eritrean border, military movements and conflicting accounts of troop deployments have heightened fears that the fighting could spread beyond Tigray. On October 8, The Associated Press reported claims by a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government that Eritrean troops had entered Adigrat earlier that week and Idaga Hamus the following day. The AP said it could not independently verify those accounts. The conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED separately reported Eritrean troops crossing the border at Zalambessa. On October 13, Reuters reported that Ethiopian government forces had advanced into Zalambessa, citing people in contact with residents and other sources. The report said it remained unclear whether Eritrean troops or Tigrayan opposition fighters were still present in the town. The differing accounts underscored the difficulty of establishing control of individual towns as the fighting shifted. The developments have unfolded amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara. On October 8, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, accused Eritrea of sending troops as far as 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopian territory in several areas of Tigray and appealed to the United Nations Security Council to respond. Eritrea has denied invading Ethiopian territory. Its government said Ethiopia’s accusations amounted to a declaration of war and called on the Security Council to take action against Ethiopia. The competing claims have raised fears that renewed fighting in Tigray could lead to a direct confrontation between the two neighbours.

events.title: Pumped hydro project scrapped after developer deems it unviable
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Oven Mountain pumped hydro scheme abandoned by Alinta Energy Plans for a pumped hydro project in northern NSW have been scrapped. ( Supplied: Snowy Hydro ) Alinta Energy has withdrawn plans to build a $1.8 billion pumped hydro energy storage project in northern NSW. The decision comes after Origin Energy scrapped its proposed 870 megawatt Skye Ridge Wind Farm near Walcha earlier this month. Energy experts warn construction costs are rising as battery storage prices plunge, leading to once-critical stored hydro projects becoming unviable. Another large-scale renewable energy project has been scrapped, with plans for a $1.8 billion pumped hydro project in northern NSW withdrawn by the developer. The 900 megawatt Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro Energy Storage scheme was one of the largest projects within the Armidale Renewable Energy Zone. An Alinta Energy spokesperson said in a statement that "economic and timing challenges on key elements including a critical transmission line" made the project unviable. It is the second state significant renewable energy project to fail this month, after Origin Energy scrapped the proposed 870MW Skye Ridge Wind Farm near Walcha in northern NSW. Listed for consideration as a state significant development, the project was progressing through assessment phases with NSW Planning. A diagram of the proposed Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro project. ( Supplied: Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro Energy Storage Project ) "We sincerely thank traditional owners, landholders, MPs and council representatives, suppliers, key agencies and many other key stakeholders who have contributed their time, knowledge and feedback throughout the development process." A pumped hydro energy storage system works by moving water between two dams, with one at the top of a hill and another at the bottom, through a turbine. Energy stored during the day is then released during peak electricity usage at night to maximise profit. Pumped hydro moves water through a turbine. ( Supplied: Australian Renewable Energy Agency ) The Oven Mountain project was planned for a site near Georges Junction at the rural hamlet of Carrai, 60 kilometres south-east of Armidale and 75 kilometres north-west of Kempsey. When it was first announced, it was identified as being critical to state infrastructure. Armidale Shire Mayor Sam Coupland said the decision to scrap the project had left him in shock, with the council only finding out about the decision this morning. Cr Coupland questioned whether state and federal planning regulations had become too onerous. Sam Coupland says he was shocked to learn about the project's cancellation. ( ABC News: James Paras ) "It seems there are too many environmental hoops to jump through," he said. "That seems to be killing important projects, whether it's this, other renewable energy projects [or] inland rail, take your pick. "There just seems to be too many hurdles to get through that are imposing a cost that makes these things unviable." Cr Coupland said the council had worked with developer Alinta Energy for several years to plan roadworks to support the project. "That Kempsey-to-Armidale Road restoration project is the biggest engineering undertaken by any council ever in NSW," he said. Michael Kemp says the Oven Mountain project cancellation is a poor economic result for the community. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds ) The state member for the coastal electorate of Oxley, Michael Kemp, said the decision was a "poor result for the community". "It's a loss for the community on the mid north coast," he said. "This project would have provided significant trades jobs, not only during the construction, but ongoing." The site location is in the steep, forested country of the Great Dividing Range and home to Thunggutti Indigenous people. Arthur Bain says reaction to the project cancellation will be mixed. ( Supplied ) Kempsey deputy mayor and Thunggutti Local Aboriginal Land Council chief executive Arthur Bain said there would be mixed feelings about the loss of the project. "If we think about the site of Oven Mountain, it's perfect for pumped hydro because it is very steep gorge country and it's got the natural falls to generate the electricity," he said. "On the other hand, its location also makes it unviable economically because it is so isolated." Cr Bain said a previous hydro project proposed for the site failed in the 1980s. "You've really got to go out there and put your boots on the ground and see what that country was like. [It's hard] to imagine just getting machinery out there," he said.

events.title: What is the FDLR, and why does its anti-Tutsi ideology endure?
events.summary: Four former FDLR officers reveal how its anti-Tutsi ideology took root and endured in Africa. Musanze, Rwanda – The Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) was built on an ideology that cast the Tutsi as enemies, according to four of its former senior officers, who say they were taught to hate them long before the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi ethnic group. “In our history and ideology, Tutsis are referred to as ‘snakes’,” said Anastase Munyaneza, a former FDLR major general. “The analogy is that if a snake bites you, it injects poison and you die. Therefore, it is better to kill the snake before it bites you.” The former officers say such ideas were reinforced through Rwanda’s political and military institutions before the 1994 genocide and persisted among those who fled into neighbouring Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), after the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) took control of Rwanda in July 1994. More than three decades later, the FDLR remains a source of regional security concerns, with its presence in eastern DRC a major point of contention between Kigali and Kinshasa. Al Jazeera met the four former officers, who defected from the FDLR, returned to Rwanda and underwent rehabilitation at the Mutobo demobilisation centre. Their accounts offer an insight into the origins of the group’s ideology, its development in exile, and the networks that have helped it survive. The roots of the anti-Tutsi ideology described by the former officers stretch back decades, to a period when ethnic identities became increasingly politicised and institutionalised in Rwanda. In November 1959, a Hutu uprising helped bring about the overthrow of Rwanda’s monarchy. The period was also marked by violent attacks on Tutsis, the killing of hundreds and the forced exile of thousands to neighbouring countries. Before colonial rule, Hutu and Tutsi identities were shaped by social, political and economic relationships. Under Belgian rule, these distinctions were increasingly formalised. In the early 1930s, the colonial administration introduced compulsory identity cards classifying Rwandans as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, reinforcing distinctions that became increasingly rigid. By independence in 1962, about 120,000 people, mostly Tutsi, had fled the country. Exiles in Tanzania and Zaire who sought to return staged attacks between 1962 and 1967. According to the United Nations, each incident was followed by retaliatory killings of large numbers of Tutsi civilians in Rwanda, prompting further waves of refugees. By the end of the 1980s, about 480,000 Rwandans were refugees. President Juvenal Habyarimana argued that population pressures and limited economic opportunities made it difficult to accommodate large numbers of returning Tutsi refugees. In 1988, exiles in Uganda founded the RPF to secure their repatriation, according to the UN. Lieutenant Colonel Idrissa Bizimana said the exiles who launched attacks against Rwanda were branded “Inyenzi”, meaning cockroaches. “When the RPF attacked in 1990, we were told that the same Inyenzi had attacked the country. We grew up being taught to hate them,” he said. Bizimana said they were also taught at school that the Tutsis had come from Ethiopia and had “ruled through hatred for 400 years”. The former officers say these narratives were carried into the military, where they shaped how soldiers were taught to view Tutsis and their place in Rwandan society. Major-General Munyaneza said the Tutsis were rarely found in the army because they were not welcome. “In the army, we were taught that the Tutsi were our enemy,” he said. He recalled that soldiers had to seek permission to marry and present their fiancees for approval. If a woman was Tutsi, permission would be denied. The justification, he said, was that a soldier’s in-laws might visit their daughter in the barracks, potentially gaining access to sensitive military information and “passing it on to the enemy”. The former officers say the ideology they encountered in the military was put into practice during the genocide against the Tutsis in 1994. Munyaneza said soldiers trained members of the Interahamwe militia, which included men who had retired from, deserted, or been dismissed from the army. The Interahamwe, the youth militia of the then-ruling National Revolutionary Movement for Development (MRND) party, participated in the massacres alongside the Presidential Guard and the army, according to the UN tribunal for Rwanda. Bizimana said members of his battalion hated the Tutsis, and took part in the killings. “During the genocide against the Tutsi, the battalion was actively involved in the genocide in the area where it was deployed,” he said. The killings began after a plane carrying Rwandan President Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira was shot down over Kigali on April 6, 1994. The incident triggered approximately 100 days of systematic mass killings, according to the UN.

events.title: Southeast Asia is hungry for AI — and the money isn't just in subscriptions
events.summary: Southeast Asia's generative AI adoption has reached 243 million users in less than three years, according to Google, Temasek and Bain & Company. Only a small fraction of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, even as adoption accelerates. Businesses have generated AI commercial value through applications ranging from e-commerce to digital advertising, Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC. Southeast Asia is embracing artificial intelligence at a rapid pace. But the business of making money from AI is about more than getting consumers to pay for it. Generative AI adoption in the region has reached around 243 million people in less than three years, according to the annual e-Conomy SEA report released Wednesday by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company. That is equivalent to 58% of the working population, with adoption occurring four times faster than the uptake of mobile internet. Yet only 1% to 2% of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, highlighting a gap between widespread adoption and direct consumer spending. Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC in an interview that businesses have found other ways to generate AI's commercial value from online shopping to digital advertising. Companies have been using AI to improve e-commerce conversion rates and handle routine customer inquiries, allowing employees to focus on other tasks, he added. Consumers may also be paying indirectly for AI when purchasing products developed using the technology. The findings come as Southeast Asia's digital economy is projected to grow 17% to $368 billion in gross merchandise value this year, with the market expected to exceed $1 trillion by 2035, according to the report. Hoppe also pointed to another factor driving the region's enthusiasm for AI: its willingness to embrace new technologies as consumers have shown what he described as "pragmatic optimism" toward AI, embracing the technology for its practical benefits. The region has historically ranked among the most active users of major digital platforms on a per-capita basis. "They're very experimental," Hoppe said, describing consumers' openness to new tools and services. He also added that in terms of individual markets, Singapore is among Southeast Asia's early leaders in AI adoption. That openness is extending to more autonomous uses of AI, with 75% of users willing to let AI agents find the best prices and complete purchases on their behalf. The report shows that confidence is also growing, with 62% of respondents saying they trust AI tools more than they did a year ago. Despite the rapid adoption, people in Southeast Asia still use AI far less than those in the U.S., with usage per person at just 10% of U.S. levels. For businesses, however, the potential returns are becoming more tangible. About 69% of shoppers use AI to compare complex purchases such as electronics, while early case studies show AI helping businesses boost conversion rates by 10% year on year and increase the average amount customers spend per order by as much as 75%. An example is Shopee, a Southeast Asian e-commerce platform, which now handles approximately 80% of customer queries through AI chatbots, helping cut its cost per customer contact by 30% year on year. In online media, Hoppe pointed to a "significant uplift" in advertising click-through rates and conversions through AI-powered advertising and improved targeting. But the benefits extend beyond online shopping. AI is helping travelers plan trips, making digital advertising more effective and enabling voice-assisted bookings for ride-hailing and food delivery services. Southeast Asia's online travel market is projected to grow 10% to $59 billion in gross merchandise value this year. Online media revenue, including digital advertising and streaming, is expected to rise 22% to $44 billion, while ride-hailing and food delivery are forecast to grow 15% to $40 billion in gross merchandise value, according to the report.

events.title: 'Musk' director Alex Gibney isn't afraid to make powerful enemies
events.summary: Director Alex Gibney's Elon Musk documentary, "Musk," is in theaters now. Jabin Botsford/Getty Images From Scientology to disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes, documentarian Alex Gibney has never met a subject too big or too controversial to tackle. Then came Elon Musk. When Gibney was approached with the idea to do a documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX CEO in 2022, his plan was straightforward: Tell the story of how Musk used his businesses to become one of the most powerful figures in the world. But when he was ready to deliver a two-hour feature film on Musk two years later, HBO issued him a directive a filmmaker rarely hears: Make it longer. It was 2024, and the breadth of Musk's influence had expanded into the political sphere. With Gibney's subject helping President Donald Trump campaign for a second term, then later spearheading the second Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency , Gibney's story had expanded. His documentary would need to, too. Elon Musk. Finn Gomez/Getty Images The result is "Musk," an incisive, nearly four-hour documentary that chronicles the personal, professional, and political life of the richest man in the world. From his controversial acquisition of Twitter, which he renamed X; to his relationships with the mothers of his children; to the accidents tied to Tesla's self-driving feature, Gibney's film is a comprehensive look at the scope of Musk's power and influence in the 21st century. Gibney even found a clever workaround for featuring Musk in the doc after he declined to be interviewed. Playing on Musk's belief that we are all living in a simulation , the director used AI to craft an avatar of Musk, who speaks in quotes amalgamated from his past interviews. Business Insider's " Director's Chair " series features career-spanning interviews with the people helming Hollywood's biggest movies and TV series. Read more stories here . Of course, a man as powerful and outspoken as Musk has already voiced his displeasure with someone else controlling his narrative. After the movie's world premiere at the Venice Film Festival in September, Musk threatened to sue Gibney's production company for defamation. Musk has also bashed the movie on X , stating: "Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don't even know me (but still have an axe to grind). He has ZERO integrity. Horrible human." Hearing from angry subjects is nothing new for Gibney, who was the subject of the Church of Scientiology's full-page newspaper ads decrying his work over 10 years ago tied to the premiere of his documentary "Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief." "With Elon Musk — and he's not unique in this, but he specializes in it — he begins tweeting horrible things about people and the next thing you know, this army of followers and bots starts to gin up the rage matrix," Gibney told Business Insider. Not that he's rattled yet. With decades of documentaries speaking truth to power under his belt, Gibney has developed thick skin and some top-secret harassment survival strategies. "Let's just say I've taken some precautions," he said. For the latest interview in Business Insider's Director's Chair series, Gibney talks about creating an AI Musk, being followed by Scientologists, and his nerve-racking experience in a self-driving Tesla. On creating an AI Musk avatar and making the movie longer Business Insider: You thought you had finished this movie in 2024. Was it daunting to go back down the Elon Musk rabbit hole when HBO asked you to? Alex Gibney: Yeah, it was daunting. We had to renegotiate the budget and all sorts of other stuff. But I got why HBO wanted that. And when Musk hitched his wagon to Trump, it was clear: This is big. I started out making a film about 21st century power, which in this case involved economic power but also tech power. Now, add to that political power, and suddenly it's a really big story. Was AI Musk in the original movie?  The idea of it was. We had put in a placeholder for it, but we were also anticipating that maybe we might get an interview with him at some point. It was kind of an epiphany to do it this way. It came out of past experience: What's the workaround for somebody who won't or can't talk to you? In "Client 9" and "Zero Days," we came up with workarounds that fit those stories. The key here was to find a workaround that would fit this story. That's how we ultimately came up with the idea of the avatar. Did it unlock anything in you regarding using AI tools in your work in the future? I think it will depend on the project. AI has become a kind of suitcase term for everything from Siri to AGI. In this instance, this was a human effort using AI tools, which revolved mostly around sync; in other words, making the lips and the body sort of move with the voice. But there was also designing the room, what he was going to wear, the gamer chair. The further we pushed it and the more interested we got in AI with the company we used, Makemake A.I., this idea of memes and looking at his own image, that's where we came up with certain scenes where you see the back of his head and he's watching himself. Those were things that we improvised on. Tesla CEO Elon Musk attending the start of the production at Tesla's "Gigafactory" on March 22, 2022 in Berlin. PATRICK PLEUL/POOL/AFP/Getty Images On the qualities Musk and Elizabeth Holmes share and Tesla's image I couldn't help but think about your Elizabeth Holmes doc, "The Inventor," when watching "Musk." The "fake it 'til you make it" ethos that's baked into Silicon Valley, has that been fascinating to observe? Both Holmes and Musk are founders who are amazing salespeople hoping that what they bet on takes off.  I think there is a similarity with Elizabeth Holmes. What was rattling around in my head through this was confidence. Musk, like Holmes, was able, through force of confidence, to convince people of things that they knew not to be true. That became a superpower. The big difference between Tesla and SpaceX and Elizabeth Holmes is that those are real products. The Tesla S is a great car. These reusable rockets are extraordinary, and we show the magnificence of that in the film. Not to take anything away from him or those companies, but there's also the bullshit factor. The idea of going to Mars and the promises. And you can see how they repeat themselves and get bigger and bigger. Oh, yeah, full self-driving!
