events.title: The U.S. market has never been more focused on one single bet—but AI’s payoff will likely take decades
events.summary: Americans have placed an unprecedented bet on the transformative power of artificial intelligence. The past 50 years of economic history suggests it won’t pay off, at least not on a timetable the market expects. Not since the Gilded Age—when, in 1885, railroad stocks accounted for more than 80% of active trading on the New York Stock Exchange—has the U.S. economy wagered so much on a single theme. When that bubble burst in the Panic of 1893, a third of railroads went bust, more than 500 banks failed, and the economy plunged into a four-year depression. Today’s frantic AI buildout may be on a similar trajectory. AI-related capital spending has surged to about 2% of U.S. GDP , from near zero five years ago. But this time, the AI wager is concentrated in far fewer companies than the railway mania ever was. In January, the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis reported that investments in information processing equipment, software, research and development, and data centers—four investment categories economists consider the closest proxies for AI investment—accounted for 39% of U.S. economic growth in the first three quarters of 2025, higher than the 28% those activities contributed in 2000, the peak of the dot-com boom. Pantheon Macroeconomics calculates that without AI spending, U.S. corporate investment in equipment was negative last year. Consumption, too, is heavily dependent on AI. The top 20% of income earners now account for approximately 60% of all U.S. consumer spending , according to Moody’s Analytics. The source of their wealth? The AI stock rally. One theme, every market AI has become the dominant theme across all segments of U.S. capital markets. In equities, the “Magnificent Seven”— Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , Tesla—boast a combined $25 trillion in market capitalization. That’s 35% of the value of the S&P 500 and the highest concentration in a handful of stocks since just before the crash of 1929. Separately, research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City shows that AI-related companies’ share of investment-grade bond issuance increased from 2% in 2023 to 10% in 2026 , highlighting the growing concentration of this kind of borrowing in credit markets. In venture capital, AI captured 81% of a record $300 billion in global venture funding in the first quarter of 2026, and just four companies—OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Waymo—absorbed two-thirds of the total. The result is a self-reinforcing loop. Hyperscalers will spend $800 billion this year on chips, data centers, and the power to run them, propping up GDP growth. Investors are bidding up AI stocks, fattening the portfolios of the richest 20%, whose spending boosts consumption. As the buildout outgrows hyperscalers’ cash flow, new investment is increasingly financed by debt and off-balance-sheet partnerships. The U.S. growth engine now runs on a narrow set of mutually reinforcing drivers. If one stalls, the others lose power too. The Bank for International Settlements warns in its 2026 Annual Economic Report that AI exuberance risks ending in a “lengthy investment bust.” The BIS flagged “circular financing” as a core vulnerability, more than half of investment in AI firms comes from other AI firms, with recipients using that money to buy their backers’ products. Profits are being funded by investors rather than end customers. The late handoff America’s AI bet is underwritten by a single assumption: That by 2027, growth driven by infrastructure will hand off to growth driven by AI-powered efficiency gains across the broader economy. I think that’ll come much later than the market expects. As I argued in Fortune a few weeks ago, five decades of digital innovation achieved broad consumer adoption yet came with a decline in aggregate productivity growth. This is the Innovation Paradox: more innovation and slower growth. Technology diffusion follows a double K-shaped pattern. Consumers adopt almost immediately; enterprises, at a glacial pace. Within enterprises, a handful of superstar firms embrace new technologies quickly while the rest struggle to make use of them. The structure of the U.S. economy makes things even worse. The U.S. has shifted from vertically-linked industrial sectors—where innovations could naturally travel through supply chains—to horizontally spread service sectors that resist transformation because they depend on human judgment. These “stagnant” sectors, as the economist William Baumol called them, now account for roughly half of GDP in advanced economies. Firms are also saddled with debilitating administrative and regulatory compliance costs, which I estimate are now past the topping point at which they strangle innovation. Adding to the paradox: the concentration of capital in AI-linked companies starves the rest of the economy of investment needed to be AI-ready. If hospitals, schools, logistics companies, and retailers can’t invest in digital infrastructure and workforce retraining, the broad-based productivity gains that justify today’s AI valuations will never arrive. AI could still defy the paradox: unlike previous digital waves, it is a cognitive technology that can reason and make judgments, precisely what’s needed to unlock productivity in labor-intensive Baumol sectors. But only deep adoption across a broad spectrum of the economy will realize that potential. Firms need to allocate capital to workers and workflows, not just chips and data centers. That’s a possible silver lining if the AI bubble bursts—that the assets financed by irrationally exuberant investors end up reshaping the economy for the better. Canals in the 1830s, railroads in the 1880s, electrification in the 1920s, telecoms and the internet in the late 1990s—each ended in painful collapse, yet the physical infrastructure created in those speculative booms laid the foundations for decades of later prosperity. Will data centers, semiconductors, and AI models prove equally long-lasting? Perhaps. But that process will take decades, not months or years. In the short term, the more concentrated the bet, the more severe the potential reckoning. No prior bubble spanned so many dimensions of the economy simultaneously—GDP growth, consumer spending, equity markets, debt markets, and venture capital all tethered to a single theme. That is not an economic launchpad. It is a vulnerability of historic proportions. events.title: James Talarico fires back at Elon Musk in Texas Senate race feud
events.summary: James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for a Senate seat from Texas, in a reply on X to Elon Musk, said, "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator." Musk earlier in the day had tweeted, "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico." Polls show Talarico leading Republican nominee Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general. Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, in September donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC that sent that money to Texas PAC, which is supporting Paxton. James Talarico , the Democratic nominee seeking a Senate seat from Texas , fired back Wednesday night at Elon Musk for an X post in which the world's richest man hours earlier had said, "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico." "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator," Talarico wrote in reply to Musk's tweet. Talarico earlier Wednesday, during a campaign speech at the UH Hilton on the main campus of the University of Houston, called out Musk. "In all likelihood, if you've seen an attack ad on your screen, that was Elon. If you've gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon," Talarico said, according to a report by Houston Public Media . "If you've received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon too," Talarico said. "Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our taxpayer dollars. He wants his very own personal United States Senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on Nov. 3, we are going to send a clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale." The sniping between Musk and Talarico came five days after news broke that Musk donated $158 million to a Republican super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, in September. That money ended up with Texas PAC, a group that is backing Talarico's opponent, GOP nominee Ken Paxton , the Texas attorney general. Musk also sent $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, another group that is backing Paxton. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Musk, who is CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla , executed the big money dump as polls showed Paxton trailing Talarico in the contest. Talarico's campaign last week said he had raised $64 million in the third quarter of this year. That was the largest tally ever reported for a Senate candidate in a third quarter, his campaign said. In comparison, Paxton's campaign raised just $18 million for the same quarter. Paxton beat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary earlier this year. His campaign didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Peter Thiel breaks with Trump over Iran war: 'We should not have done it'
events.summary: Peter Thiel, cofounder and chairman of Palantir Technologies Inc. Bloomberg/Getty Images Thiel criticized the US-Iran war, diverging from Trump's foreign policy stance, POLITICO reported. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made," Thiel said at a lecture earlier this month. Despite his criticism of the war in Iran, Thiel highlighted his continued support for Trump. Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel said he's skeptical of the US war with Iran and does not believe the United States should have launched it, putting the major Republican donor at odds with President Donald Trump over one of the administration's defining foreign policy decisions, POLITICO reported . Thiel's remarks, delivered on October 12 at a private event, are his most explicit statements to be revealed publicly about the war with Iran and come less than two weeks before the midterm elections in which Trump's party is grasping to maintain power in Congress. The audio of Thiel's comments was obtained by Decoded by POLITICO from a lecture earlier this month. "I'm skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it," Thiel said. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made." Thiel added, "Maybe we don't have the hard power. Maybe we're going to lose the soft power war." In the full lecture, Thiel made clear his strong opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars. Despite his criticism of the Iran war, Thiel highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president. Still, Thiel's break over the war represents one of the most important examples to date of a fierce Trump ally sharing deep concerns about the conflict. The comments were part of Thiel's lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has documented since their start this fall . In the latest lecture, Thiel issued extensive warnings about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on comments from Bush-era figures Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney. "I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late," Thiel said. "And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran." Thiel also discusses meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after the October 7 attack, where he said he asked the president about his plans in Gaza. Thiel said Netanyahu told him, "I can't just Dresdenize it," referring to the Allied bombing of the German city of Dresden during World War II that killed roughly 25,000 people. The first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016, and then have a high-profile speaking role at the Republican National Convention that year, Thiel was also the biggest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance 's Senate campaign in 2022. POLITICO reported in March that Vance was "skeptical" of the U.S. striking Iran in the lead-up to the beginning of the war. Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. events.title: Mark Zuckerberg considered leaving California over the billionaire tax
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg considered moving out of California because of a proposed billionaire tax. Zuckerberg would get $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" if the billionaire tax passes. Meta made the offer to Zuckerberg to help keep him in California after he considered leaving. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg considered moving out of California because of its proposed billionaire tax, Meta disclosed in a new SEC filing on Wednesday. Next month, Californians will vote on Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the assets of the state's billionaires. The filing said that Zuckerberg told a special committee formed by Meta that he was considering moving. In response, the committee concluded that it was "critically important" for Zuckerberg to keep running Meta close to its Silicon Valley headquarters — particularly to its AI division, Meta Superintelligence Labs. The filing said the committee got Zuckerberg to agree to remain in California or any other jurisdiction where Meta has its corporate headquarters for eight years, barring unforeseen circumstances. As part of its efforts to ensure he can remain in charge as it raises more cash for its AI initiatives, the company is granting the Meta CEO a new stock class. The shares would give Zuckerberg $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" to cover the tax by selling stock without losing control of Meta, if the tax passes. The new shares wouldn't add to Zuckerberg's net worth or increase his percentage ownership of Meta. "The goal is to keep Mr. Zuckerberg continuing to lead the Company from California," the filing says. Meta declined to comment. A person familiar with the matter said that the new class of shares, which totals $150 billion, is also intended to raise capital, compensate employees, and keep Meta's stock price on the right track. Meta's filing showcases how tech billionaires are responding to the tax proposal. Some, including Google cofounder Sergey Brin and former CEO Eric Schmidt, poured hundreds of millions of dollars into attack ads against the proposal. While Zuckerberg has taken a lower-key approach, it's clear he's been taking the proposed tax seriously. The Meta CEO, who is worth about $240 billion according to Forbes, has multiple residences in California, including in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe. He also has a sprawling property portfolio outside the state, including a doomsday bunker in Hawaii, a waterfront mansion in Miami, and a castle in Ireland. Have a tip? events.title: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
events.summary: Two critical vulnerabilities, collectively known as “PHP2Shell,” could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers. Governments worldwide have issued urgent security warnings, while Google, OpenAI and other tech companies have worked to identify vulnerabilities and protect affected systems. Amazon detected attempts to exploit the flaws before their public disclosure, but said it remains unclear how attackers obtained information about them. The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet. The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems. The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks. The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible. The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk. Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore , the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems. Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure. Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches. OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure. The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals. Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates. The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

events.title: Australia’s ASX says ‘turning point’ reached after trading outages
events.summary: The ASX has faced a number of trading outages and settlement delays over the past three years, following a failed technology overhaul. SYDNEY – The Australian Securities Exchange’s chair said on Oct 22 the company had reached a turning point in addressing its regulatory troubles, and maintained its lower dividend payout ratio and higher cost guidance for the year ahead. The ASX has faced a number of trading outages and settlement delays over the past three years following a failed technology overhaul, which led the Australian Securities and Investments Commission to order the exchange to hold an extra A$150 million (S$135 million) in capital and renew its infrastructure. “My clear view is that ASX has reached an important turning point,” ASX chair David Clarke told shareholders at the company’s annual meeting on Oct 22. “We did not get here through one action or one appointment, but through several years of confronting difficult issues, making important changes and rebuilding key foundations step by step.” To help meet the regulator’s order issued in December 2025, ASX cut its dividend payout ratio from 85% to 75% of underlying net profit. Clarke said on Oct 22 the payout ratio would remain at 75% for at least the interim dividend period in the current financial year. Some investors had pushed the ASX to increase the payout ratio as the exchange was ahead of schedule in meeting the capital charge. “The board believes that we must achieve the right balance between continuing to provide returns to shareholders, strengthening ASX’s financial resilience and investing in the critical market infrastructure we operate,” he said at the company’s annual meeting. New ASX chief executive Anthony Attia said the exchange would record growth of 18% to 21% in operating expenses in the current financial year, and capital expenditure would be between A$180 million and A$200 million. Both expenses and capital expenditure forecasts were raised earlier in 2026 to fund the ASX’s ongoing technology overhaul. ASX shares were trading 0.3% higher on Oct 22, as the S&P/ASX 200 index was down 0.35%. REUTERS

events.title: Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world
events.summary: Precautionary takedowns come as experts say bad actors could exploit vulnerability in language used by 70% of sites Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites . The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks. WordPress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday as a precautionary measure until they could be patched. The organisation behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”. Because a fix is now public and AI tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers ⁠jumped to get ahead of the updates. AI was powering a “race to exploit”, said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet”. Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at Surrey University, said: “It was very surprising and troubling because of the extent to which PHP was used around the world. PHP issued a patch very quickly. The big thing is for everyone using it to get that in to make sure their systems are safe. “The troubling part is there is going to be a long tail of websites who may not be maintained as well and they are going to remain vulnerable, which means we may see weeks and months of ongoing attacks. For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly.” Woodward said there was a window of opportunity for bad actors. “There is this race and some people unfortunately don’t even know they are in the race.” OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they used models available to the public. Cybersecurity company Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on 1 August and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The vulnerabilities remained hidden ‌in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said its security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy “honeypot” systems on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding that it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo. In a statement, the ​White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday. In the UK, websites belonging to Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford councils were taken offline. In France, local government websites including that of the Paris police prefecture went offline on Wednesday, as did in the Netherlands the national digital identity service, the website of the house of representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre. The Australian Signals Directorate was temporarily affected by the outage overnight local time, with the national cyber defence agency noting other government websites may have been similarly affected. Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said.

events.title: Newly single and 42, I left Connecticut for Montreal on a whim. People told me I was brave.
events.summary: Moving from Connecticut to Canada gave Erin Levi a panic attack. Provided by Erin Levi Last summer, Erin Levi left Connecticut and moved to Montreal on her own . She barely knew anyone in the city, and relocating at 42 gave her a panic attack. Moving to a new city while working for herself was hard, but it made her feel brave. Last summer, I left my life in Connecticut behind and moved to Montreal on a whim, without a plan. People told me I was brave. Really? I'm a travel journalist. I've followed a snow leopard expert across Nepal; I've lived with a family in Uzbekistan who didn't speak English; and I've had a private encounter with the King of Bhutan. Montreal is only a 6-hour drive from my hometown in Connecticut. It didn't seem brave to me. It seemed, frankly, safe. Yet moving here at 42 gave me a panic attack. I hadn't been to Canada in more than 12 years and barely knew anyone. After my parents dropped me off, we spent a few days exploring my new city together, where it's easy to get by without a car — it felt like the start of another semester abroad. Except this time, I was older and had no plans to leave. The last time I'd been in Montréal with my parents was in the summer of 2003, before I left for a semester abroad in Hanoi. I had my first pho in Montréal's Chinatown. So why Montreal? A Facebook post on a full moon in May changed my life. My lease in Ridgefield, Connecticut, was up. So was my relationship. My landlord wanted an extra $500 a month for the lofty, 1,100-square-foot, one-bedroom apartment in the woods that I had been sharing with my now-ex. That would bring the rent to $3,250 a month, not including utilities, which often reached $700 during the winter because of the high ceilings. I saw all of this as signs to leave. But I was about to write a check for $5,985 upfront for a $1,995-a-month, 900-square-foot, one-bedroom duplex nearby and buy a car. Then a Canadian friend shared that her 638-square-foot, one-bedroom apartment near Montréal's Little Italy was available for 6 months at a writer-friendly rent: 1,100 Canadian dollars, or about $775 a month, including utilities, WiFi, furniture, and a beautiful patio. My friend is a professor and works abroad for half the year. Ever since my first job at Tourisme Québec's New York office — the role that ultimately launched my travel-writing career — I'd wanted to live in Montreal. I also speak French. It seemed like a no-brainer, so I said "oui." I found out that Americans can spend up to 6 months in Canada per visit. However, anyone who spends more than 183 days in the country in a calendar year may have to pay taxes. Foreign media workers like me also don't require a work permit. I consulted an immigration lawyer about staying in Canada. Watching the Stanley Cup semi-finals at a bar in Montreal. Provided by Erin Levi My new life in Canada Since moving, I've learned to row. I take weekly lessons at the Olympic Basin, where beginner courses cost CA$200 each. Gliding hundreds of meters solo in a scull has been one of the best antidotes to my anxiety. Socially, though, I should've joined the dragon boat team. My neighborhood, La Petite-Patrie, is home to some of the city's top restaurants, including Vin Mon Lapin, Pasta Pooks, and Limbo. And Marché Jean-Talon — the largest open-air market north of Mexico — is my local grocer. Some cultural highlights have included celebrating Jewish holidays at Leonard Cohen's shul, attending my first F1 race, cross-country skiing in Parc du Mont-Royal, and going to a hockey game solo. Sure, there's been loneliness. There's been longing. It's not easy moving to a new city when you work for yourself. Nor is it easy being more than 10 minutes from my parents — and their delicious cooking. But I've also made new friends, hosted old friends, and opened my heart. Brave, eh? Perhaps I really am. events.title: US media group Comcast planning significant job cuts as part of reorganisation
events.summary: The company has been losing cable TV subscribers for some time as customers cut the cord in favour of streaming options. Comcast plans major job cuts as part of a wider restructuring of its cable TV, broadband and wireless businesses, sources said. The aim is to make the company more agile and save cash for growth. The changes come as Comcast loses cable and internet customers to streaming, fibre and fixed wireless rivals. It has tried to fight back with five-year price guarantees and a free wireless line for one year. The restructuring is linked to Comcast’s split from NBCUniversal in 2027. Brian Roberts has also reshaped senior management, while the company had 179,000 employees at the end of December. PHILADELPHIA, Pennsylvania – Comcast is planning a significant number of job cuts as part of an overall restructuring of its cable TV, broadband and wireless businesses, according to sources familiar with the company’s thinking. The reorganisation is designed to put Comcast in a stronger position to operate as an independent company after it spins off the NBCUniversal businesses in 2027, said the sources, who asked not to be identified because the plans have not been made public. The cuts, which could be announced in a matter of weeks, are aimed at creating a more nimble workforce and freeing up cash to invest in more growth opportunities, among other long-term goals. The Philadelphia-based media and telecommunications conglomerate has been losing cable TV subscribers for some time as customers cut the cord in favour of streaming options. More recently, Comcast has also been shedding internet customers with rivals such as AT&T, T-Mobile US and Verizon Communications pushing attractively priced fibre optic or fixed wireless connections. Comcast has been promoting broadband by offering five-year price guarantees and a free wireless line for one year. The company is due to report earnings on Oct 22. Comcast has adjusted its portfolio to boost its stock price, which was down about 21% in 2026. Cable TV networks like CNBC and MS Now were spun off as Versant Media Group in January. Co-chief executive Brian Roberts has made changes to senior management to address the subscriber losses. He promoted Steve Croney to chief executive of the broadband and wireless business, and hired Jon Gieselman, a former Apple and DirecTV executive, as chief growth officer. Michael Angelakis, a former chief financial officer, is returning to lead Comcast after the NBC separation. The company had 179,000 full- and part-time employees as at Dec 31, 2025. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says Muse and Reality Labs are highly unprofitable — for now
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Meta's AI agent, Muse, is unprofitable due to "very high compute costs," CEO Mark Zuckerberg says. Meanwhile, Meta expects Reality Labs, its AI glasses division, to lose $15 billion next year. The social media giant has a plan to fix that. Meta says some of its biggest cash incinerators could finally start turning profits. The social media giant, which generated over 97% of its quarterly revenue from ads, has faced persistent questions from investors about the lack of profitability in its AI and hardware initiatives. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg addressed those concerns head-on during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday. Zuckerberg said that Muse, the AI assistant it launched last month, is unprofitable since it's "very compute intensive to run." Meta expects to start turning that around next year by massively improving Muse's efficiency. "If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years," he said. Meta plans to make money from Muse by taking a small transaction fee off of purchases it drives, Zuckerberg said at Meta's Connect conference last month. Zuckerberg added that Muse, which launched only in the US and Canada, wasn't launched globally due in part to the amount of compute it requires. (Meta's North American users are generally its most lucrative.) Zuckerberg also struck a positive note about its cash-hemorrhaging Reality Labs division, which makes products like Meta Ray-Bans and virtual reality glasses. Meta expects Reality Labs to narrow its losses to about $15 billion in 2027, down from the $18 to $19 billion it expects to lose this year. The division should start trending toward profitability next year, as Meta's AI systems make it more useful, Zuckerberg said. "I continue to believe that the path to delivering holographic experience, of bringing together the physical and digital worlds and everyday glasses, will come through VR first," Zuckerberg said. events.title: Eight months of US-Iran war turns China petrochemical glut into a crunch
events.summary: Products made by such chemicals include plastic bottles, rubber for car tyres and electrical insulation. China’s petrochemical glut has shrunk fast after the US-Iran war cut oil and naphtha flows. Inventories are now near the bottom, and prices are rising across many industrial products. The tightest supply is in aromatics and downstream goods like rubber, resins, bottles, paints and coatings. JPMorgan said consumers are already seeing inflation, and China’s producer prices hit 5% in September. Higher feedstock costs may force buyers to pay more, but the rally may not last. China still has overcapacity, and new global polyethylene capacity is set to rise sharply, risking future oversupply. China has burnt through much of a petrochemicals glut built up by years of overproduction as the US-Iran war chokes oil flows, setting the stage for higher prices for an array of industrial materials. The squeeze is most acute in the so-called aromatics chain and the downstream products made from these chemicals, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co and commodities data provider ICIS. That includes rubber for car tyres and electrical insulation, resins, and plastic bottles, as well as various paints and coatings. Energy exports from the Persian Gulf may have recovered in recent months, but Iranian crude, favoured by some Chinese private producers, has completely dried up due to the United States’ blockade. Exports of naphtha, a chemicals feedstock, from the region remain constrained, while Beijing has prioritised gasoline and diesel output, forcing refiners to draw on petrochemical stockpiles accumulated before the war. “Inventory levels are basically near the bottom,” said Parsley Ong, head of Asia energy and chemicals research at JPMorgan. The tightness in Chinese markets has already affected consumers with “inflation happening across most products”, she said. The price rises have fed through into China’s producer price index, which tracks inflation at the wholesale level, and has gone from below zero in February to a faster-than-expected 5% in September. These price gains are also being exported, given the country’s role as a major supplier of petrochemicals and downstream products to global markets. Unlike China’s vast crude reserves that were amassed for strategic reasons, the scale of the country’s petrochemicals inventories was an unintended consequence of years of overcapacity and overproduction as refiners expanded deeper into chemicals. Rongsheng Petrochemical and Hengli Petrochemical are some of China’s biggest producers. The glut became an inadvertent cushion when the US-Iran war disrupted energy supply. Around 95% of the end-use chemical inventories built up in 2025 have now been depleted, Goldman Sachs Group said in a note in October . Overall, stockpiles remain high by historical standards, but the bank said the de-stocking is unsustainable over the longer term as China seeks to maintain buffers against future supply shocks. Petrochemicals are split into two main types of hydrocarbons: aromatics – used to produce benzene, toluene and paraxylene – and olefins such as ethylene and propylene, materials that are commonly used in packaging, coatings and plastic piping. Across China, port inventories of the aromatics grades are all at multiyear lows, said ICIS senior analyst Jenny Yi. Robust Asian demand for toluene in gasoline blending is also diverting supply away from petrochemicals, she said. As the stockpiles shrink, fresh production becomes more important. Overcapacity had already pushed margins for some petrochemicals below zero before the war. The surge in oil and feedstock costs is now putting more pressure on producers. For producers to increase output in the fourth quarter, downstream prices need to rise enough to restore margins, said JPMorgan’s Ong. Petrochemical buyers are “just going to have to accept a higher price”, she said, adding that she does not expect a sharp rally. The higher prices may not last, given that China is still saddled with overcapacity in the sector. ICIS sees China’s cracker operating rate recovering to 81% by the end of 2026 from 79% in October as plants return from maintenance. That is well below 88% before the war, however. The overcapacity is still increasing. Bloomberg is forecasting that almost 21 million tonnes of new global manufacturing capacity for polyethylene – one of the world’s most common plastics – will be producing or ramping up, a record increase. That leaves an unusual combination of depleted inventories and abundant underlying capacity. “Higher feedstock prices, when passed through the supply chain, are leading to short-term inflationary pressures on Chinese consumers,” said Salmon Aidan Lee, principal at ICIS. “This goes against fundamentals, though, and those products facing overcapacity will eventually return to that oversupplied state.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Tesla says it will start selling Cybercabs by end of year
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Tesla said Wednesday it will start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year, even as federal regulators investigate whether the vehicle meets vehicle safety standards . The gold-hued, autonomous two-seater lacks a steering wheel and other traditional controls. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Lars Moravy, vice president of engineering at Tesla, said the Cybercabs produced today are all destined for the company’s own robotaxi fleet. As that fleet grows, the company will “mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers,” he said, noting that it will start small. The company will scale as it learns about delivery, ownership, and fleet management of autonomous vehicles, Moravy added. Tesla first floated the idea of selling the autonomous vehicle to third parties last month around its Cybercab event in Austin and even posted a form for people interested in buying robotaxis. But it wasn’t clear if Tesla would follow through, or how. Tesla CEO Elon Musk has talked for years about building a massive fleet of low-cost robotaxis, but until recently, those plans centered on turning privately owned Tesla vehicles into self-driving taxis with a software update. That plan has yet to materialize, and Musk’s comments on the call show how his views have shifted. Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to Full Self-Driving (Supervised), an advanced driver-assistance system that automates many driving tasks but still requires the driver to take control. The company continues to push out software updates to the system to improve its capabilities, but a human driver is still required to remain engaged and ready to take over — even though many videos show drivers testing the limits of that rule. Musk said Wednesday that an unsupervised version of FSD, the fully self-driving version, would be rolled out to customers sometime in the second quarter of next year, yet another delay for Tesla owners, many of whom bought or subscribed to the software years ago. If both timelines hold, it would mean third-party fleet customers would be able to buy the autonomous Cybercab and potentially operate it as a robotaxi service before Tesla owners would get access to the same autonomous capability in their own cars. Musk said the Cybercab is meant to be a ride-hailing vehicle, not a car people own. “Cybercab is primarily going to be something that is offered as like transport as a service, whereas our other cars would be more, you know, the cars that you’d want to own, like the 3 and the Y and whatnot, and the Roadster, obviously,” Musk said Wednesday on the call. “But, you know, the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transported as a service.” There is at least one obstacle that could throw off Tesla’s Cybercab fleet plans. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the federal auto safety regulator, announced last month that it had opened an investigation into the Cybercab, just hours after the vehicles began operating on public streets in Austin. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) require manual controls like brake pedals, as well as other features such as rearview and side mirrors. Automakers traditionally self-certify whether their vehicles comply with FMVSS rules, and Tesla did the same. Current regulations don’t accommodate vehicles without manual controls, though the Department of Transportation recently proposed removing those requirements for vehicles that are designed to be autonomously driven. In the meantime, NHTSA said it would investigate the Cybercab to “examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.” The outcome of that investigation could affect whether Tesla, or anyone else, can legally operate the Cybercab. events.title: Inside India newsletter: Asia’s hottest data center market aims to quell concerns over water and power use
events.summary: India plans to roll out a data center policy as several U.S. big tech companies pour billions of dollars into the country to set up digital infrastructure. Expert says the proposed policy indicates a shift in direction from "primarily encouraging the data center investment" toward now balancing it with infrastructure readiness and sustainability. Amazon and Google's $15 billion data center projects in India are facing public backlash. Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. India is touted as one of the hottest markets for data centers, with several U.S. Big Tech companies investing to set up capacity in the country. But of late, some projects have faced public backlash over the use of water and power resources. Now the Indian government is taking steps to address the situation. Will it work? Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team. Several U.S. Big Tech companies that are spending billions to set up digital infrastructure in India are facing growing public anger over resource sharing and environmental concerns, prompting the government to step in and calm tensions. On Oct. 14, Jitin Prasada, a junior minister for electronics and information technology, announced that India will roll out a policy for data centers, calling the country a "fertile ground for hyperscalers." The minister reportedly said India wants to avoid a situation where consumers have to pay more for power because they have to compete with data centers for supply. Globally, data center companies are facing public backlash as communities raise concerns over electricity, water and land use. India is also grappling with similar issues that pose a threat to its ambitions to host the whole world's data . As per local media reports, Amazon's data center near Mumbai is facing resistance from residents who are worried that the U.S. company's facility would receive priority access to water and electricity during shortages. Meanwhile, environmental activists have been demanding the cancellation of permissions given to AI data centers in Visakhapatnam, where Google is constructing its $15 billion project. Amazon told CNBC that it is committed to being a "good and responsible neighbor," and said it is engaging with the community through educational sessions. They denied using water for cooling and added that their data centers "do not draw electricity from the local distribution network that supplies homes, shops and businesses." The American firm also said it "will be a part of industry consultations with the government to advise on India's data center regulations." Google did not respond to CNBC's request for comments. Experts told CNBC that the government plans to roll out a policy directive to pacify local resistance to some projects across the country. It will also lay down clear approval guidelines that will minimize the risks data center developers face from public pushback and execution challenges, they added. The proposed policy indicates a shift in direction from "primarily encouraging the data center investment" to now balancing it with infrastructure readiness and sustainability aspects, Jaspreet Singh, partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, told CNBC. Last week, Niti Aayog, an Indian government think tank, shared a framework for local governments to evaluate data center projects for sustainability and to provide suitable locations, based on grid readiness and water supply availability. It underscored the need to establish guidelines "before constraints emerge," adding that data centers should get faster approvals only in cases where resource readiness, local safeguards and public value are proven. Experts who are part of consultations expect the new policy to lay down clear and consistent rules, which will also help the industry overcome challenges around land acquisition and simplify a fragmented approval process. "India does not have a dedicated national policy for data centers, and it is high time that this gap was addressed," Shobhit Agarwal, chief executive of real estate consultancy ANAROCK Capital, told CNBC. He explained that projects are currently approved under existing environmental and building rules, and every state has its own "variations and incentives." While the Indian government has been enthusiastic in welcoming the hyperscalers to invest in data centers in India, even giving them 20-year tax sops , regional governments are the final decision-makers when it comes to providing land, water and power resources. Nikhil Narendran, a partner for technology at law firm Trilegal, who works with U.S. Big Tech companies, said local governments are proposing data center projects in locations that are already facing constraints in terms of electricity, water and other infrastructure.

events.title: Germany’s SAP hits $14.3 billion quarterly revenue milestone, lifts 2026 view
events.summary: Cloud revenue rose 26% in the third quarter, with CEO Christian Klein saying that artificial intelligence was “the main driver behind customers’ move to the cloud”. SAP hit a record €10 billion quarterly revenue, with cloud revenue up 26% to €6.67 billion and operating profit up 18% to €3.03 billion. The cloud backlog rose 26% to €24.14 billion, showing strong demand. CEO Christian Klein said “AI was the main driver” as customers moved to the cloud. SAP lifted its 2026 outlook to the top of its range, while CFO Dominik Asam warned the fourth quarter faces a gloomy backdrop, with oil prices and US interest rates adding pressure. WALLDORF, Germany – Europe’s largest tech company SAP on Oct 21 achieved a €10 billion (S$14.3 billion) quarterly revenue milestone for the first time, while reporting a 26% rise in current cloud backlog and lifting its 2026 revenue outlook to the upper end of its range. Cloud revenue rose 26% to €6.67 billion in the third quarter while non-IFRS operating profit rose 18% to €3.03 billion. SAP’s cloud backlog at constant currencies grew 26% to €24.14 billion, ahead of the 24% to 25% growth UBS had forecast. SAP held its operating profit outlook at €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion at constant currencies, a range trimmed in July for its recent acquisitions. SAP’s order book is watched as a gauge of enterprise tech spending worldwide as its software suite runs accounting and payroll at many of the world’s biggest companies. A miss on the measure in January sent the shares down 15% in one day. “AI was the main driver behind customers move to the cloud,” in the quarter, CEO Christian Klein told analysts, with companies signing subscription contracts to get access to SAP’s Joule assistant platform connecting to over 70 AI models. “SAP is not committing to a preferred model,” he said. CFO Dominik Asam said the fourth quarter would decide how the year lands, describing a gloomy backdrop with rising oil prices and US interest rates that “start to develop teeth”. SAP said growth in cloud revenue was helped by customers returning from “financial distress”. Its profit margin widened to 29.5% from 28.3% while free cash flow rose 36% to €1.72 billion. SAP now expects 2026 subscription revenue – access to software customers rent remotely rather than buy and run themselves – towards the top of its €25.8 billion to €26.2 billion forecast, up 23% to 25%. Including the declining classic licence business, it sees revenue of €36.3 billion to €36.8 billion, up 12% to 13%, at the top of its range. Klein called it “an outstanding quarter”. Customers are “investing in the technology behind” the company’s AI strategy, he said. New cloud customers included AstraZeneca and Infineon. REUTERS

events.title: NAB staff speak out after mass job cuts revealed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NAB staff speak out after mass job cut announcement NAB workers have spoken out after the bank announced plans to shed staff. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton ) Entire teams of National Australia Bank workers are having to reapply for their jobs and compete among themselves as part of a major restructure. Staff say the writing was on the wall as they witnessed the bank pushing to offshore workers and take up AI. The major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June next year, with 1,500 expected to be out the door before Christmas. National Australia Bank (NAB) workers have accused the banking giant of a "spill and fill" redundancy strategy, forcing entire teams to reapply for their positions as part of a sweeping restructure. Earlier this week the major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June , including 1,500 before Christmas. This is about 6 per cent of its total workforce, with corporate roles bearing the brunt. Several workers who spoke to the ABC on condition of anonymity said the writing was on the wall as the bank pushed the uptake of AI and moved work offshore. "Until today, it's been a lovely place to work," said Dylan*, who has worked in NAB's technology team for a decade but learnt he could be unemployed by the end of the year. His team will have to reapply for their jobs in what is known as a "spill and fill" type of workforce restructure, where existing roles are made vacant and current employees have to fight for a smaller number of positions. There is a two-week consultation period for Dylan's team and, for those being shown the door, their last day will be December 2 or 17. Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au Andrew Irvine says the changes are "expected to improve outcomes for customers". ( AAP: Mick Tsikas ) NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said in a note to staff he encouraged colleagues to be "thoughtful" and check in on one another, and indicated support would be offered to those "impacted personally". The bank said in an ASX announcement that the mass redundancies, which are estimated to cost the bank about $300 million in restructuring costs, were part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers". The bank declined to comment to the ABC on staff members' claims. The looming redundancies have sparked serious concerns about offshoring among staff, as the banking heavyweight bolsters its Indian and Vietnamese headcount while it cuts staff based in Australia. A leaked workforce plan seen by the ABC shows Dylan's team in technology, which consists of just under 500 people, is currently 53 per cent Australian-based. The rest are based in NAB's offices in India (14 per cent), Vietnam (13 per cent), or are external contractors. But, under the plan, the number of staff would be reduced to 400 by the 2027 financial year while the percentage of offshore workers would increase. The Australian-based workforce would be cut to 40 per cent, with the Indian and Vietnamese offices upping their numbers to 30 and 20 per cent respectively. NAB announced mass redundancies on Tuesday. ( ABC News: Yiying Li ) James* resigned last Friday, just days before NAB announced it was going to slash staff, because of fears about the longevity of his business banking role. He shared an email NAB sent in March, which stated the bank would be "expanding out teams in NAB India" to help in its goal of "focusing on digitising and simplifying processes, including increasing automation to speed up turnaround time" and "investing in our global teams". James said the messaging in NAB had changed so drastically in the past six months that he no longer felt safe in his job and had left the banking industry. "People are feeling the anxiety," he said, adding that he had moved to a service-based industry because, "I can't be replaced realistically for the next five to 10 years." AI is also an issue on everyone's lips. While there was no direct reference to AI, NAB did refer to "rapid technological change" in its announcement to the market and experts say its impact is clear. MST Financial analyst Brian Johnson said that for a long time it was politically unacceptable to essentially replace people with AI. Brian Johnson says it is becoming more acceptable to replace people with AI. ( ABC News ) "Technology will supplant a lot of functions at jobs. You can just do things better and faster." events.title: Zuckerberg told Meta directors he might leave California, where he could lose billions to a wealth tax. Meta answered with a new class of stock
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg intends to maintain control over the company he founded in 2004 and a new class of stock will help him do just that. On Wednesday as Meta released third quarter earnings results, the company announced that it would issue a new share class of Class C stock. The share class, which is technically a one-for-one stock dividend of new Class C shares, will be distributed to all shareholders. It was conceived following months of extensive negotiation that grew contentious at times between Zuckerberg and board members, including DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Ambassador Robert Kimmitt, and ex- Microsoft executive Charles Songhurst. Xu disclosed his personal friendship with Zuckerberg but said it wouldn’t impair his judgement. At one point, the committee even talked about resigning if they couldn’t come to a resolution. According to a Meta filing with the Securities & Exchange Commission, Zuckerberg wanted to be able to maintain his voting control, meet his pledges to fund the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative with his Meta stock, and be prepared to pay billions to the state of California if a proposed wealth tax is approved by voters in November. The proposed wealth tax, however, came around the same time as a decision by the company in late 2025 that Meta needed to raise outside capital to help fund the AI boom. Zuckerberg holds about 60.6% of voting control at Meta, while his stake is about 13.4% of the company. Like other major tech companies, Meta maintains a dual-class share structure, where Class A shares trade on Nasdaq as a one-vote-one-share stock. Conversely, Zuckerberg’s holdings are made up of mostly Class B shares, which carry 10 votes per share, which is how he maintains majority control. The condition on the supercharged Class B shares is if Zuckerberg sells them, they convert to Class A. Many companies require this condition for super-voting shares to ensure that outsiders don’t start to gain control of companies from founders seeking liquidity.  The rub is if Meta issues more Class A shares, which it does in order to make equity grants to employees, make acquisitions or raise capital, Zuckerberg’s stake gets diluted. Meta has long offset the dilution with stock buybacks, which helped buoy his voting power from 53.7% in 2013 to 60.6% now. But the buybacks also drain cash that Meta wants to use to fund the AI buildout. The company’s SEC filings show Meta repurchased $26.3 billion in Class A stock in 2025, but hasn’t bought back any shares in four straight quarters. Meanwhile, in the first nine months of this year, Meta posted $21 billion in stock-based compensation. Meta’s third quarter results , released Wednesday, help explain why the share class came about. Revenue this quarter rose 26% to $64.6 billion while capital expenditures hit $34.9 billion. Meanwhile, free cash flow dipped to negative $2.1 billion, compared to $10.6 billion a year ago. Meta also forecast capex for 2026 at $135 billion to $140 billion, raising the low end up from $130 billion. Meta forecast fourth quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion.  As a solution to the crunch, the new Class C stock will carry no votes, the company said. Meta will use them to pay employees, fund acquisitions, and raise capital without Zuckerberg losing majority voting control. He can also sell some of them without giving up votes, and more importantly, pay a potentially massive wealth tax bill looming in California without having to tap into his Class B shares. His current level of control is such that he can personally elect all the directors on the board and determine most of the issues proposed to shareholders for a vote, which won’t change following the recapitalization. With the new shares, Zuckerberg can sell 20% right away, and the remaining 80% are “stapled”—meaning he can sell them only if he sells or converts an equal number of his voting shares. Proposition 40 in California, known as the wealth tax, is up for a vote on Nov. 3 and if it passes, it could hit Zuckerberg and the wealthiest in the state with a multibillion bill. The Bloomberg Billionaires index lists him at #5 with a net worth of $246 billion. In July, Zuckerberg told Kimmitt, who is Meta’s lead independent director, that selling his Class B stock to cover what he might owe for the wealth tax could cut his voting stake back down to 53%. The tax came up in a conversation between the two after negotiations between Zuckerberg and the committee appeared to grow tense. The committee had suggested shareholder-friendly sunset provisions that would see the Class B shares convert into regular stock within a year of Zuckerberg’s eventual death or departure from Meta—or if he sold more than half his holdings. During a call with Kimmitt in July, the two discussed the wealth tax and noted that Zuckerberg had only taken a $1 salary from Meta since 2013.  Later that same month, Zuckerberg again brought up Prop 40, this time raising concerns about whether it might impact his ability to stay a California resident. The following week, Zuckerberg’s lawyers sent a letter asking for a pay package similar to those made to other tech founders, partly so Zuckerberg could pay a potential tax bill. Like SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, many founders in tech have moonshot performance pay packages, in which rigorous stock price growth is tied to massive pay hurdles. According to the filing, Zuckerberg refused to consider any changes to his voting shares, including sunset provisions, and told the committee he was “considering establishing residence outside of California.” The next day, the committee hashed over Zuckerberg’s stance and went over Meta’s analyst coverage and commentary, and the tightening of credit conditions for hyperscalers. Meta had seen relatively looser demand for its July bond issuance for a Texas data center. The committee wanted to keep Zuckerberg in California, close to its artificial intelligence lab.  Later that same day, August 4, Zuckerberg proposed a dividend of 20 shares of Class C stock for each share of Class A and B shares, paid to all shareholders. He told the committee he wouldn’t agree to sunsetting his Class Bs or support equity financing that diluted his voting control. Then, he upped the stakes. Zuckerberg told the committee “he intended to establish residence outside California, which he had been advised he would need to do before the November. 3, 2026 election,” the filing states. The committee met again August 5, but viewed the 20-for-1 proposal as “excessive,” the filing states. By late August, all sides were dug in after various proposals had been issued and objected to. Eventually, committee members discussed dissolving the committee or resigning from the board if Zuckerberg wouldn’t make concessions for the benefit of all Class A shareholders.  At a September 9 board dinner, Zuckerberg told directors he planned to list his Palo Alto estate for sale on September 13. events.title: Tesla cuts spending before potential SpaceX deal even as Musk bets future on AI, robots
events.summary: Tesla beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter revenue as deliveries rose from the previous quarter. Tesla cut 2026 capex to about US$20 billion and posted US$1.53 billion free cash flow. Lower AI and robotics spending helped cash, but raised doubts about growth plans. Musk said a Tesla-SpaceX merger is a “good idea” and special committees are discussing it. The deal could link AI, energy, robotics, transport and space. Tesla revenue was flat but beat estimates, while net income fell 43%. Deliveries rose to 486,532, and Musk said demand is “exceeding our production by a significant margin”. Tesla cut its annual capital expenditure forecast by a fifth and posted surprise positive free cash flow for the third quarter on Oct 21 after spending far less on AI and robotics than Wall Street expected. The unexpected cash generated in the quarter comes at a critical moment for Tesla, as chief executive Elon Musk explores combining the EV maker with his far more capital-intensive space venture, Space X . While the lower spending strengthens Tesla’s financial position ahead of any deal, preserving cash at the expense of investment – in AI, robotaxis and humanoid robots – could undermine the very growth story investors are betting on. Tesla shares, which had risen 2% in after-hours trading after the company reported positive cash flow, higher gross margin and market-beating revenue, reversed course to trade down 2%. They have fallen about 14% in 2026. “The free cash flow beat was a pleasant surprise, but when combined with the lower-than-expected capex, raises questions on the next step for the automaker,” said Ryan Lee, senior vice-president of product and strategy at Direxion, which offers ETFs tied to Tesla. “Lower capex suggests less of an ‘all-in’ approach to the AI arms race than one would expect from Elon.” Tesla said it expected capital expenses for 2026 to be roughly US$20 billion (S$25.56 billion), down from its previous forecast of more than US$25 billion, but did not say what it would spend less on. In the third quarter ended Sept 30, Tesla spent US$4.7 billion in capex, double that of a year ago, but lower than the US$7.5 billion analysts on average were expecting, according to LSEG data. Tesla reported free cash flow of US$1.53 billion, compared with an expected US$4.92 billion cash burn. Musk said on Oct 20 that a merger between Tesla and SpaceX was a “good idea” and that the companies had formed special committees to discuss a deal. On Oct 21, Musk said on a conference call with analysts that he had no more to say on the matter. A merger would create a single company at the centre of Musk’s long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications and transportation on Earth and beyond. Still, investors will seek evidence that Tesla is investing enough to turn Musk’s ambitions into commercial businesses, with the robotaxi rollout lagging behind his promises. Tesla’s energy unit has recently offered a counterweight to its auto business, which remains under scrutiny as rivals globally launch newer, often cheaper models. Tesla still leans heavily on the ageing Model 3 and Model Y. “The merger still faces a high bar, but tonight’s numbers make the financial logic harder to ignore,” said Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com. “The main takeaway is that Tesla’s surprisingly positive cash flow quarter did not come from stronger profits, but from spending billions less than planned at a time when SpaceX is preparing to invest up to US$40 billion in a single quarter.” Revenue was flat from a year earlier, despite the end of US tax credits that supported sales in 2025. That was enough to top Wall Street targets. Net income plunged 43%. Tesla said in a statement that it ended the quarter with the largest backlog for its passenger vehicles in four years. High gasoline prices have stoked demand for EVs, especially in Europe. With 486,532 vehicles delivered in the third quarter, Tesla is on track to increase annual deliveries for the first time in three years. “Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It’s exceeding our production by a significant margin,” Musk said on the conference call with analysts. “In a nutshell, after many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we’re now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth.” The FSD (supervised) attach rate reached over three-quarters of new vehicle deliveries in North America, an increase of nearly 20 percentage point from the second quarter, Tesla said. Automotive gross margin, excluding regulatory credits, came in at 18.1% in the third quarter, higher than analysts’ estimates of 16.7%, according to Visible Alpha data. Tesla said it was aiming to produce 5 million vehicles a year by about 2030, up from an expected 2.5 million this year. REUTERS

events.title: Meta offers Zuckerberg new shares to keep him in California
events.summary: Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg previously said he was considering leaving California because the state’s proposed wealth tax could leave him with a multibillion-dollar bill, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. Meta agreed a share deal with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him in California for eight years, or wherever Meta’s headquarters moves, while he stays in full-time leadership. The plan gives him non-voting Class C shares and immediate sale rights for 20% of them, helping him cover a possible tax bill from California’s proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40. Meta said keeping Zuckerberg at headquarters is “critically important” for its AI race, and the move also counters claims that a wealth tax would drive billionaires out of California. Meta Platforms signed an agreement with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him living in the same jurisdiction as the company’s headquarters after the chief executive said he was weighing leaving California if the state passes a wealth tax. Zuckerberg would “remain a resident of California, or any other jurisdiction in which the company maintains its corporate headquarters, for eight years”, Meta said in a filing on Oct 21 . Meta said that Zuckerberg was considering leaving California because the state’s proposed wealth tax could leave him with a multibillion-dollar bill, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. The company said in the filing it was issuing Class C shares in a deal partly designed to prevent that outcome. Zuckerberg, the world’s fifth-richest person, gets non-voting shares he can sell for liquidity without reducing his voting control. In return, he has committed to remain in California – or wherever Meta is headquartered – while he remains in a full-time leadership role. Under the agreement, he can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, the equivalent to 10% of his overall economic stake. That would give him liquidity to help cover a potential tax bill triggered by Proposition 40, the name of the ballot measure that California voters will decide in November . While the remaining 80% of the Class C stock is initially restricted, those limits gradually lapse over eight years as long as Zuckerberg continues leading the company. Zuckerberg has a net worth of US$247 billion (S$315 billion), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Proposition 40 has been pushed by a healthcare workers union and progressive politicians in the state, including Congressman Ro Khanna. The levy would impact people whose net worth exceeded US$1 billion on Jan 1, 2026. Some of the world’s wealthiest people, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, have opposed the tax and left the state. Recent polls show a tight race. The arrangement offers a counterpoint to one of the main arguments against Proposition 40: that a wealth tax would push billionaires out of California. Meta’s special committee said keeping Zuckerberg working from the company’s headquarters was “critically important”, particularly as he works closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs during the intensifying race over artificial intelligence. The special committee also noted the “difficulties” the company faced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg was away from the management team, and said it did not want to face similar challenges. Zuckerberg had been discussing the California tax and how it would impact his ownership in the company for months, the Oct 21 filing shows. The subject came up in July, when the CEO briefly discussed the upcoming election with Robert M. Kimmitt, Meta’s lead independent director. At the time, Zuckerberg warned that the proposal could force him to sell down his Class B common stock, leaving him with less than 53% voting interest in the company. Within weeks, Zuckerberg’s legal counsel sent a letter to a special committee of the board warning the committee that he was considering leaving California in the light of the proposed tax on billionaires. He also suggested that Meta should create a class of non-voting stock that would allow it to raise the equity capital it needed to fund its AI ambitions. The letter also asked that the special committee discuss with Zuckerberg a revised compensation arrangement “comparable to those recently approved for other founders of a similar profile and importance to their companies”, Meta said on the filing, “consisting of equity grants tied to rigorous performance benchmarks”. Meta’s chief financial officer Susan Li said during the company’s quarterly earnings call that the Class C shares will primarily serve as a financing tool, giving the company more flexibility to fund its AI ambitions without diluting existing voting power. She did not mention the Zuckerberg-specific elements detailed in the filing. Bloomberg

events.title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn to New Mexico in Cambridge Analytica data-privacy case
events.summary: Jury had found Meta misled consumers after Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained user data without consent A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump ’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users ⁠without their consent. “Facebook’s wrongdoing – ⁠over the course of ​years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn. A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Settlements over the social networks’ safety are growing so large that Meta is reporting significant drags on its business. In its quarterly earnings report, issued the same afternoon as the announcement of the judge’s order, the company said its net income came in significantly below Wall Street analysts’ expectations because of a $9.9bn settlement payment in the US. In August, the social media giant agreed to pay $17bn to settle a nationwide lawsuit by dozens of state attorneys general, who alleged it intentionally designed addictive products that harmed children. Despite the hefty payments, Meta still reported a 26% increase in quarterly revenue up to $64.6bn. New Mexico’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica , ⁠a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta ​of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had ‌access to their data, how the ‌company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to ‌users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said. Meta has faced a wave of lawsuits over the course of the year related to user safety, with the culmination of several cases being referred to as a big tobacco moment for social media. The company will report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday. Jurors on 25 September found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43m violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement. State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per ‌violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico’s school system, New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on 1 October, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had ​asked Mathew to award the state between $35bn and $40bn, saying that would be supported by the US constitution’s protections on due process and the jury’s verdict. “This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45bn, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the ⁠state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove ​that any consumer had actually been misled, the ​company said in court filings. The ​verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the ​state of New Mexico against ‌Meta Platforms. In the first trial, ​which ended in March, a ​Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375m in civil penalties. After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567m into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.
