events.title: Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines
events.summary: Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. Automotive revenue fell 3% from a year earlier. Tesla shares are down 14% this year, underperforming the rest of megacap tech. Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock slid more than 3% in extended trading. Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. 43 cents estimated Revenue: $28.05 billion vs. $27.9 billion estimated Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up. "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger. Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information. "I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," he said. Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, according to the earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion. Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion. Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders. Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a share, a year earlier, Tesla said. The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter. Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million. "We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck. Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to its forthcoming FSD (Unsupervised) systems around the second quarter of next year. Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but it's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service." The company plans to bring Cybercab to cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning. Musk said the company's driverless Robotaxi fleet will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027. That fleet now includes 362 Model Y Robotaxi, and 449 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in Texas, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles, "It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year." Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, Musk predicted that Tesla "will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely." Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit. Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications. One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas.

events.title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
events.summary: The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea. After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund. Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding housed in the National Wealth Fund. A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks. It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go? It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time. "The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said. "If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds." On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth. The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's. "Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me. It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said. Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 16 hours ago It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era. The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories. Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996. The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s. I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund. Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic. It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future. While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance. UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits. Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that. Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past? How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills? events.title: Democrats accuse Trump of using prosecution threats to pressure election officials
events.summary: Democratic groups sued the Trump administration Tuesday, accusing it of using unfounded voter fraud claims to muscle its way into how states run elections. Why it matters: The groups say the administration is issuing a stream of threats to intimidate and bully both voters and election officials. They're asking a judge to declare the administration's actions unlawful and block further interference. Driving the news: The lawsuit condemns the administration for targeting state voter rolls by insisting that local officials review federally compiled lists of alleged noncitizens on their voter rolls. The suit also alleges that the administration is improperly demanding that states deny ballots to registered voters based on those federal lists. The Democrat-aligned groups also claim the administration has attempted to intimidate state and local officials by threatening them with jail time or prosecution. Case in point: The lawsuit cites a Department of Homeland Security claim that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. The department later claimed that it had confirmed 185 of those people were noncitizens. State records later indicated that all 185 were citizens. The DOJ also demanded that California deny ballots to more than 20,000 people based on a federal list that flagged them as suspected ineligible voters, the lawsuit says. A preliminary investigation by Los Angeles County investigators found that more than 25% of those flagged listed a U.S. birthplace, and others already had their voter registrations canceled. What they're saying: "Department of Justice and DHS officials have sought to bolster their interference efforts through a persistent stream of threats and intimidation directed towards state and local election officials across the country," the groups' attorneys wrote. "Defendants' coercive threats of legal retaliation against state officials, including even potential imprisonment, for simply following state law and aiding registered voters in casting their ballots objectively intimidate voters and election officials alike, in violation of Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act." The suit, brought by Democratic organizations including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic leaders and a voter, names Trump, the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, and their respective heads as defendants. The other side: "The Justice Department enforces federal election law, and election integrity is a top priority," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement "Every action the Department has taken to protect the integrity of this year's elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court. Ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted is a requirement of federal law." "We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn't permit this willful blindness." The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: The suit also argues that the president has no constitutional authority to decide who gets to vote or dictate how states count ballots. Investigations and audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud. Research shows noncitizen voting is rare, and there's no evidence it occurs on a scale that could swing elections. events.title: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroad
events.summary: Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseas Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place. "I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails." More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey , external of 15,000 final year university students. Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high. UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report , external . For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading? Australia: 'The weather's beautiful, even in the winter' While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show. , external In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme, , external British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years. Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than London Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First. She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London. Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched. "People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life." Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures , external from the UK's Office for National Statistics. It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived. After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US. Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunities Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University. West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching. "I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live. "In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences." Europe: 'If you can work across the EU there are more opportunities' The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult. One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends. Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from Finland This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design. Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020. "Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently." Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon. "To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities." Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.

events.title: Scoop: Dems quietly guide super PACs to boost spoiler House candidates
events.summary: House Democrats' campaign arm is instructing allied super PACs to promote minor candidates in several key House races, Axios has learned. Why it matters: This allows Democrats to steer outside groups toward siphoning votes from Republicans without violating laws against direct coordination. An Axios review of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "redboxes" — publicly available webpages laying out what PACs should say in ads and which voters to target — found references to minor candidates in five races. The DCCC included language on four of those pages promoting a third-party or independent candidate with language touting their conservative, pro-gun or anti-government bona fides. "Registered Republicans under the age of 55 need to see ads," the redbox for Colorado's 5th District says, "showing that ... Christopher Mitchell, a libertarian, is the true conservative running for Congress." The page for Virginia's 2nd District says white, college-educated men should see that independent J. Matt Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment" who will "defend our constitution." In Virginia's 5th District , the DCCC wants the same group of voters to know that independent Cooke Harvey "will fight for Virginia's farmers against big government." Republican women in Nevada's 2nd District should be informed that American Independent Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values," the DCCC says. Zoom in: In several cases, the redboxes urge super PACs to steer Democratic and left-leaning voters away from minor candidates who could siphon votes from the DCCC's recruit. The redbox for Alaska's at-large district — where Democrats are backing independent Bill Hill — says voters need to know Eric Hafner is a "fake Democrat" despite being listed on the ballot as one, noting he is an inmate in New York with no clear ties to Alaska . The page for Virginia's 2nd District urges PACs to ding the progressive credentials of another independent candidate, Geral D. "Bishop" Staten , a self-identified "Democrat Socialist." Black voters should hear that Staten "said that he would vote for Donald Trump in 2024 and said that President Obama is a quote 'puppet and a clown,'" the DCCC redbox says — though he has denied supporting Trump. Between the lines: In the post-Citizens United era, redboxes have emerged as a way for campaigns to give messaging guidance to cash-rich outside groups that often have less localized knowledge of their turf. The practice is so named because the websites often put a red box around the instructions. The NRCC has its own publicly available redboxes , though it shies away from encouraging PACs to boost spoiler candidates. The big picture: There have been several other isolated examples this year of both parties allegedly boosting spoiler candidates, including with redboxes. Democrats successfully sued last month to get a Green Party candidate who they alleged was a GOP plant booted off the ballot in Pennsylvania's 7th District. Republicans in Alaska tried and failed to do the same with unaffiliated candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who they allege is a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his race against Democrat Mary Peltola. It's even happened in party primaries: The campaign of Rep. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.) put language on its redbox promoting Republican Zachariah Wooden in the hopes of keeping progressive challenger Mai Vang out of the general election.

events.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
events.summary: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together . Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. During Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said he had nothing further to add about the prospect of a merger but quipped: "I feel like I'm tap-dancing through a minefield." Musk said that calling the merger a certainty would be "overstating" things. Tesla reported a slight drop in third quarter sales which came in at $28.05 billion compared with $28.1 billion at the same time last year. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models . Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.

events.title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan
events.summary: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborate Investors were paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX. But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter. “With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX , I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.” On a call with SpaceX investors on Tuesday, Musk said it would be a “good idea” to combine the two companies and that “there’s a lot of merit” that would come with it. Musk said on Tuesday that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders. On Wednesday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share. Still, the company came in at a slightly lower revenue than last quarter , which was $28.23bn. And its automotive revenue dropped 3% from the year prior. “We maintained strong momentum on many projects spanning Super Intelligence (SI), robotics and renewable energy that will be critical to building a future of Amazing Abundance,” the company wrote in its report . Despite the stronger-than-anticipated quarter, Tesla has experienced a rough year with falling stock and increased competition from cheaper Chinese automakers. The company’s share price has fallen by more than 11% this year, although it appears to have rebounded some since last week with the news of the possible SpaceX merger. Last week, Musk unveiled the company’s electric sports car , the Roadster 2, which he said uses technology from SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. At a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas, a remote-controlled version of the car drove up a steeply curved ramp and then used jet-like thrusters to flip over, hover and land. The vehicle is priced at upwards of $200,000. “Flying cars are real … It can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics,” Musk said at the event, adding: “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.” During Tesla’s earnings call on Wednesday, he added that the event was “the coolest demo of any product ever”. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Tesla’s vehicle sales are not as crucial to its market performance as they once were, as the company has pivoted towards robotics, autonomous driving and AI. Tesla’s Optimus robot has faced production hurdles, however; and its driverless taxi service, Robotaxi, has hit road blocks in scaling its fleet and expanding to new cities. “Tesla’s leaders continue to make big claims about autonomous mobility and physical AI. The company has achieved remarkable things but continues to miss some of its leaders’ bolder bets,” said Paul Miller, a principal analyst for market research firm Forrester. “Tesla robotaxis are undeniably carrying passengers, but not yet at anywhere near the levels the company promised.” Musk has long declared the Robotaxi will have near-infinite demand and that “probably half the population of the US” would be using the autonomous ride-hailing service by the end of 2025. Similarly, the CEO has forecast the manufacture of as many as 1m Optimus robots each year. As Miller pointed out with Musk’s promises, he has failed to reach those lofty targets and rollout has been slow. Musk once again touted the robots on Wednesday, saying: “I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on earth and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on earth.” He added that no other company compares to Tesla in developing humanoid robots – this is despite Chinese competitors making vast strides in the technology.

events.title: Meta beats expectations but legal penalties hit profit amid AI race
events.summary: Meta reported US$9.86 billion in profits from July to September, almost 50% below investor expectations. Meta beat third-quarter revenue expectations, but profit fell after an “US$18 billion” legal settlement with nearly all US states and a new “US$25 billion” New Mexico ruling. Susan Li warned of more legal and regulatory risks, including youth-related trials. Meta shares rose as much as 7% after the results. Meta is spending heavily on AI, Reality Labs and smart glasses, while planning a new class of non-voting stock to raise cash and protect Zuckerberg’s control. SAN FRANCISCO - Meta beat investor expectations for third-quarter revenue on Oct 21 as it doubles down on a global AI race but the social media giant’s profits took a hit due to an US$18 billion (S$23 billion) legal settlement with nearly all US states. The company reported US$9.86 billion in profits from July to September, almost 50% below investor expectations, which Meta said was dragged down by a US$9.9 billion charge related to the settlement. Meta reported its earnings just hours after another financial penalty was announced related to a case in New Mexico. A judge ruled that Meta must pay US$25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” CFO Susan Li said on Oct 21 on a call with analysts. Meta still faces “a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States”, Li continued. The company has been spending aggressively to build out its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, and investors are looking for signs that the investments are paying off. “We expect that the (profits and losses) of Reality Labs to improve from here ... and trending towards profitability,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on the call. Reality Labs is the company’s hardware division which is developing devices like AI-powered glasses. In September, Meta unveiled several new AI wearables including an audio-only, camera-free version of its smart glasses, amid global concerns about privacy and the filming of women and girls without their consent. Its AI model known as Muse will be “the centerpiece of our vision” for wearables, Zuckerberg said in September at the company’s annual Meta Connect conference. Smart glasses let wearers take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant. During Connnect, Meta also announced the Muse Charm, a tamagotchi-like AI device that will allow users to interact with their Muse agent, a type of autonomous AI assistant, separately from a smartphone. “We’re about to ship Muse Charm, which will have gone from concept to a hardware device in people’s pockets in less than a year,” Zuckerberg said on Oct 21. And 10 million people already use its Muse model in the US and Canada, the company said. But AI models consume large amounts of computing, which has sparked an industry-wide race to build out new data centers around the world. Meta said it spent US$35 billion on capital expenditures – which include buying property and equipment – in the September quarter, below investor expectations of US$41 billion. The company has spent over US$85 billion so far in 2026, it said in an investor document. In July the company had increased its spending estimate for the whole year to US$145 billion, up from US$130 billion, which is nearly double what it spent in 2025. Meta also announced that it would issue a new class of stock, though the new shares would not have voting rights, which will allow it to raise more money for its ambitious AI roadmap. It might also be leverage to encourage its founder and chief executive to stay in California. In a securities filing, Meta expressed concern that Zuckerberg’s voting power “could drop to approximately 53 percent or lower” if he has to sell a significant portion of his shares to pay increased taxes. That is a possibility due to a controversial tax on billionaire wealth, Proposition 40, that could pass in California this November. Existing shareholders will be given one new Class C stock for every share they already own – meaning Zuckerberg will also gain new shares and could eventually sell them to pay the new tax without diluting his voting power. events.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
events.summary: Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to do Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning. The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests. Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds. The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace. "House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC. "So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises." According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes". The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions. A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders. Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules. While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said. If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree. Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees. TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail. One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place. They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts. events.title: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira says fears over AI-buildout debt are overblown
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Private equity giant Blackstone is putting itself at the center of the AI boom, firm veteran Jas Khaira discussed last week on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt. It is writing checks via various strategies, ranging from offering massive loans to data centers to investing in frontier AI models and applications. Earlier this year, the firm launched Blackstone N1 (BXN1), a San Francisco-based central hub for its AI initiatives. The group is led by Khaira, who relocated from New York to be at the epicenter of AI. Unlike earlier tech cycles such as mobile or SaaS, which allowed companies to reach significant scale with moderate capital, the transition to AI requires staggering amounts of investment. That need for capital is precisely why Blackstone, with its $1.3 trillion in assets under management, could play such a critical role in this tech shift. Khaira emphasized that Blackstone sets itself apart from traditional venture capitalists through its focus on compute financing and its ability to offer flexible capital structures, ranging from debt to equity. And it has been investing aggressively. “We’re the largest owner of compute outside of the hyperscalers today, whether it’s investments in neo clouds, investments in data centers, and being able to use that compute strategically to support companies,” Khaira said. For instance, BXN1 played a key role in several compute-related deals, among them Crux AI, a neocloud launched in partnership with Google to commercialize its custom TPUs, to which Blackstone committed $5 billion as an investor. It also backed four-year-old Etched , a chip startup whose rapid development has caught investor attention. Neoclouds are cloud providers that rent out AI GPU infrastructure. Blackstone pioneered a financing structure that allowed it to lend massive sums to venture-backed cloud neoclouds by analyzing both committed customer contracts and using GPUs pledged as collateral. Blackstone’s first such deal came in 2023 with CoreWeave, shortly after that neocloud saw demand explode following the launch of ChatGPT. Despite having only “30 million of revenue and minimal profitability” at that time, according to Khaira, CoreWeave approached Blackstone for a $2.3 billion loan. CoreWeave was borrowing against the considerable value of its large collection of Nvidia GPUs, with Nvidia also an investor. Blackstone also grew more comfortable with the loan because CoreWeave had contracts with blue-chip customers like Microsoft. That transaction quickly became the financing model for how Blackstone and other credit institutions provided billions in follow-on debt to CoreWeave and rival neoclouds. “One of the primary things that we’re looking to is the nature of the customer. And if the customer is an investment-grade customer — let’s say it’s Microsoft or let’s say it’s Meta — the risk gets priced relative to that customer,” Khaira said. Building on its success with CoreWeave, Blackstone struck other neocloud financing deals, including co-leading alongside Coatue a $10 billion credit facility for Australian GPU provider Firmus earlier this year. Khaira acknowledged that in recent weeks, the large debt burdens accumulated by these companies and other neocloud operators have begun to raise red flags. Coreweave’s debt alone has since ballooned to about $50 billion , causing Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner to note in a recent CNBC interview, “The collateral that CoreWeave is putting up which is really only GPUs is not good enough anymore. They used that in the past to get cheap debt.” Khaira said that on the credit side, the market jitters stem from a combination of factors. Interest rates ticked up in September, and hotter-than-expected inflation signals that borrowing costs may keep climbing. The flood of AI infrastructure debt offerings isn’t helping either. “We’re also seeing higher credit spreads,” Khaira said, explaining that lenders are charging higher premiums on top of already higher base interest rates to finance the AI buildout. “The cost of capital to price in debt for a Meta or a Microsoft has widened out,” he added, pointing out that even tech giants with massive balance sheets and solid earnings are paying more to borrow. Concerns about the rising cost of debt have spilled into the stock market. Shares of CoreWeave dropped over 20% in recent days, while Firmus scrapped its planned IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange at a target valuation of roughly $30 billion. “Ultimately, the market wasn’t there at that valuation, and so I think as a result, that deal didn’t get done,” Khaira said about Firmus’ cancelled listing. “The market is thinking what is the right price for neoclouds, what is the right price for these businesses in this moment when interest rates are moving up,” he said.

events.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
events.summary: CoreWeave's stock is down 29% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening. The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds. CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $34 billion, with its stock down 29% this month. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%. The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 164% in the past year and 30% in October. It last stood at nearly 1,067 basis points, or 10.67%. The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 27% this month, while IREN's stock is down 32%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions. U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month. A representative from Nscale declined to comment. CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft . That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing. Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing. "Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options. "Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant." CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet. One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027. "Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter." Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary? Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it. On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence. During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.” Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.” The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able ). events.title: Mine on tropical island plans to pump pit water into ocean
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South32 plans to pump water from Groote Eylandt mine pit into ocean The Groote Archipelago is home to several Anindilyakwa communities and the GEMCO manganese mine. ( ABC News: Erin Parke ) South32 wants to build pumps and pipelines on Groote Eylandt to take up to 80 gigalitres of water per year from the mining pit to the ocean. The plan has the support of traditional owners and environmental approval, and comes as the company tries to address massive water management costs. Further consultation is required as the infrastructure would be partially built on Aboriginal-owned land. South32 plans to spend $100 million to pump water from its Northern Territory manganese mine into the ocean as it battles to keep the site open. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) has faced huge financial challenges due to ongoing flooding in its pits on the remote island, and the company is planning redundancies. GEMCO, majority owned by South32, plans to construct about 12 kilometres of pipelines to take up to 80 gigalitres per year from the mine and discharge it into the island's Milner Bay. The plan has the support of traditional owners via the Anindilyakwa Land Council (ALC), and it has environmental approvals from the NT government. Traditional owners expect the mine to close in the early part of the next decade. The new water infrastructure would be in place for the rest of the mine's life. Mining operations on Groote Eylandt filled with water from Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) It is understood South32's production costs have nearly doubled due to excess water management, and it needs to cut about $129 million out of the business. In its quarterly report, released this week, the company said all production forecasts for next financial year were dependent on the infrastructure being built. Production for 2025/26 was also below initial forecasts. In a statement, an ALC spokesperson said it had been discussing the plan with GEMCO and the NT Environment Protection Authority (NT EPA) for more than three years and had confidence in the environmental plans in place. Further consultation is required because the infrastructure extends beyond GEMCO's mining leases and into Aboriginal-owned land. Work cannot begin without traditional owner consent. "The ALC is satisfied with the NT EPA's response, and this coupled with the other environmental practices are designed to meet the traditional owner expectations that risk for environmental harm is minimised," the ALC spokesperson said. An NT government spokesperson said it wanted the mine to continue operating and that the plan had been approved with strict environmental conditions. "GEMCO is one of the Territory’s most significant mining operations and a major employer and contributor to the Groote Eylandt economy," the spokesperson said. "The ALC acts for the traditional owners, and on Aboriginal land its consent is a legal requirement. Those discussions are continuing. "The NT government has supported these discussions where appropriate, while respecting that the agreement is required between independent parties." The MV Anikitos crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt due to Tropical Cyclone Megan. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said the water would be clean and it would work to "safely and effectively manage elevated water volumes". "GEMCO currently manages excess water through a range of pathways, including bush discharge and riverine discharge … water is also used at processing facilities and for dust suppression," the spokesperson said. "The excess water disposal project is intended to become GEMCO’s primary pathway for managing excess water." The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in 2024, but it is understood heavy rain in multiple wet seasons was also a factor. South32's website says it is the world's largest producer of manganese, a key alloy in the production of steel and aluminium.

events.title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday. During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026. Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing. Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control. All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.” Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas , Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax. But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models . In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes. events.title: Tesla targets shipping Optimus to customers by the end of 2027
events.summary: A prototype of Tesla's Optimus robot. CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images Tesla has begun production of its humanoid robot, Optimus, in Fremont, California. Musk said he expects to begin delivering Optimus to customers at the end of 2027. Musk said it will take at least a year to produce 20,000 Optimus units a week. Tesla has begun producing its long-awaited humanoid robot, Optimus, at its Fremont factory, the company said in its quarterly earnings report. "The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured," Tesla said, saying the current manufacturing process is "suitable for a commercial product." "There's still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration," CEO Elon Musk said on Tesla's Q3 earnings call. "It can't, like, wear out after a month." Musk said the company will take at least a year to scale up Optimus production to 20,000 units a week in Fremont. He said he expects to begin delivering Optimus to customers at the end of next year. Musk tempered expectations about how quickly Tesla can scale up Optimus production because it is "such a radically new product." He said the early stages of production will be "somewhat bumpy" because "there's like 10,000 things that have to go right" to build the robot. One of the big challenges Musk outlined is building robot hands. Musk said Tesla is building an "Optimus Academy," where robots will practice tasks and generate data to improve the AI models that power them. The company also plans to install its next-generation AI5 chip in Optimus in April, which will give the robots more computing power and be a "big step change in intelligence," Musk said. The latest version of Optimus has not been unveiled. Musk said he expects to release a video of Optimus within one or two months. He previously said Tesla was keeping the robot under wraps to prevent competitors from copying its design. Tesla stopped producing the Model S and Model X at its Fremont, California, plant earlier this year to make room for an Optimus line designed to eventually produce a million robots a year. A second line under construction in Austin is planned to have an annual capacity of 10 million robots. Tesla is competing in a crowded humanoid market. Agility Robotics, which plans to go public, has deployed its Digit robot across nine customer facilities, while Figure AI has announced deployments in logistics and distribution centers this year. events.title: Airbnb limits chores for guests, sparking backlash from hosts
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Airbnb is taking steps to limit the chores that hosts can require of guests prior to checkout, addressing a long-standing grievance among customers who often pay cleaning fees and are told they must do a list of tasks themselves. In a new policy update , Airbnb prohibits hosts from mandating that guests strip beds, wash and put away dishes, start laundry, or remove trash from the property. This new guideline will apply to reservations made on or after November 20. This change comes in response to years of backlash regarding overly burdensome checkout instructions and hefty fines for not disposing of trash. Many guests have voiced their frustrations on social media, questioning why they should be responsible for cleaning tasks after already paying a cleaning fee. However, some hosts aren’t pleased with the update. Within Airbnb’s community forums , some argue that basic cleaning responsibilities are essential for maintaining sanitary conditions and protecting their properties. They point out that hosts must manage the costs and practical demands of preparing their properties for the next guests. One host expressed concern that the new policy leans toward a hotel-like model, which detracts from the unique appeal of Airbnb. “Guests are given complete freedom to be lazy while the hosts bear the risk,” the host wrote. “The major distinction between commercial hotels and my private home is the personal touch. Guests can certainly be expected to wash their dishes or put them in the dishwasher and remove their dirty linens. In exchange, they enjoy a personal connection and a unique environment that a hotel simply can’t provide. Plus, every potential guest has the opportunity to read the listing beforehand and decide what they prefer. If these restrictions are removed, it could lead me to withdraw my listing and bid farewell to Airbnb after twelve years.” Airbnb has outlined some exceptions to the new policy, though. Hosts may still ask guests to conserve water during droughts or use bear-proof trash containers in areas where wildlife poses a risk. The policy change highlights the challenge Airbnb faces in balancing the expectations of guests versus hosts and is another step taken in addressing guests’ concerns. The company faced scrutiny in 2024 over price transparency from hosts tacking on cleaning fees after guests booked their listings. In 2023, the company said more than 260,000 hosts had reduced or eliminated their cleaning fees. In May 2025, Airbnb began displaying total prices — including fees but excluding taxes — by default in search results worldwide. It will be interesting to see how many hosts decide the new restrictions make Airbnb less attractive as a platform. But the move could also draw in more travelers who want the convenience of a rental without feeling as though they are both paying for housecleaning while still expected to clean the home themselves. events.title: White House to Politico: Retract stories or face "consequences"
events.summary: The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct recent stories about alleged staff drama, or it would suffer unspecified consequences. That deadline expires Thursday. Why it matters: The White House demand threatens to escalate already tense relations with Politico specifically and, more generally, the press corps that covers President Trump in Washington. Politico, CNN, and MS NOW are already banned from covering Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One because the president does not like their coverage. Trump blocked all three outlets from the White House grounds as well, but a judge on Oct. 13 restored their access. CNN threatened legal action Wednesday to regain access to Air Force One and the "pool" of television networks that accompany the president. Zoom in: In his letter to Politico, White House Counsel Will Scharf singled out three stories concerning White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles despite "on-the-record refutations" or contrary evidence supplied by senior staff and even the president. 1) Oct. 15: In a story headlined " Trump's ice maiden is under fire ," Politico Playbook reported that Trump was considering a replacement for Wiles. Trump called it "fake news." 2) Oct. 16: Politico Playbook wrote that the prior day's story had caused a "freakout" and that the president "blew up" over it. A White House spokesman called it "unbelievably stupid and false." 3) Oct. 16: In a story headlined " Susie Wiles helped set up Fox interview ahead of press secretary's exit ," Politico insinuated the chief of staff set up Katie Zacharia to fail in a Sean Hannity interview on Fox the night before. The White House and Fox News denied the reporting. And White House officials provided text messages to Politico before publication showing Zacharia — not Wiles — set up the interview, which the New York Post reported the following day. "Politico has not corrected or retracted its false reporting. Instead, a Politico reporter confirmed that Politico declined to remove Ms. Wiles from the story because she was the 'hook' for the story — a legally fraught and alarming admission to say the least," Scharf wrote. What they're saying: Scharf wrote that "freedom of the press is not a professional exemption from accountability. I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives." Otherwise, he wrote, the White House would conduct an "immediate review of Politico's relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies." A Politico spokesperson did not return a message seeking comment. White House officials fault the new management at Politico for pushing its reporters to engage in what Scharf called "gossip-peddling." The letter was addressed to global editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger. Zoom out: Trump has had an ongoing love-hate relationship with the press. He is available to reporters for far more question-and-answer sessions than any recent president, but he's quick to anger and threaten press bans for coverage he doesn't like. Early in his second term, Trump banned the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One access after it balked at calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. A federal judge reinstated AP's access months later. The New York Times reported this week that Trump has mused about removing the press entirely from the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room and building a swimming pool there. What's next: Scharf would not specify what consequences Politico faces, but a White House official said "all options are on the table" and described Trump's counsel as "uncharacteristically enraged." Trump is highly litigious with media organizations and, advisers say, his appetite for launching lawsuits hasn't diminished. Some advisers outside of the Trump White House noticed that administration officials may be telegraphing another avenue to attack Politico as a malign foreign influence because it's owned by a German company, Axel Springer. "Politico is a foreign-op designed to interfere in American politics and meddle in our elections with disinformation and misinformation," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote on X Saturday.

events.title: Tesla posted a highlight reel of its robotaxi avoiding collisions with rivals Waymo and Avride
events.summary: Tesla posted a highlight reel showing off its robotaxi navigating real-world road conditions, including robotaxis getting in the way. Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images Tesla posted footage of its robotaxi driving without a safety driver ahead of its Q3 earnings call. Two of the clips included footage of a Waymo robotaxi and Avride encroaching on Tesla's path. The clips showed the Tesla Robotaxi slowing down. Tesla took some subtle jabs at its robotaxi competitors ahead of its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday. On a website Tesla created for its robotaxi safety report, the company uploaded clips of its self-driving cars maneuvering in real-world conditions without a driver behind the wheel. Obstacles and hazards included stormy weather, a pedestrian crossing at a green light, stray pets, and rival robotaxis getting in the way. Ashok Elluswamy , Tesla's VP of AI, also posted the video on X, calling it "Robotaxi B-roll." Robotaxi B-roll https://t.co/NWO7Ak2h1I — Ashok Elluswamy (@aelluswamy) October 21, 2026 At around the 1:44 mark of Elluswamy's post, the video shows a robotaxi coming to a complete stop in its own lane as a Waymo makes a wider-than-usual right turn. The Waymo can be seen encroaching into Tesla's lane before it returns to its own path. A Waymo spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment. In another short clip, the Tesla robotaxi is seen driving at night, braking for an Avride car that pulled up from the right, a little too far into the Tesla's path. Avride is a robotaxi company that offers robotaxi rides through Uber in Dallas and is testing rides with a safety driver behind the wheel in Austin. A spokesperson for Avride did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Tesla posted the footage as it seeks to make its case publicly on robotaxi safety. The company began offering a limited number of autonomous rides without an in-car safety monitor in Austin in January. In the newly posted safety report, Tesla said its robotaxi service has driven 3.3 million miles autonomously — relatively small compared to Waymo's more than 271 million miles driven as of June. Tesla said during its Q3 earnings call that it will launch unsupervised Cybercabs in Dallas in November. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Calls for rent cap to stop WA's spiralling rental market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tenant advocacy groups say cap on rents across Western Australia well overdue Veronica Johnson has felt the brunt of rent increases in the Kimberley region. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) West Australian housing advocacy groups are calling for an urgent cap on rental prices after a report finds two-thirds of people would struggle with a $20-a-week rental increase. The Make Renting Fair Alliance says "runaway rents" have outpaced both inflation and wage growth. The WA government has ruled out capping rents, arguing the move could reduce investment in rental housing and hurt tenants. Rent increases would be capped annually across Western Australia under a new plan pushed by housing advocacy groups. The "Cap Still Fits" report, released today by the Make Renting Fair Alliance, argued Perth tenants could save almost $33,000 over the next five years with a 2 per cent cap on rental increases this year. Regional renters could save about $30,000 based on an average rent of $710 a week, according to the report. Tenants in metropolitan suburbs Churchlands, Scarborough and Fremantle could save the most, with renters in regional locations like Karratha, Exmouth and Port Hedland tipped to save up to $58,812 over five years. The Make Renting Fair Alliance says "runaway rents" have outpaced both inflation and wage growth. ( ABC Kimberley: Gareth McKnight ) Alliance spokesperson Kate Miller said stabilisation of the rental market was long overdue. "Rent shouldn't be a free-for-all where renters are expected to cough up infinitely," she said. "We need a system that gives renters and landlords certainty and stops housing costs from spiralling further." Financial counsellor's 'rental nightmare' It is a situation Broome financial counsellor Veronica Johnson is all too familiar with, for both professional and personal reasons. Working regularly across the Kimberley to help the region's vulnerable residents with monetary problems, she was recently "looking down the barrel" of homelessness herself after her lease ended. Ms Johnson had rented a unit in the town, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, since 2021, with rent jumping from $480 to $740 a week over that period. Veronica Johnson says without assistance from her employer she was facing potential homelessness. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) The only suitable option was an almost identical unit in the same complex, but on a different floor, at $1,000 a week. "We're looking at exactly the same unit in the same complex," she said. "That's over a 100 per cent increase and I can't imagine any mortgages would be that much. "People are shocked to find someone that is actually representing people and assisting people can no longer actually be able to afford to live here." There are calls for a cap in WA to nullify soaring rental prices. ( ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills ) Ms Johnson was only able to afford the rent after her employer chipped in to help. After more than a decade of consideration, the WA government introduced a swathe of rental reforms in 2023 , including restricting landlords to one rent increase a year. But it stopped short of rental caps or freezes, arguing substantive change could have unintended consequences on the rental market. Maiy Azize says renters are being forced to make "dire" choices. ( Supplied ) But renter advocacy group Everybody's Home argued increases as low as $20 a week were increasingly unaffordable for the average tenant. Spokesperson Maiy Azize said a separate survey of 1,100 renters, home owners and people in temporary housing found rising costs had tenants at their absolute limit. "Even these amounts that can seem small really add up (after) years of relentless rent increases," she said. "Fuel costs have really gone up in the last couple of years, the cost of food has gone up … [and] electricity bills." Ms Azize said tenants were too afraid to report maintenance issues, fearing it could result in higher rent orleases not being extended. Critics warn of unintended consequences Real Estate Institute of WA president Rob Mandanici said caps offer short-term protection for current renters at the expense of those looking for somewhere to rent. "Rent caps might sound appealing, but they come at a significant cost to the broader rental market," he said. "A cap may benefit existing tenants, but it does nothing to address the underlying shortage of rental homes. "Instead, it risks discouraging investment, driving rental property owners out of the market and making an already difficult situation worse.

events.title: Meta creates a new stock class to keep Zuckerberg in control
events.summary: Meta wants to continue its "founder-led model" — so it's creating a new stock class. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta established a new class of stock to ensure Mark Zuckerberg stayed as CEO. The stock class will "continue the founder-led model that has driven the company," Meta said in its third-quarter earnings. Zuckerberg has taken a leading position in Meta's AI era. Meta's board wants Mark Zuckerberg to stick around. The company announced a new category of non-voting Class C stock in its third-quarter earnings report. It listed several reasons for creating the new class — one of which is to keep the CEO in control.
