events.title: Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores
events.summary: Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.” The change, which applies to all bookings made on or after November 20, quickly sparked outrage after it was announced in an email to Airbnb hosts on Wednesday. Many began fuming online about losing the right to make their guests clean up after themselves. “As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official forum for hosts. “The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves.” “Airbnb is like an abusive partner,” wrote one user on the Reddit community r/airbnb_hosts. “I'm alive long enough to recognize how truthful those few words are,” another person replied . “Until and unless I see substantive changes, I'm finally out.” A different self-described host declared that going forward, the kitchens in their rentals will be “stripped down to only bare essentials.” Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out. “The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.” Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by putting cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites include asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers. In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit Save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read “Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task.” Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.” If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed or be banned from the platform entirely. In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike. “Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.” Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.” (Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable but against current Airbnb policy.) “First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’” another person said , though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans. Unwanted smoking and other serious scenarios—like letting dirty dishes become “ health hazards ,” leaving “permanent stains on sheets,” and creating “mountains of rotting garbage”—were invoked by several hosts.

events.title: Tesla's profits are under pressure
events.summary: Tesla's earnings call was on Wednesday, a day after Elon Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call that he'd back a merger. Bloomberg/Getty Images Tesla is facing some profitability headwinds. Its operating income fell 56% year over year as AI and research and development costs climbed. The company is still in the green, and it surprised earlier this month by delivering 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter. Tesla is still selling plenty of cars . Making the same amount of money on them is getting harder. On Wednesday, the Elon Musk-led automaker reported that its operating income fell 56% year over year to $718 million in the third quarter — below Wall Street's estimates of $746.3 million — while overall revenue of $28.05 billion came in a smidge below analysts' estimates. Tesla pointed to higher operating expenses tied to its AI efforts, or "SI"/"Super Intelligence" as Trump prefers , and other R&D projects. Lower regulatory credit revenue and weaker energy storage gross profit also weighed on profitability, while lower vehicle prices hurt revenue. "While we continue to execute on innovations to reduce the cost of manufacturing and operations, over time, we expect our hardware-related profits to be accompanied by an acceleration of SI, software and fleet-based profits," the company reported. It's not all bad news for Tesla's profits. The company is still solidly in the green, and it beat on the bottom line. Tesla reported 48 cents in adjusted earnings per share, above the 44-cent analyst consensus estimate. Free cash flow of $1.5 billion was also a surprise after Wall Street had expected negative free cash flow of $4.92 billion. The automaker also sees areas of profit growth in its future: autonomy subscriptions are trending up, and Tesla said it's offering the right, region-specific product mixes. During the earnings call, Tesla's chief financial officer, Vaibhav Taneja, said the company is experiencing its "highest backlog" of vehicles in four years. The company, he said, is trying to increase vehicle production. He also added that Tesla has secured $30 billion of borrowing to support expected capital expenditures, but the company doesn't expect to "make any draws under any of the new facilities in this calendar year." "The main takeaway is that Tesla's surprisingly positive cash flow quarter did not come from stronger profits," Thomas Monteiro, senior analyst at Investing.com, said after the report. "Added to the equation is the fact that Tesla's AI spending remains broadly inefficient, with research costs up nearly 70% and operating margins down to just 2.6%, while at SpaceX AI is already one of the biggest sources of revenue," the analyst added. The new quarter has already made waves The Tesla story continues to play out in real time, and it's had a busy month since the fourth quarter kicked off in October. On Tuesday, during SpaceX's earnings call, Musk said that Tesla and SpaceX had each formed committees to explore a potential merger. Both companies are helmed by Musk — and he owns billions of dollars in stock of each. Anticipation of the potential mega-merger has been building around the companies for much of 2026, and has only increased since SpaceX went public. Musk said he was not included in those committees and that calling the merger a foregone conclusion "would be overstating it." It also came less than a week after Tesla held its high-flying demo for the Roadster . The sports car performed a gymnastics routine, including briefly jumping into the air and twirling over a lineup of other Tesla vehicles. Tesla had a high-flying demo for the coming Roadster. It came nine years after the company first floated the sports car. Tesla It came nine years after Tesla first promised to relaunch the Roadster. Musk first showed off a prototype of the vehicle in 2017 and predicted a 2020 product launch. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump administration wants to reconsider permit for offshore wind project
events.summary: The Trump administration is asking a federal judge to let it reconsider a major federal permit granted for a large offshore wind farm, making it the fourth project the Republican leadership has targeted in recent months WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration is asking a federal judge to let it reconsider a major federal permit granted for a large offshore wind farm, making it the fourth project the Republican leadership has targeted in recent months. The Interior Department wants to reconsider its own approval for the “construction and operations plan” for the New England Wind project off of Massachusetts. The plan was approved in 2024 during the Biden administration. The Justice Department said in a filing Tuesday the court should remand the permit, sending it back to Interior, because the plan was approved despite major adverse impacts. The developer, Avangrid, declined to comment Wednesday. Construction has not begun. The Trump administration is using executive orders, agency actions and the courts to try to stop the development of offshore wind, an industry and technology that President Donald Trump has attacked as “ugly” and unreliable compared to fossil fuels such as coal and natural gas. It started buying back offshore wind leases after federal judges blocked its efforts to stop construction on five major East Coast projects. U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat, warned that the administration now risks derailing a legislative effort to speed up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects. The Senate reached a bipartisan deal in September on a permitting bill, which has not yet been voted on. “This is how you blow up a permitting deal,” he said in a statement Wednesday. The Interior Department also wants to reconsider its prior approval of the construction and operations plan for Revolution Wind, a wind farm for Rhode Island and Connecticut that has finished construction, and for the Maryland Offshore Wind Project, which has not yet begun construction. In August, a judge granted the administration's request to reconsider the permit for the stalled New Jersey project Atlantic Shores. That project had been halted soon after Trump returned to office because co-owner Shell walked away from it . Last year, a federal judge said the Trump administration could reconsider the permit granted to the Massachusetts project SouthCoast Wind days before the president’s inauguration. Pasha Feinberg, an offshore wind strategist at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said the Trump administration’s attacks on offshore wind are escalating at a time when Americans are struggling with surging utility bills. The National Ocean Industries Association, which represents offshore industries including oil and wind, said it's concerned about the uncertainty that comes with reopening federal approvals for offshore energy projects, particularly those already under construction or in operation. The plans for New England Wind call for up to 129 wind turbines that could supply as much as 2,600 megawatts of clean energy to power more than 900,000 homes each year. Couple charged in fatal shooting of 17-year-old on her way to zoo Some changes are coming for Medicare as open enrollment begins Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Its federal approval was challenged in court by ACK for Whales, a group of Nantucket, Massachusetts, residents who say they are concerned about the negative impacts of offshore wind development. The lawsuit in District Court for the District of Columbia contends that the federal government failed to comply with numerous statutes. The federal defendants in the case filed a motion Tuesday stating that remand of the permit is warranted, so Interior could make a new decision. The government also told the court in 2025 it wanted to reconsider New England Wind’s approval. Interior said Wednesday that the latest filing complied with a briefing schedule, and was not announcing a policy change. It says its position on offshore wind has remained consistent throughout this administration. Avangrid built another wind farm, Vineyard Wind, off the coast of Massachusetts in a joint venture with Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners. Construction finished in March , making it the first project to reach this stage during Trump’s time in office. Vineyard Wind was one of the projects the administration tried to halt construction on , citing concerns over national security. McDermott reported from Providence, R.I. events.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
events.summary: Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this year Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices. A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data. "The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices". Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful. The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety. New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal. That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time. New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added. Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been. They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable." The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter. He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order. While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine. It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices. Campaigners welcome Meta and YouTube's defeat in landmark social media addiction trial Published 27 March Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant Published 7 August New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children. The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children". As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race. Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people. "Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said. To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn. The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.

events.title: Trump denies ordering Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, says he doesn't know who did
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink in Ukraine. "I don't know who did it," Trump said when asked if SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk was behind the change to the satellite service. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Musk ordered the slowdown and discussed it with Trump. President Donald Trump on Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX 's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know if Elon Musk was responsible for speed-capping the critical satellite service. Trump's latest denial came one day after The Wall Street Journal , citing unnamed U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, reported Musk ordered the slowdown and discussed it with Trump. "I wasn't involved," Trump told a reporter when asked about the decision as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in South Carolina. When pressed to answer if Musk, SpaceX's founder and CEO, ordered the slowdown, Trump said, "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved." The recent disruption of Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, rendered some Ukrainian drones effectively useless, weakening defenses against Russian attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said his military still faces "speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in different parts of the front." "No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," he said. The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk and Trump discussed the move to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, citing two people familiar with the matter. One of the people who spoke with the news outlet claimed Musk discussed the matter with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump himself, prior to imposing the Starlink speed cap. Trump and Musk have both recently ramped up their criticism of Zelenskyy. But neither of them has yet identified who ordered the Starlink disruption. Musk said on X last week that Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government" and that any speed or usage limits are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Earlier Wednesday, Zelesnkyy said he and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik "discussed in detail launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors." "We will involve partners who have the capacity to provide support," Zelenskyy said in an X post . Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday morning that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."

events.title: New Mexico AG lawsuit accuses Epstein's attorney and accountant of facilitating sex trafficking
events.summary: New Mexico's attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein's long-time personal lawyer and accountant for allegedly facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation. The suit alleges the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico. New Mexico 's attorney general on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit accusing Jeffrey Epstein 's long-time personal lawyer and accountant of facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation. The civil suit alleges the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico. Indyke and Kahn are beneficiaries of Epstein's 1953 Trust, co-executors of Epstein's estate, and administrators of the revocable trust, whose name comes from the year of the convicted sex offender's birth. New Mexico's suit asks a judge to block Indyke and Kahn from receiving payments from the estate as the case proceeds in U.S. District Court in New Mexico. The suit alleges the two men participated in a sex trafficking venture in violation of the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act; and that they violated New Mexico's Racketeering Act by engaging in kidnapping, criminal solicitation and conspiracy. Attorney General Raul Torrez's office said Epstein's estate is currently valued at more than $107 million, and the suit says Indyke and Kahn are eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million, subject to the availability of funds. "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," Torrez said in a statement, which was released as he appeared at a press conference flanked by two survivors of abuse by Epstein, Anouska De Georgiou and Julia Molchanova. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working "The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences." The suit comes a month after The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York had opened an investigation into Indyke and Kahn. De Georgiou said at the press conference that her abuse by Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, "did not happen in isolation." "It could not have continued for as long as it did without people facilitating it, looking the other way, or choosing to do nothing to stop it," De Georgiou said. "Accountability cannot end with Epstein and Maxwell. It must extend to those who knowingly made their abuse possible, especially those who stand to profit from it. That includes anyone who knowingly helped make Epstein appear legitimate to conceal his abuse of women and girls." Daniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, in a statement to CNBC, said, "Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr. Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him." "They are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them," Weiner said. "Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," Weiner said. "Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have given multiple depositions in civil lawsuits and have testified at length before the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform," the attorney said. "Had the New Mexico Attorney General wanted to learn the actual facts of their professional services for Epstein, the Attorney General or his staff could have reached out to schedule interviews. Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so." The lawsuit alleges Indyke and Kahn personally profited from their relationship to Epstein, who killed himself in a federal jail in New York in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on child sex trafficking charges. "Between 2011 and 2019, Indyke received more than $16 million from Epstein and related entities, and Kahn received more than $10 million," Torrez's office said in a statement.

events.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet, its answer to Meta and OpenAI's personal agents
events.summary: Ami Vora, Anthropic's chief product officer, and Daniela Amodei, its president. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Anthropic has its answer to AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots. Claude Duet, built on Anthropic's flagship model, has entered the personal agent frenzy. Karan Ahuja, a recent departee from Meta, led Claude Duet's development. Anthropic is joining the personal AI agent craze . The company announced the new app Claude Duet on Wednesday, billed as a "proactive agent" that can run in the background, surface tasks to a user, and handle a variety of work. The tool is in research preview for now with a waitlist, meaning it won't immediately compete for the larger market with other new agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots . Still, the announcement ramps up the pressure on those companies — Anthropic says it built Duet around its flagship Opus 5.5 model, which was released in late September and has already become one of the industry's most popular. Recent model breakthroughs have made AI better at handling work on its own, spurring a rush to build these "always-on" personal agents. "It can have the discernment and judgment around when to be proactive, when to act on your behalf," said Mike Krieger, a co-lead of Anthropic's Labs team, said in a Duet launch video. The tool, Anthropic says, will send users a brief each morning about what's happening on their connected apps, and message them when something needs attention. Like other companies' offerings, it runs outside a user's computer, sends notifications, and asks for approval on certain tasks. Anthropic announced Duet on the day of Meta's earnings report and used the opportunity to mention a new poach from Mark Zuckerberg's company. Karan Ahuja led product management for Meta Superintelligence Labs until July, according to his LinkedIn, before starting at Anthropic in August and leading Duet's development. He wrote on X that he's been using Duet to build Duet, and said the team "built it for professionals and small business owners juggling a lot at work and at home." Ahuja also wrote that Anthropic is letting people into Duet from the waitlist "as quickly as possible." The news didn't go unnoticed at Meta. Alexandr Wang, who heads Meta Superintelligence Labs, posted a meme about Duet's similarity to Muse. Anthropic is fast approaching a giant initial public offering, which could value the company at as much as $2 trillion. Like other AI players, the company navigates a high-wire competition to win over users, secure computing power, build state-of-the-art models, and deliver AI-native products. The data firm Apptopia estimates that Muse had more than 14 million installations as of Wednesday. It found that Claude users who installed the Muse app were using Claude more than before, though still for fewer minutes per day than they spent on the Meta product. Have a tip? events.title: Nasdaq leads Wall Street gains as SpaceX, Super Micro boost AI sentiment
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading, on Oct 21, in New York City. Nasdaq led Wall Street higher as SpaceX and Super Micro lifted AI shares. SpaceX posted its first profit as a public company, and Musk said a SpaceX-Tesla merger would be “a good idea”. Super Micro rose 9.6% after forecasting revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates. This eased worries about AI spending and helped HPE and Dell gain too. The S&P 500 rose 0.58% and the Nasdaq gained 1.05%, but communication services fell 1.3%. AT&T, Netflix and Alphabet dragged on gains, while investors watched more earnings. NEW YORK - The tech-heavy Nasdaq led Wall Street to a higher close on Oct 21, after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer improved investor appetite for artificial intelligence-related stocks while weakness in communication services stocks capped gains. SpaceX shares finished up 7.8% after Elon Musk’s rocket and space technology firm posted its first profit as a public company. Musk said, following the report, that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea”, also boosting Tesla shares. Elsewhere in earnings, Super Micro shares jumped 9.6% and it was among the S&P 500‘s top gainers after the AI server maker forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, signalling that AI demand remained resilient. The report also benefited peers HPE, which rose 3.7%, and Dell, which rose 5.3%. The reports provided some reassurance to investors who have been worried about the sustainability of massive spending on AI buildouts and their profitability. The technology sector was hammered last week by a selloff in AI-linked stocks, with data centre operator CoreWeave at the centre of the storm. The SpaceX news “pushes back on some of the investor worries” about AI along with some help from Super Micro, according to Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. Kourkafas said the reports will not “answer all the questions investors have on returns on AI investments, but it’s a good start.” As a result, the S&P 500 Information Technology index finished up 1.6%, the biggest gainer among the S&P 500‘s 11 major industry sectors. “It’s really a positive technology story for almost anyone that is somewhat involved in the artificial intelligence ecosystem,” said Marc Dizard, chief investment officer at Huntington Bank. “The technology market reaction has been a reaffirmation that the artificial intelligence trade is still intact,” he added. However, Dizard said sentiment can quickly shift around AI and that investors will seek reaffirmation when they monitor earnings reports from other companies. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09, the S&P 500 gained 44.60 points, or 0.58%, to 7,757.17 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 278.04 points, or 1.05%, to 26,702.86. Within technology, one of the strongest areas was chips with a 2% rally in the Philadelphia Semiconductor index, which has had a volatile month so far including an eight-session selloff. Gains in the benchmark S&P 500 were limited however by a 1.3% decline in communication services stocks. The biggest losers included telecom operators such as AT&T, which sank 6.5% even as it beat third-quarter revenue and profit expectations. The SpaceX results, along with a recent wireless spectrum purchase, fanned fears that it could become a formidable competitor in telecoms, according to Dizard. T-Mobile US shares fell 2.5% and Verizon Communications lost 2.2%. Also in communications services, Netflix shares sank 5.3% after the video streaming company issued a weaker-than-expected forecast for its fourth-quarter profit. Google’s parent Alphabet also declined 1.6%. Abbott Laboratories shares dropped 1.9% after the medical device maker cut its 2026 sales growth forecast. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.37-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 131 new highs and 221 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 2,690 stocks rose and 2,068 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.3-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 26 new 52-week highs and 3 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 216 new lows. On US exchanges roughly 16.11 billion shares changed hands compared with the 17.10 billion average for the last 20 sessions. REUTERS

events.title: GM's OnStar gets an AI makeover — but humans will still answer when airbags deploy
events.summary: GM executives confirmed to Business Insider that humans are still staffing OnStar call centers to handle emergencies. General Motors GM says it's keeping humans in its OnStar call centers to help with emergencies. It comes as OnStar is getting a fresh makeover, complete with AI. "The stakes are too high," an exec told BI about the human-in-the-loop. GM is giving OnStar an AI overhaul. The automaker says it is not coming for the person who answers when your airbags deploy. On Wednesday, during the company's tech conference, GM Forward, Ed Nightingale, GM's vice president of digital products, told Business Insider that the automaker would continue to use human OnStar staffers on emergency calls to contact first responders. "That's something that isn't changing," Nightingale said. "We feel that, when it comes to a crash or a problem being solved, they want to make sure that there's a human in the loop. The stakes are too high." After publication, a GM spokesperson told Business Insider that OnStar Advisors "aren't going away" and will remain a core part of the OnStar experience. Humans-in-the-loop are a notable constraint on GM's AI ambitions compared to other software companies. Other AI-enabled companies, such as SpaceX, have recently highlighted how few customer calls are routed to humans. GM said that keeping people involved in complex or sensitive situations is an intentional part of its AI strategy. Technology handles more routine interactions, while humans take the call during an emergency. It also comes as the company gives OnStar — its 30-year-old in-car emergency service — a much bigger job. GM showed off OnStar AI on Wednesday. It's a new voice assistant designed to understand a vehicle and the driver using it. The automaker said it can answer questions about vehicle alerts, control some functions, plan routes around bad weather, and offer more context-aware suggestions, including from information through a driver's digital calendar. The assistant will arrive first on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq via an over-the-air update in the coming months, GM said. Other vehicles will follow. GM also plans to unify its brand-specific mobile apps under the OnStar AI name next summer. Onstage, Sterling Anderson, GM's chief product officer, said the company was turning the 30-year-old service into "an intelligent platform." The shift is part of a large bet from GM. GM is focusing heavily on its tech capabilities. On recent earnings calls, CEO Mary Barra has highlighted GM's subscription products . Anderson previously told Business Insider about how AI has allowed the company to cut product development time in half , starting with the GMC Hummer EV, which only took 20 months of development. Industry-average product development is typically around 5 years. On Wednesday, the company also highlighted the development of its hands-off, eyes-off self-driving features, set to make their debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. GM still has to persuade drivers that the new tools are valuable enough to use — and, in some cases, pay for. Nightingale said subscriptions only retain customers when drivers can see the benefit. events.title: The 'Fourth Wing' TV show has cast its Violet and Xaden. Here's everything we know so far.
events.summary: Two actors have been cast in the "Fourth Wing" adaptation. TheStewartofNY/GC Images/Getty Images/Red Tower The "Fourth Wing" TV show has its Violet and Xaden. Amazon MGM Studios and Michael B. Jordan's Outlier Society are adapting Rebecca Yarros' series. Amazon announced in October that the show had found its two lead actors. At this point, it's hard not to be familiar with Rebecca Yarros' "Empyrean" series about dragon rider Violet Sorrengail. When "Onyx Storm," the third book in the romantasy series , was released in January 2025, it became the fastest-selling adult novel in 20 years. Yarros is working on the fourth installment in the series, and she recently released a collection of short stories set in the "Empyrean" universe called "Threshing Day." However, it will still be a while before book four is ready for readers. In the meantime, though, we're getting closer to a series adaptation of "Fourth Wing," which officially found its lead actors. 'Fourth Wing' is becoming a TV show In October 2023, Deadline announced that Amazon MGM Studios and Michael B. Jordan's Outlier Society were developing "Fourth Wing" into a TV series. Yarros is an executive producer for the show. Outlier Society produced Jordan's " Creed III " and is developing a slate of other series and films in addition to "Fourth Wing." Deadline also reported in October 2023 that Amazon MGM Studios had acquired the rights to the entire "Empyrean" series. In her January 2025 Variety interview, Yarros said she had shared the "five-book arc" for the "Empyrean" series with Amazon. "Fourth Wing" by Rebecca Yarros. Red Tower Publishing "They have the five-book arc, which went a little awry in Book 3 just because the positioning, but they already know that," she told Variety. "But they have the five-book arc and the general big points of what happens in between each book, but they don't have the specifics between Book 4 and Book 5, because I'm getting ready to go to my crazy plotting board and plot out every single event that happens in each book, so that I make sure that I'm within my two books there." A new showrunner In July 2024, Outlier Society announced it had hired Moira Walley-Beckett, who worked on shows like "Breaking Bad" and "Anne with an E," as the showrunner for the series. In a January 2025 interview with Variety, Yarros said Walley-Beckett was "great" and "phenomenal," but in July 2025, Walley-Beckett exited the project. Variety reported in September 2025 that Meredith Averill was taking over as showrunner. Averill was previously the showrunner of the Netflix series "Locke & Key" and a producer on shows like "The Good Wife" and "The Haunting of Hill House." Meredith Averill is set to be the showrunner for the "Fourth Wing" series. Jemal Countess/FilmMagic/Getty Images Amazon declined to comment on this piece when contacted by Business Insider, but Yarros shared a screenshot of a Deadline article about the showrunner announcement on her Instagram when it dropped. "Welcome to the team, Meredith Averill! Guys, I love everything this wonderful woman has worked on and I'm so excited to have her joining us," Yarros said in her caption. 'Fourth Wing' is in the works In January 2026, Jordan assured fans the "Fourth Wing" show was on its way in an interview with Deadline. "We are making sure that this is going to be an exciting show that delivers on all of the things the fans want and some of the things that they won't be expecting either," Jordan said. He also told the outlet that he's aware of how much fans of "Fourth Wing" care about the series. "But trust me, I know how beloved this franchise IP is," he said. "It's early stages, but I feel how much people care about this one. It's not lost on us." And on May 11, 2026, Jordan announced the show had been ordered to series for Prime Video at the Amazon Upfront, an annual event where Amazon offers a sneak peek at its coming content. Rebecca Yarros, Lisa Joy, Meredith Averill, and Michael B. Jordan onstage at the Amazon Upfront in May 2026. Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Amazon Yarros and Averill joined Jordan onstage at the event, as did Lisa Joy, an executive producer on the show who will direct the first episode. Joy has previously worked on shows like HBO's "Westworld" and Prime Video's "Fallout." Meredith Averill, Michael B. Jordan, Rebecca Yarros, and Lisa Joy at the Amazon Upfront in May 2026. Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images for Amazon Yarros posted about the event on her Instagram story, sharing a photo of herself, Jordan, Averill, and Joy, writing, "What an absolutely wild night! So grateful for this team!" Meet Violet and Xaden The Amazon Upfront seemed to build momentum for the show, as it was announced in October that the Prime Video series had cast its Violet Sorrengail and her enemy turned lover Xaden Riorson. Deadline first reported the casting on October 15, 2026, though the streamer didn't confirm that news until October 21. Esther McGregor will play Violet. McGregor, the 24-year-old daughter of Ewan McGregor, appeared in " Babygirl " and "We Were Liars," another Amazon adaptation. Esther McGregor in New York City in May 2026. TheStewartofNY/GC Images/Getty Images Meanwhile, 30-year-old Emilio Sakraya has been cast as Xaden. The German actor is known for projects like "Rheingold" and the popular Netflix series "Warrior Nun." Both actors are relative newcomers, though, with their "Fourth Wing" casting marking a big step in their careers. McGregor reshared Amazon's post about her casting to her Instagram story, writing, "So beyond excited. Honored. Thrilled." Sakraya also shared the post to his Instagram story, but he captioned it with a quote from "Iron Flame," the second book in Yarros' series, in a fun nod to the text: "My house. My chair. My Woman." Emilio Sakraya in November 2025 in New York City. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images In a statement shared by Amazon , Yarros said, "I'm so grateful to our producing and casting team for conducting a thorough, worldwide search to find Violet and Xaden. It will be incredibly exciting to see these talented actors, Esther and Emilio, bring our beloved characters to life on screen." Yarros said at a London event in August 2024 that she intentionally never shared any hopes for which actors may be cast in the show. "I will never say who my perfect fan cast is because the cast is so diverse, and I want to open that up to more diversity," she said. "And I feel like the second I say who I think this character is, that's who everyone will accept. That's only who they will accept." "I kinda hope they find, like, an up-and-coming generation," she added. "But I would never put my fan cast in your heads." At the same event, she clarified that she wouldn't be involved in the casting process, but that she had shared one hard-line casting request with Amazon and Outlier Society. "They know how staunch I am against whitewashing Xaden," she said. "I think that's the biggest thing.

events.title: AI uncovers massive flaw in web's foundational code
events.summary: Security officials are sounding the alarm over two critical vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI . Why it matters : The bugs, which researchers found partly with an OpenAI model, proves AI can uncover critical flaws humans missed for decades — raising the stakes for defenders racing to fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them at machine speed. What's happening: There are two problems hackers could easily exploit in an open-source programming language known as PHP that's used on nearly 70% of all websites . Government officials from the U.S. to Japan are warning companies to apply a patch to fix the bugs, or consider taking down their sites to avoid an attack. OpenAI touted the role its model played in discovering one of the vulnerabilities, which allowed PHP researchers to create a fix. Between the lines: Security researchers have been skeptical of AI-generated vulnerability reports, many of which have turned out to be minor bugs or false alarms. But the PHP discovery could force the cybersecurity community to reckon with the reality of AI threats. "It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post Wednesday. Threat level: If exploited, the PHP flaws would allow malicious hackers to take control of vulnerable web servers without needing a password or other credentials. Since PHP runs under a wide variety of internet applications, that access could allow hackers to take over websites, steal sensitive information and tamper with a website. Some website owners took their sites down earlier Wednesday, including certain services at Wikipedia and 4chan , until they had time to patch their systems. "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," researchers at Wiz wrote in a post. The big picture: AI-driven bug discoveries are shining a light on the fragility of the modern internet, which is heavily reliant on a slew of open-source software powered by volunteers . The two flaws in PHP existed for decades, but demonstrated that it was possible for a hacker to exploit them required "an exceptionally complex chain of steps," researchers at Wiz added. "Defenders have always relied on the gap between 'vulnerable' and 'exploitable' to buy time to patch," Michael Leland, field CTO at Island, said in an email to Axios. "That gap is rapidly closing." What to watch : Cybersecurity defenders are on guard for what could be a wave of incidents where websites and organizations are hacked using these two vulnerabilities in the next few weeks. events.title: Walmart rolls out AI agent shopping features while Amazon tries to curb the tech
events.summary: Walmart is adding tools it says will make AI agent shopping easier. Bloomberg/Getty Images Walmart is rolling out two new tools to help third-party AI agents shop on behalf of customers. The company says the tools give people more control of their bots, and help bots be more accurate. Walmart's move contrasts with Amazon's approach, after it blocked Meta's agent Muse from its site. Walmart wants your bot to shop. The retail giant said Wednesday that it has two new tools to help third-party AI agents shop on customers' behalf: agent profiles and an agent gateway. The agent profiles link all transactions to the bot that performed them, and allow Walmart customers to manage authorizations and spending limits as they would for an additional user on their credit card account, the company said. With agent gateways, bots no longer have to navigate a website that is designed for humans . Instead, Walmart is granting access through a model text protocol that it says will help agents work more quickly and accurately. Walmart's move contrasts with Amazon's approach, which recently blocked Meta's agent Muse from its site, saying agents violate Amazon's conditions of use. Amazon has also pushed back on other third-party agents, including a lawsuit against Perplexity and restrictions on agents from Google and OpenAI. "As customers begin using agents to help them shop, we're building connections, permissions and options that complement those tools and support how customers want to use them," the company said in a statement. The company also said the gateway protects the information that Walmart has about its customers, and only provides what is necessary for completing a given transaction. In particular, the gateway can share a relevant pattern or preference — such as a customer's favorite laundry detergent brand — without sharing their entire purchase history with the agent. The company also laid out a set of terms and conditions regarding how AI agents are expected to operate when shopping. Under the terms, the company said it will honor its usual returns policy and that agents will always see the same pricing that a human would see on Walmart.com. events.title: TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026: Everything you need to know
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. TechCrunch Founder Summit is a full-day gathering in Boston on November 4 where founders across all stages connect with top VCs and experienced entrepreneurs to gain tactical insights on building and scaling their companies. It’s the latest in our long line of founder-centric events, which are smaller and more hands-on than Disrupt. For the founder looking to really get in the weeds during a one-day crash course, Founder Summit is the ideal place to get a head start on your 2027 plans for everything from hiring, establishing product market fit, finding investors, improving your leadership skills, and more. Before you dig in on the event details, you can get info on all of our tickets, which are available for a $100 discount for investors and founders, right here . Even if you’re a student and an aspiring founder, or an investor looking to meet the next wave of East Coast innovators, we have an option for you. Who is TechCrunch Founder Summit for? All founders end up wrestling with the extensive, complicated mechanics of building a company from the ground up. There’s fundraising, hiring, legal, marketing, PR, and leadership, as well as the investors needing the means to vet, invest in, and develop founders as they build out their skills. Founder Summit is the best way to cover all of the challenging questions with community members who have been there, and lived to tell the tale, through constructive failure and massive success. When and where is TechCrunch Founder Summit? The event takes place on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, at the SoWa Power Station in Boston. It’s accessible via public transportation and a short walk from the Back Bay and Tufts Medical Center stops on the Orange Line, or the Broadway stop on the Red Line. What’s on the TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda? To deliver on that promise of equipping founders for success, this year’s agenda and speakers lean hard into fundraising, AI-native building, and leadership. Sessions include: Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself: Toast Co-founder and Director Steve Fredette shares his insights on keeping a company relevant amid evolving technologies and changing customer expectations. The Boston Founder Playbook : HqO co-founder and CEO Chase Garbarino on building a category-defining company outside Silicon Valley, having raised $200 million and scaled to 30+ countries. Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale : Bessemer Venture Partners ‘ Kent Bennett on validating demand and avoiding scaling before the fundamentals are in place. Built for AI From Day One : 7AI co-founder and CEO Lior Div on what changes when AI is the foundation of a company rather than a bolt-on feature. Not Every Dollar Is Equal : Cogent Security co-founder and CEO Vineet Edupuganti on evaluating investors and cap-table trade-offs beyond valuation. How to Spot the ‘King of the Hill’ Company : TDK Ventures investment director Tina Tosukhowong unpacking a framework for evaluating startups on economics, scalability, and timing. Your Pitch Has to Near the Next Conversation : TrueVentures Partner and Edisyl CEO Dave Balter instills the importance of making sure your pitch doesn’t just wow, but that it sparks a continued conversation throughout every minute of its delivery. We’re glad you asked! Founder Summit will once again feature the much-requested So You Think You Can Pitch? competition, during which three early stage startups will try to impress a panel of judges within four minutes each. Their approaches, and the judges’ feedback, is invaluable for improving your own pitches. Didn’t this event have a different name? Yes. Founder Summit was formerly known as Early Stage and All Stage . This year, we have the same mission, but with a new name. Keep that in mind if you want to do any more research before attending. Is TechCrunch Founder Summit just panels, or is there more to it? Founder Summit is far from a series of panels, though the agenda does provide a ton of valuable insights for founders and investors. In addition to all of those sessions, we also have our breakout sessions, where even more intimate panels discuss vital topics for the community to dive deeper into. There’s also networking available via the Braindate app to help connect investors with founders, or facilitate founders with similar challenges to bring their expertise together to reach shared solutions. Or that time is the perfect opportunity for students to build out their nascent network. Then there’s Founder Summit week, taking place November 1-7. That’s when all of our Side Events are held , expanding the opportunities for you to gather with the community. And if you’re especially eager to take part, you can apply to host your own Side Event right here . How much does a ticket cost, and how can I get the best price?

events.title: Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention. He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders. “Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping. Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content. Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said. Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay. Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales. “On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.” Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year. Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].” “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added. events.title: Southwest Airlines cuts 2026 profit forecast on higher fuel
events.summary: Southwest cut its 2026 profit forecast as another jump in fuel prices is eating into its bottom line. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks this month. Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said travel demand remains strong despite higher fares. Southwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares. The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share. Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG: Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expected Revenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expected Southwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year. "Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release. The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people. Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors. For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion. Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. Both of those airlines reported top- and bottom-line misses for the third quarter. events.title: Student-loan borrowers win as Trump drops legal battle to narrow a major forgiveness program for public servants
events.summary: The Trump administration agreed to drop its appeal of a ruling that blocked its plan to limit Public Service Loan Forgiveness. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images The Trump administration agreed to drop its appeal of a Public Service Loan Forgiveness ruling. The ruling blocked Trump's plan to limit PSLF eligibility from taking effect. An advocacy group said it's a victory for borrowers pursuing PSLF. Student-loan borrowers pursuing a major forgiveness program got a rare legal win. On Wednesday, the Trump administration agreed to drop two of its appeals of a June ruling that had blocked its plan to narrow eligibility for the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years. The Education Department intended to implement a plan on July 1 to exclude employers from PSLF who did not align with the administration's definition of "public service," listing actions like assisting with gender-affirming care or 'acts of terrorism. A judge ruled at the end of June that the plan was unlawful and would not take effect. This followed a series of lawsuits filed by advocacy groups and nonprofits, including Student Defense, which said the education secretary did not have the authority to roll out those changes. The administration appealed the ruling at the end of August. With the appeal set to be dismissed, borrowers will not face any immediate changes to PSLF. Another appeal in a separate PSLF lawsuit is still pending. "The Trump administration's attempt to weaponize public service loan forgiveness against organizations it disagrees with was anti-democratic and unlawful from the start," Dan Zibel, chief counsel at Student Defense, said in a statement. "This is a significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service." The Education Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Undersecretary of Education Nicholas Kent previously said that the rule had been intended to "ensure federal benefits go to our Nation's teachers, first responders, and civil servants who tirelessly serve their communities." Borrowers pursuing PSLF are still facing challenges . The Education Department recently removed some borrowers' payments toward forgiveness, citing Biden-era coding errors. Others have reported delays getting their payments counted toward relief, leaving them in limbo. A department spokesperson previously said that the agency "remains committed to ensuring that every qualifying payment is properly credited to a borrower's account." Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation. The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled. Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company. Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT. Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn , a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it. The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.) The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.” The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched. They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump-aligned super PACs pour millions into once-safe GOP House seats
events.summary: Trump-aligned super political action committees are spending millions in districts Republicans won comfortably in 2024, including Ohio’s 10th, Michigan’s 4th and North Carolina’s 11th, a sign the GOP is being forced to defend a broader House map. Trump’s main super PAC, MAGA Inc., reports spending $300.5 million through Oct. 14 and still held $164.3 million in cash three weeks out from Election Day, new filings show. The spending comes as Republicans defend an expanding House battlefield and Trump’s approval rating sits at 36% in a new New York Times/Siena poll. President Donald Trump has made good on his claim of having put more than $300 million of his political war chest into the 2026 midterm election . New campaign finance filings released Tuesday night show millions flowing into House districts that were barely competitive two years ago, underscoring how far the GOP's problems have spread in the final weeks of the campaign. MAGA Inc. , Trump's main super political action committee, reported $300.5 million in disbursements through Oct. 14, with a quarter of that election cycle total — $75.5 million — being spent in the first two weeks of October, according to new Federal Election Commission filings. It still held $164.3 million in cash, and Trump said Tuesday his political operation would spend more than $400 million by Election Day. Much of the money is moving through two new Trump-aligned groups. MAGA Inc. has sent $200 million to No Going Back PAC and $25 million to Safety & Affordability PAC , which have already reported more than $209 million in independent expenditures between them, according to FEC filings. The spending is also likely to ease months of Republican anxiety that Trump would sit on his massive war chest rather than deploy it in the midterms. GOP operatives had worried as recently as September that MAGA Inc.'s cash would remain largely on the sidelines. Safety & Affordability has spent $3.76 million in Arizona's 1st District, $1.84 million in Maine's 2nd, $1.6 million in Wisconsin's 3rd, $1.48 million in North Carolina's 1st and $1.4 million in Ohio's 10th. It has also put more than $1 million each into Pennsylvania's 8th, Ohio's 9th and Michigan's 7th, according to a CNBC analysis of the PAC's filing . Several are established battlegrounds. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates Wisconsin's 3rd, North Carolina's 1st, Pennsylvania's 8th, Ohio's 9th and Michigan's 7th among its 21 "Toss Up" races. Other places Trump is donating show Republicans being forced onto less familiar terrain. In Ohio's 10th District, Safety & Affordability PAC has spent about $1.4 million defending Republican Rep. Mike Turner, who won by 18 points in 2024. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee now lists the seat among a new tier of possible 2026 pickups , while the National Republican Congressional Committee only began spending there this month, according to AdImpact. No Going Back has also spent roughly $5 million each in Republican-held Michigan's 4th and North Carolina's 11th, while putting another $14.4 million combined into Democratic-held Florida's 14th and 25th, according to a CNBC analysis of the PAC's FEC filing . At the same time, other Republican groups are beginning to triage. The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson , stopped spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st, New Jersey's 7th, Michigan's 8th and Ohio's 1st, the Associated Press reported last week. Trump-aligned groups, meanwhile, have spent about $1.4 million across those four races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Republicans still hold the advertising edge in 25 of the 42 House races rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report, according to AdImpact . But the political environment continues to move toward Democrats. Of the 21 House races Cook rates as "Toss Ups," 16 are Republican-held and five are held by Democrats. Trump's PACs have also spent big in the Senate, according to the new filings. No Going Back has spent nearly $30 million in Michigan , $27.8 million in Ohio , $11.8 million in New Hampshire and $9.9 million in North Carolina , according to a CNBC analysis of the new FEC filings . Those four races alone account for roughly $79 million. Trump's own standing may help explain the pressure. A New York Times/Siena College poll released Wednesday put his approval rating at 36%, with 59% disapproving. Voters in the poll disapproved of his handling of the cost of living by 69% to 29% and gas prices by 73% to 24%. Democrats led by 10 points when voters were presented with the House candidates actually running in their districts. Trump's allies are also trying to solve a turnout problem: getting voters who backed him in presidential elections to show up when he is not on the ballot. MAGA Inc., in its latest filing , reported a $16.2 million Oct. 8 disbursement labeled " voting education .

events.title: Meta narrows capex forecast as it leans into the AI agent wars
events.summary: Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, has spent big on infrastructure for its AI development. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta spent $34.91 billion in capital expenditures in its third quarter. The company is spending big on data centers and other infrastructure for its AI development. Meta predicted $135-145 billion in capex for 2026, aligning with analyst expectations. Meta is making it rain for AI. The company spent $34.91 billion in capital expenditures during the third quarter of 2026. That's up from the second quarter's sum, $31.08 billion. For the year 2026, Meta said it expects to spend between $135-145 billion in capital expenditures, narrowed from its prediction of $130-145 billion last quarter. Meta's forecast includes the yearly capex prediction that analysts expected: $139.79 billion. As Meta bets big on AI, it is investing heavily in its development. It has built massive, costly data centers and spent big on computing power. The spending uptick was expected. On the "Cheeky Pint" podcast earlier this month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg recounted early conversations about the investment — and said he'd bet up to $200 billion on AI, before he knew the models would work. Investors haven't loved Meta's massive capex forecasts in past quarters. The stock tumbled almost 10% last quarter after earnings per share missed Wall Street estimates , and sank 6% the quarter before on raised capex guidance . This quarter, Meta has a new hero product: Muse. The AI assistant has reached over 2 million daily users and 3 million downloads. It quickly scaled the App Store. Muse users told Business Insider they chatted with it to help plan trips and ace exams. The energy around the company is ebullient, as Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, continues to post memes of Muse's squishy-looking mascot. At Meta's Connect keynote event in September, Zuckerberg said Muse "has a novel business model." "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens with the expectation that over time, we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," he said. Muse could help justify the capex guidance for some investors. The stock was trading up 4.12% after-hours at the time of publication. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Another bank announces job cuts — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ASX closes lower, Meta ramps up AI expansion, another bank announces job cuts — as it happened The Australian share market has closed lower after gains on Wall Street. In response to an independent review, the government agreed with KPMG to a further extension of the pause on KPMG bidding for Australian government work until February 28, 2027, after the audit leaks scandal. Meanwhile, another Australian bank, Westpac, announced job cuts, with the union accusing the bank of using NAB's mass redundancy announcement as "cover" for its own restructure. Look back at the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our business blog. Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice. Australian dollar: -0.2% to 70.15 US cents Brent crude: +2% at $US111.1/barrel Choose what information you see below by using filters The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February, following a review that found "serious ethical failings" by its leadership and some of its senior partners. Meta has raised the lower end of its annual spending forecast to help fund its AI expansion, at the same time it copped a staggering $35.6 billion fine. Westpac was accused of quietly cutting jobs while NAB's shocking 2500 mass restructure acted as a 'cover', according to the union. And it's a bye from me too. This will be my last blogging shift in a while. I bid you all adieu! KPMG says it is working on 'lasting change' as ban on government work continues Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into the Big Four firm, following allegations its audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it. KPMG CEO John Sams and its chairman Michael Ebeid said they accepted the findings and recommendations of Mr Watt's review. The firm had appointed Kerry Schott to provide independent oversight and said "while we are making important progress, we know that changing culture takes longer than changing individual roles, structures or controls". "Confidence in KPMG's suitability for Commonwealth work must be earned through evidence of effective, lasting change," the KPMG leadership statement said. KPMG ban on government work extended after 'serious ethical failings' NextDC best performer on today's trade, after horror time yesterday Datacentre operator NextDC came out well and truly as today's winner, with stock prices surging 7.5% by market close, making it the best performer. But don't be deceived — its stock price jump comes after plummeting about 40% yesterday. The firm shed close to half its value in trading yesterday, hitting an eight-year low following a market update. NextDC told investors there would be a delay in supplying electricity to its M3 Melbourne data centre. Management subsequently lowered its earnings target to $245 and $265 million, from between $385 and $410 million. The ASX 200 closed lower Thursday, dropping 0.4% to 8,793 points . Energy was the worst-performing sector, while real estate was the best. Here were our top and bottom performers by individual stock. Tesla's flying cars just a publicity stunt: experts Tesla's flying cars will be as much of a reality as… flying cars, at least according to experts. Earlier this week, Tesla's CEO Elon Musk posted a video of one of the company's 'Roadster' models driving up a wall and then using rocket thrusters to land. "It can basically fly like a rocket. It can do rolls; it can do like crazy gymnastics. Whatever you want really," Mr Musk said. But experts are sceptical, saying safety risks and regulation might prevent widespread availability in Australia. According to them, don't expect them to be driving on (or flying above) Australian roads any time soon. Elon Musk's latest sci-fi dream a 'slick publicity stunt' David Chau's chart of the day: Fortescue's China problem Hello there! Every afternoon, I'll give you a sneak peek at what I'll be discussing on my 7pm News finance report . One thing that caught my eye was Fortescue , which saw its share price drop 4% today — and it's down 34% since the year began! The mining giant has also wiped out all its gains in the past 15 months. Earlier today, Fortescue released a trading update saying it might be forced to mine less iron ore, which will hurt its bottom line. The company has been locked in tense negotiations with China's Mineral Resources Group, a state-owned enterprise that coordinates iron ore purchases for the country's steel mills.
