events.title: Tesla starts Optimus robot production in California as profit falls 43%
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Tesla has started production of its Optimus humanoid robot at its factory in Fremont, California, in a manufacturing space once dedicated to making electric vehicles, the company announced Wednesday. “The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its third-quarter letter to shareholders. “While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product.” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on a conference call that he considers this “early production” and that the ramp will be slow and “somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product.” He nonetheless claimed Tesla will be able to make 20,000 of them per week by the end of 2027. “There’s still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration, so it can’t, like, wear out after a month,” he said. “And there’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks.” That forward-looking development wasn’t enough to lift the company’s otherwise middling third-quarter earnings, results that typify a company in the midst of a major bet. Tesla’s revenue was flat and its expenses skyrocketed as it pressed the accelerator on its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving. The end result was a 43% drop in profits. The company’s revenue was largely driven by EV sales, which were flat year-over-year at $20 billion. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the previous quarter, but fewer than in the same period last year. Tesla’s total third-quarter revenue was $28.04 billion, a skosh below the $28.09 billion it generated in the third quarter of 2025. Tesla’s third-quarter revenue was also about $200 million lower than the previous quarter’s haul of $28.23 billion. Tesla saw a 16% year-over-year decline in revenue from its solar and energy storage business to $2.8 billion, which it blamed on tariff-related customer refunds. There was some positive revenue growth in its services business, a category that includes customer subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance software. Tesla’s services business grew 33% year-over-year, bringing in $4.6 billion and accounting for a record $734 million in gross profit for the quarter. None of this was enough to outpace Tesla’s spending on artificial intelligence projects and its Optimus robot, which took a big bite out of profits. The company reported $787 million in net income, a 43% drop from the same period in 2025, when it earned $1.37 billion. Lower regulatory credit sales also put pressure on its profitability. Tesla executives on the earnings call, including Musk, CFO Vaibhav Taneja, and Ashok Elluswamy, vice president of AI software at Tesla, all took bullish positions on the company’s FSD product, even as the timeline to give consumers the “unsupervised” version was delayed yet again. Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to a supervised version of the software that requires the driver to pay attention and be ready to take over at any time. The unsupervised version would be the equivalent of Level 4 autonomous driving capabilities similar to those used in robotaxis. “We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet,” Elluswamy said, referring to when privately owned Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD (Supervised) would receive a software update enabling unsupervised driving. Musk said during the company’s earnings call in April that the unsupervised version would “probably” be released in the fourth quarter of this year. This story has been updated with information from Tesla’s quarterly conference call. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. events.title: ATO criticised for 'not going in to bat' for millions of Australians underpaid super
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Workers say ATO not doing enough to recoup unpaid superannuation Pauline Devin and Angela Noack are still trying to recover thousands in superannuation their former employer never paid. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) Workers and industry experts are calling on the Australian Taxation Office to be more proactive in responding to unpaid superannuation claims. Data shows one in four workers are underpaid super, and only 15 per cent of that is recovered by the ATO. The ATO says it is serious about ensuring employers are paying super. One in four Australian workers are underpaid superannuation by their employers, amounting to about $6 billion each year, with independent reports showing only about 15 per cent is ever recovered by the tax office. The figures come as no surprise to Pauline Devin and Angela Noack, who were underpaid about $5,000 and $3,000 respectively in super while working at a Brisbane dental clinic two years ago. Early last year, the oral health therapists filed separate complaints with the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), and the regulator found in their favour in April. Millions of Australians have discovered they haven't been paid all of their super. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) But 18 months later, neither have seen a cent returned to their super fund or received any further information from the ATO. "All I ever used to get was, 'No, we can't give you any information because it's an invasion of privacy'," Ms Devin said. "I wasn't asking for financial details or anything like that. "I just wanted to know when I could maybe, possibly, think about getting that superannuation paid to me." The long wait and lack of information from the ATO has left Ms Devin and Ms Noack feeling helpless. Angela Noack says the ATO doesn't "seem to be really going in to bat" for her. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) "I have come to the conclusion I'm probably not ever going to get my super paid from [my employer] at this point, and the ATO don't seem to be really going in to bat and doing anything about recovering that either," Ms Noack said. "The ATO is just useless and hopeless." Pauline Devin says the situation has left her feeling like she's stuck in limbo. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) The ATO declined the ABC's request for an interview, but a spokesperson said in a statement it was "serious about ensuring employers comply with their super obligations and dedicates significant resources to educating employers, undertaking audits and debt recovery actions after liabilities have been raised". The spokesperson also reiterated the ATO's position that "tax secrecy and privacy laws limit what the ATO can disclose to employees" and said where the tax office collected unpaid super on behalf of employees, it advised them accordingly. Funds hire private firm to recoup super Industry Fund Services collects unpaid super on behalf of three super funds, in a role similar to the ATO's regulatory responsibilities. But the firm's executive manager of super recoveries Natalie Lister said the organisation took a more "proactive approach" to super debt recovery. Natalie Lister says her team specialises in recovering unpaid super. ( ABC News: Scott Jewell ) "We'll use digital communications, SMS, email … outbound calls and that's where our specialist team really come in … and [get] an understanding of the employer's situation and working with them to actively resolve it," she said. "If we don't have any success early on, we then have escalation processes, so we'll follow up with … what we call a final demand call and then at that point, we will actually threaten to take legal action." Ms Lister said in most cases, the digital communication and phone calls were enough to successfully engage employers, with only about 10 per cent of cases escalated to the "final call and letter of demand". She said the firm had for years used data provided by its super fund clients to contact employers who were not paying super, avoiding the need for employees to discover and then flag the discrepancy themselves. "We'll try and contact the employer as soon as we can to find out if there is any super payments overdue," she said. "Our experience has largely seen that the ATO, if they are going to intervene, it's much further down the track." Payday super needs to be 'backed in action' On July 1, the ATO introduced payday super , meaning employers are now required to pay workers their super at the same time as their wages. Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said the reform was a game-changer for the industry because it offered workers and the ATO real-time visibility of their super.

events.title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI. Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months. Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop. The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist. Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification. Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory. Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second. On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint. The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time. The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video , it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference. Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations. Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher. If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.” The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster. events.title: Scoop: Senate Republicans fear Mississippi is in play
events.summary: Senate Republicans are weighing three last-ditch spending moves that would have been unimaginable six months ago: a cash infusion for Mississippi and even more money for South Carolina and Kansas. Why it matters: It's been 94 years since Kansas elected a Democratic senator, 44 years for Mississippi and 28 for South Carolina. But panic is spreading through the Republican Party. "The wall has broken. The enemy is inside the fort," one national Republican political operative told Axios. "We are now fighting hand to hand." The Senate map, which once looked impregnable for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is now full of vulnerabilities. Democratic challengers are polling within the margin of error in more than half a dozen deep-red states, according to internal GOP polls. The other side: "We're nervous about Alaska. We're nervous about Michigan. We're still going to hold the Senate at the end," said another operative. Zoom in: Two weeks ago, when Senate Leadership Fund decided to take out a $5 million "insurance policy" in South Carolina, operatives took a hard look at Idaho, South Dakota and Mississippi. At the time, they concluded they didn't need to spend any money in those states, according to a person familiar with the matter. But Senate Republicans are now reviewing the Mississippi race and may need to spend there to protect Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith from a surprisingly competitive bid by Democratic district attorney Scott Colom . Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, announced a $1.2 million investment in the race on Tuesday. Zoom out: In early June, SLF started to reinforce a Midwestern red wall to protect the GOP majority, reserving $28 million in TV advertising in Ohio and $11 million in Iowa . Those investments have ballooned to $93 million in Ohio and $53 million in Iowa. After an initial $5 million buy in South Carolina, SLF's spending has increased to $8.5 million, according to AdImpact. And a super PAC linked to Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) is spending another $500,000 in South Carolina. SLF, which is linked to Senate GOP leadership, has earmarked $14 million for Kansas, and has spent nearly $12 million there so far. "No Republican seat is safe this cycle," another operative told Axios. What we're hearing: Some GOP Senate candidates do, in fact, appear safe this cycle. Republicans aren't overly concerned about Sens. Ashley Moody in Florida or Mike Rounds in South Dakota. The intrigue: The National Republican Senatorial Committee raised $31.4 million last month, but its coffers appear to be drained. It took out a $20 million loan as it spends aggressively on its coordinated campaign strategy. SLF ended September with $155 million in cash on hand, according to its FEC filing. The group has spent or reserved $169 million worth of video ads since Oct. 1, according to AdImpact. Even President Trump promised to unload another $100 million before Election Day in a Tuesday post on Truth Social, bringing the total from his super PACs to $400 million. The bottom line: Republicans can still maintain their Senate majority, but none of the polling is giving them a great deal of confidence that they will do so.

events.title: Meta’s revenue surges to $64.6 billion, but billions in settlements and skyrocketing AI spending turn screws on profit, free cash flow
events.summary: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta Platforms topped Wall Street revenue targets in the third quarter and forecast continued top-line growth, even as billions in legal payments for teen mental health litigation cut its operating margins in half, and massive AI investments pushed free cash flow into negative territory. The company also said it create a Class C stock share class to help it fund the AI buildout, pay employee stock compensation, and fund acquisitions. Investors ignored the short-term pain for the potential of a future AI payoff, cheering early signs of traction with the recently released Muse AI agent, sending Meta shares up as much as 5% in after-hours trading on Wednesday. “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in a prepared statement on Wednesday, later adding on the conference call that plans were underway to monetize Muse. “The average revenue per American user for our existing ‘family of apps’ users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place,” Zuckerberg said. Meta’s third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, above the $63.3 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. And the company forecast revenue for the final quarter of the year to range between $73 billion and $76 billion, compared with the $73.75 billion expected by analysts. But Meta’s operating income of $13 billion was down 37% from the $20.5 billion it posted in the second quarter of 2025 as a result of a $10 billion settlement Meta struck with a group of attorneys general over youth safety. The terms of the settlement will see Meta pay about $18 billion to the states over the next decade, depending on cooperation from TikTok and Google’s YouTube. Without the charge, operating income would have been $22.9 billion and earnings of $7.40 a share, rather than $13 billion and $3.83. Legal issues may continue to take a bite out of Meta’s results. Hours before Meta announced its Q3 results Wednesday, news broke that a New Mexico judge had ordered the company to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal. Meta plans to appeal. Net income in Q3 totaled $9.9 billion, or $3.83 a share, versus $2.7 billion, or $1.05 a share in the year-ago period. Meta is plowing unprecedented amounts of capital into AI infrastructure and services, joining companies like Alphabet , OpenAI, and Microsoft in a race to develop the most advanced AI models. To continue funding the AI effort, Meta said it would reallocate investments from its money-losing virtual reality business, Reality Labs, and that it would create a new nonvoting class C common stock. Capital expenditures, which have tech investors on tenterhooks, clocked in at $34.9 billion, compared with $31 billion in the second quarter and $19.4 billion a year ago. Meta slightly tweaked its full year capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion, from $130 billion to $145 billion.  Free cash flow, which has been a sore spot for Meta, was negative $2.1 billion, compared with $784 million in the second quarter and $10.6 billion a year ago.  Monetizing the Muse The results also come a week after Meta’s Superintelligence Labs launched Muse Wonder to the public, its first frontier model , and a little over a month since Meta released its Muse virtual assistant. Zuckerberg said that more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had already set up Muse assistant since it was released. “Because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we have not launched it globally yet,” Zuckerberg said on the earnings conference call with analysts. Asked about Meta’s traditional playbook of monetizing new products after they reach 1 billion users, Zuckerberg said that the steep costs of running Muse and the inherent suitability of AI agents like Muse to play a role in retail transactions meant that the company would look for ways to generate revenue sooner. “My guess is, I think that we are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook,” he said. Zuckerberg also said he was optimistic about the potential for business customers to use Muse. Few companies are as well positioned as Meta to capitalize on the agentic AI opportunity, Zuckerberg said, though he noted that the company needed to continue making progress on compute efficiency. “It’s going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out,” he said. Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha research at S&P Global, wrote in a note before the results that consensus capex for 2026 had risen more than $14 billion since April to about $140 billion—almost double that of 2025. She noted that investors continue to want clarity on how that spending will translate into shareholder returns.  Overall in tech infrastructure spending, capex is expected to continue ballooning in 2026 to $790 billion, according to Otto, almost double what it was in 2025 at $404 billion. And it won’t stop there. For 2027, capex is expected to rise to $1.2 trillion, meaning companies will have spent nearly $2 trillion on the AI build-out in two years.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Poll shows big lead for South Dakota Republican Rounds
events.summary: Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota leads in his Senate race by more than 20 points, according to a new poll shared first with Semafor, a sign that any blue wave in November will have its limits. Rounds is trouncing independent candidate Brian Bengs 57% to 36% in the deep-red state, according to a new poll conducted in mid-October by Quantus Insights. That’s a larger lead for Rounds than many surveys have previously shown; some surveys even showed Bengs with a slight lead. South Dakota is one of three states, including Idaho and Nebraska, where Democrats have coalesced behind an independent Senate candidate. Nebraska is the most competitive of the three races. Bengs lost to Senate Majority Leader John Thune in 2022 as a Democrat, but he insists if he wins he’ll create an independent caucus and not align with Republicans or Democrats.

events.title: Automattic begins layoffs following board upheaval and executive departures
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Automattic, the parent company to WordPress.com , WooCommerce, Tumblr, and others, has begun layoffs, and insiders tell us they are bracing for more cuts to come. Over at least the past week, the cuts have impacted its communications team, social team, WordPress.com, and its VIP enterprise business. The departures represent more turmoil at Automattic, whose team is still reeling from the board’s failed attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg in September, resulting in a complete board turnover and other exec departures, including its CFO, interim CFO , and chief legal officer. Automattic’s director of communications, Megan Fox, posted about her departure last week on LinkedIn, saying the move was an “unexpected end” and that her role had been “eliminated.” Meanwhile, after TechCrunch reported that Automattic’s interim CFO Jeremy Klaperman left earlier this month , only weeks after the board shake-up, Mullenweg posted on X suggesting Klaperman may have been “offended” by the company’s decision to seek external candidates to fill the role. (Internally, however, Mullenweg had asked Klaperman to reconsider leaving, we had heard.) At one point, Mullenweg also shared personal information about one of the recently departed execs in the company’s internal Slack, according to screenshots viewed by TechCrunch. The post was related to a health matter impacting the person’s spouse and claimed that the company was not providing this person with much-needed COBRA insurance. Mullenweg said the exec was threatening to sue over this. Mullenweg also shared that his own fiancée had been impacted by the same health condition. Some employees told us they were shocked that the CEO would share something so private and personal in such a forum. Throughout this month, TechCrunch has heard from different sources that members of Automattic’s team have also been let go, including those in marketing and product at WordPress.com. Reached for comment about the layoffs last week, Mullenweg said the terminations were not above its normal numbers. Asked on Wednesday about the growing total, Mullenweg said that today he was “mostly focused on PHP.” (He posted on X about the PHP security issue hitting the internet, which is taking priority.) The company’s About page lists the total number of staff at 1,397, but insiders tell us that the plan is likely to spread out the layoffs over the months ahead, in the hopes of improving Automattic’s Q4 revenue figures ahead of a debt renegotiation that’s coming up in June. In a statement shared with TechCrunch, Automattic spokesperson Chenda Ngak said, “We’re staggering our organizational changes to be more generous with severance and allow more time with each Automattician.” Updated after publication with Automattic’s statement. events.title: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
events.summary: General Motors is hoping to reduce the time it takes to develop vehicles, targeting a roughly two-year cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software. GM says it is using artificial intelligence, simulation and more concurrent engineering to shorten development and reduce physical testing. The automaker is also expanding in-vehicle AI and plans to introduce eyes-off highway driving beginning with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market. The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half. GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models. "All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan. The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers. "Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation. Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity How lower fuel economy targets could boost pickups and V-8 engines Stellantis CEO urges incentives for carmakers who build in Europe as Chinese rivals gain ground GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal. The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage. GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities . Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses. He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad. "There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise." GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines. The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems. That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features. The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs. GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact. GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them. "We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them." GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development. The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.

events.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
events.summary: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal in New Mexico. The penalty comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data. A New Mexico district court judge said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind schedule Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act.

events.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
events.summary: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties Wednesday after a jury found in September that the social media giant misled users about their data privacy. Why it matters: The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke and signal that Big Tech can face significant financial consequences for misleading users about their privacy. Driving the news: Judge Francis Mathew determined the penalty amount Wednesday, handing New Mexico a win as the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled. Mathew concluded New Mexico was entitled to $219.5 billion based on the state's maximum $5,000 penalty multiplied by 43,899,720 violations. He reduced that to $25 billion. Meta did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The company has previously said it expects to appeal the decision. Catch up quick: In September, a New Mexico jury said Meta had committed 43 million "willful violations" of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act. Mathew found that Facebook's privacy controls failed to give users meaningful control over their data and that third-party app developers could access their information through the platform's systems. Mathew found Mark Zuckerberg knew users didn't understand how data privacy works, and exploited that, noting that the CEO had once written that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates." Zuckerberg also wrote that the company should give users "a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it." Zoom out: The suit followed reporting that revealed data firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from more than 50 million Facebook users to craft political ads during the 2016 election. After the scandal, Facebook promised more transparency, but the court found Meta failed to consistently inform users when their data was misused. events.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
events.summary: International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet. The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon. Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leading bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline. The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape. Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities. The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X , external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix. "These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote. Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue. And in a post on X , external , Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? Published 1 hour ago The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities. "We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said. That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday. Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors. They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment. Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are " temporarily down for maintenance , external " without specifying the reason. The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet. Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language. OpenAI said in a blog post , external that the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms. The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered. "Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post. It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure. While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday. It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale. The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website. Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note , external . Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning , external . "PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said. Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers. The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said. "The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.

events.title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
events.summary: BlackRock's Rick Rieder is bullish on this area of the credit market for the first time in a "long time." The CIO of global fixed income lays out his fourth-quarter fixed-income outlook in an exclusive interview. Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration. "Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance." While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC) , which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit. Best opportunities include hyperscalers Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July , that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised. "Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield." Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be." The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out. Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle , which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve , which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool . The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said. "They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure." Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

events.title: GM is betting compute and AI will help it compete with Chinese automakers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When GM announced its new fourth-generation EV platform on Wednesday, what the automaker didn’t share was almost as notable as what it did. The new EV platform, part of a series of technology-focused announcements made during its annual GM Forward event in New York, didn’t talk about suspension geometries, dash-to-axle ratios, and torsional rigidity, all nerdy automotive terms that translate to how people will experience a car. Is it supple or sporty? Does it have a refined stance? When it hits a pothole, does it feel like a bank vault or a paper plate? Instead, GM’s announcement centered on novel battery chemistries, revamped electric motors, and an entirely new central computing platform and electrical architecture that will connect every system in the car, including acceleration and power, steering, braking, and active safety features as well as software. Lots and lots of software. “We think vehicles can become a more capable and helpful part of everyday life if we make them spaces that understand context, reduce friction, and give people back moments that would otherwise be consumed by the demands of the road,” Sterling Anderson, executive vice president, global product, and chief product officer at GM, told TechCrunch in a recent interview. That sure doesn’t sound like a traditional automaker’s pitch. Then again, since the arrival of Tesla, Rivian, and Chinese automakers, the industry hasn’t been the same. Ride and handling still matter, but they’re table stakes. What sets vehicles apart today is largely defined by software. Anderson has talked about this future GM before. Last year, the company announced plans to overhaul the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant. This year, GM is providing more details and dates. This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also roll out an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over. The software race includes hardware European and U.S. automakers have spent years chasing the prospect of software-defined vehicles but have often fallen short. Volkswagen Group had so much trouble with its own in-house effort, including its troubled Cariad unit, that it struck a $5.8 billion joint venture deal with relative newcomer Rivian. GM has been on its own capitally intensive software adventure. The company has bet heavily on software in recent years. It ditched the popular smartphone projection technology Apple CarPlay for nearly all of its EVs, and instead turned to a Google-based infotainment system, which is actually quite capable even if it doesn’t yet live up to the standards set by Tesla and Rivian. It’s poured billions into software and autonomous vehicle technology development too. GM’s capitalized software amortization expense in 2025 was $866 million, which gives a sense of how much it is spending even as it spreads out the cost over years. Like many legacy automakers, GM has come to the conclusion that the old approach to electronics, which scattered computer chips throughout the vehicle, was holding it back. For fourth-generation EVs, GM will centralize much of those functions on a central compute unit (CCU) that’s 40x more powerful than its existing systems. Eliminating smaller chips on the edges will help trim wiring by 30%, saving weight and simplifying assembly. GM notes that this new CCU will work on fossil fuel models, too, though it will debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ, a vehicle that is shaping up to be the automaker’s technological flagship. The CCU will handle the usual propulsion and chassis controls, as well as perception and active safety. That should help pave the way for more advanced autonomy features, which GM also announced on Wednesday. Such a move was perhaps inevitable. Pressure on automakers has been building on all sides. Domestically, Tesla has been pushing the boundaries of autonomy, in part because it developed a true software-defined vehicle. Automakers like GM are also feeling pressure from Chinese manufacturers, which have shortened development cycles to two to three years, down from the usual four to five years. GM intends to match that cadence. Alongside announcements about battery chemistries and autonomy, GM outlined how enterprise AI tools have sped up vehicle development across every sector as it pushes to slash its traditional four- to five-year development timeline in half. GM gave a brief glimpse of its revamped development strategy.

events.title: Meta ordered to pay $25B in case related to Cambridge Analytica scandal
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The tale of the Cambridge Analytica data scandal is long — and it keeps costing Meta gargantuan sums of money. On Wednesday, a judge ordered the social media giant to initiate its biggest payout yet: $25 billion to the state of New Mexico for the tech giant’s role in deceiving resident users over its data privacy practices, The New York Times reports . The huge sum follows a two-week trial in which a New Mexico jury deliberated over the company’s alleged wrongdoing. The jury found that the company behind Facebook and Instagram had committed 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws, each of which carried a $5,000 penalty, the outlet notes. Part of the case revolved around the company’s handling of a third-party app linked to the Cambridge Analytica data breach, The Wall Street Journal reports . Other parts involved its data privacy policies and its efforts to mitigate misinformation on its platform. Cambridge Analytica was an outgrowth of a British defense contractor, SLC Group, that specialized in influence operations and other political work. The company notably worked with the Trump campaign during the 2016 presidential election. It was also involved in a number of controversial initiatives . “We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez told journalists at a press conference, commenting on the case’s resolution. Meta said that it will appeal the decision. “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” said C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, in a statement shared with TechCrunch via email. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge,” he added. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) An open date has been set for the long-awaited Southwest Metro after a two-year project to replace the 130-year-old line. The first driverless service is expected to depart early morning on Friday, October 30. It is hoped the new service will cut travel time with connections including from south-west Sydney to the CBD. The long-awaited Southwest Metro extension now has an opening date, after extended works to replace the 130-year-old train line. NSW Premier Chris Minns said the $23 billion project would officially open with the first service departing at 4:31am on Friday, October 30. The new metro offering will connect south-western suburbs to the Sydney CBD, North Sydney and north-western suburbs. From next Friday, the NSW government said passengers would have access to trains every four minutes during weekday peak hours in places including Bankstown, Punchbowl, Wiley Park, Lakemba, Dulwich Hill and Marrickville. "The new Metro will deliver 50 per cent more passenger capacity than the old T3 Bankstown Line it replaces, along with faster journeys and direct connections to more jobs, education and opportunities across Sydney," a spokesperson said. The opening was delayed until 2026 due to the project's complexity and industrial action. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) They also said services would run every five minutes during the day, and every 10 minutes in the evenings and on weekends. On the first weekend, between October 31 and November 1, services will increase to accommodate increased interest. Mr Minns said it was an investment that would "make a real difference" to communities for "generations to come". "This is about giving people in south-west Sydney the same fast, reliable public transport connections that other parts of our city enjoy," he said. Buses replaced trains on the south-west line for more than two years, and pink-coloured buses became a regular sight on major roads between Sydenham and Bankstown. It meant some commuters faced lengthier travel times. Mr Graham says the time for pink buses is over. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) Transport Minister John Graham said communities "have been very patient" and the wait for the new line to open "will be worthwhile". "The pink buses have really played a big role moving people around, but the time for them is over," he said. "We know this has had an impact, though, on communities, on passengers, on businesses as well. "There's no easy way to upgrade the line in this way; it has taken time. Now it's here, I think people will immediately see the benefits." Mr Graham said the new line will transform the way people travel around Sydney. "You won't need to check the timetable, you'll simply be able to turn up at the station and jump on a metro within minutes," he said. The pink Southwest Link buses will continue to operate on the opening day and weekend. Station improvements and line upgrades The new metro line runs from Sydenham to Bankstown. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) About 48,000 trips are expected to be made across the metro line on a typical weekday during the 8am and 9am peak. Upgrades include platform screen doors, new lifts and station upgrades, updated customer information systems and enhanced security technology along the line. Improvements have also been made at stations to improve accessibility for prams and people living with a disability, with accessible lifts at Wiley Park, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Punchbowl and Canterbury for the first time. The T3 Bankstown Line between Sydenham and Bankstown ceased operations in September 2024 to convert the 130-year-old heavy rail line to a metro line. The Sydney City and Southwest Metro station under construction at Martin Place in 2020. ( ABC News: Rachel Pupazzoni ) The conversion deadline was pushed back due to industrial action and complexity issues. It was initially meant to take 12 months. It is the final stage of Sydney's M1 Metro North West and Bankstown Line, which will connect Bankstown to Tallawong along a 66-kilometre stretch. The state government has warned passengers there may be "minor teething issues as services get underway".

events.title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. Now it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart president and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Meta plans nonvoting shares, eyeing more stock sales to fund its AI dreams
events.summary: Meta plans to introduce new non-voting stock, the company announced, which suggests it’s likely to lean heavily on new share sales to fund its AI buildout. The plan, earlier reported by Semafor, will allow the company to issue new stock — for acquisitions, to lure top AI talent, and to pay for chips — without diluting Mark Zuckerberg’s control. Alphabet made a similar move in 2014, executing a 2-for-1 stock split that introduced non-voting shares alongside super-voting shares, which allowed the combined control of co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin to remain at just over 50%. That made it easier for the company to issue $85 billion of new stock earlier this year to pay for AI investments; half of the new shares carry no voting rights . Big tech companies have historically been able to balance out the new stock they issue by buying back shares in the market. But they have paused stock repurchases as the cost of their AI investments mount, and now find themselves as net issuers of shares, which risks diluting insiders’ stakes.

events.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the world went offline , Reuters reported, after AI discovered critical security vulnerabilities that impacted the programming language PHP . The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could. But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js , the open source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity. In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code, the company shared in a post on X on Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published to PyPI (Python Package Index), Docker Hub , and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted. The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems. LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to follow the remediation guidance it provided. And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra, had its private keys compromised , potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. Security pros have called this a massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed.” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library.) These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which the company announced on Monday. Other hackers have been exploiting four patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity company BeyondTrust warned customers to patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August. Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. events.title: Will an AI-cloned free tool spell the end of expensive software?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts An AI-cloned free tool is being dubbed 'the end of software' Some developers want to use AI tools to break the power of big tech and "take back the internet". ( Getty: Malte Mueller ) It is being called "the end of software" and the dawn of a new era of AI-powered piracy. New AI tools are disrupting the tech industry, making it relatively easy and fast to clone an existing piece of software and replicate its features. Earlier this month, a small team of developers used AI tools to create near-identical, free versions of two commonly used products: Microsoft Office, with programs such as Word and Excel, and Adobe Creative, which includes Photoshop. A licence to use Adobe's Creative Suite costs more than $1,000 per year, but the cloned version is free. ( Supplied: Artcraft ) Around the same time, a different tool called Reverse Engineer Anything that helps developers use AI to deconstruct and replicate features in other pieces of software shot to the top of trending projects on software repository GitHub. For some, this new generation of tools will disrupt software in the same way MP3 file-sharing networks in the late 1990s changed how we listened to music and watched movies, replacing CDs and DVDs with streaming. But whether this will give more power to users or further concentrate power in the hands of AI companies remains to be seen. 'Set the clock back' to the 1990s internet Brandon Thomas is one of the developers who recently announced they had used AI tools to copy the Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative suites. A 15-year veteran of the US tech industry, he sees himself fighting a "war" for the future of the internet. In the 1990s, "Everything [online] was nerdy, hackable and weird," he told the ABC. "Everything in this era could be inspected, copied, shared with friends, remixed. It was amazing." But over time, the internet became more standardised and bland. Spaces for innovation and personalisation, like Geocities or Myspace, were replaced by closed ecosystems that tightly controlled user access. This is "enshittification", a term coined by writer Cory Doctorow in 2022 to describe the perceived decline of online spaces. Social media platforms like Facebook initially attracted users with clean, chronological feeds and personal connections, then pivoted to intrusive ads and sponsored content. Search engines became crowded with sponsored ads and affiliate-marketing spam, pushing out organic search results. Software makers shifted to subscription-only models with automated billing and predatory cancellation fees, in some cases worth 50 per cent of the annual contract. The cloned version of Adobe Photoshop, Photocraft, has similar features and layout. ( Supplied: ArtCraft ) For some, AI is part of the problem, as "slop" content floods online spaces. But for Mr Thomas, AI is the solution. "AI flips the tide of this war in a way legislation never did," he said. AI data centre company cold calling about buying land, inquiry told Tech giant shares plunge 40pc after delays to Melbourne data centre Embattled AI company Firmus still wants funds for Tasmanian data centre A small group of AI companies are creating a lopsided US economy "We can build anything, even triple-A video games and operating systems. "This is the most excited I've felt for the future in a long time. "I think we have a great opportunity to take back the internet from the monopolistic platforms that became rent-seekers and behaved badly to us as users and customers." How AI is making software easier to copy Think of a piece of software like a cake from a bakery. To copy the recipe, you could break into the bakery and steal the list of ingredients (the source code), for which you would be quickly prosecuted. Or you could reverse engineer the cake by tearing it apart, tasting it, and studying it under a microscope. This is known as "decompiling". You can then bake the cake based on what you learnt. Each time you bake the cake, you tweak the recipe so the result more closely matches your description. Queensland University of Technology (QUT) digital economy expert Marek Kowalkiewicz said AI dramatically sped up this process. "[AI-powered reverse engineering] is not very different from having a bunch of human software developers doing the same thing, but it's way faster and cheaper," Professor Kowalkiewicz told the ABC. Experts say AI's dominance of the US market brings risks all of its own. events.title: Investors eye proxy fight at Mattel
events.summary: A big Mattel shareholder is preparing to mount a proxy fight at the toymaker and push the company toward a sale, according to people familiar with the matter. Southeastern Asset Management has been considering whether to nominate new directors at Mattel as part of a proxy fight, the people said. The activist has been pushing the company for months to sell itself, following double-digit sales declines in Fisher-Price and other key segments, as well as profit-margin pressures. The issues became more acute after Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz left to join Skydance: Mattel shares, which are down 15% so far this year, dropped by 5% on the news of his replacement, former Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch. The stock rebounded following a Wall Street Journal report that the company had drawn takeover interest by Authentic Brands Group. Southeastern’s plans could change, the people cautioned, and no decision has been made. It’s unlikely the activist could secure full control of Mattel’s board, but a proxy fight would serve as a referendum on the direction of the company. Under Mattel’s bylaws, an investor can only nominate two directors, except in specific circumstances. Separately, Ariel Investments, another big Mattel shareholder, has told other investors that it believes a change needs to happen at Mattel, according to another person familiar with the matter. In a recent CNBC appearance, Ariel founder John Rogers said the company should sell itself, an unusual posture for a famously management-friendly investor. Mattel said in a statement that it engages with all shareholders but declined to comment further. Ariel and Southeastern didn’t respond to requests for comment.
