events.title: US stocks nudge higher as SpaceX, Tesla and Nvidia climb
events.summary: The U.S. stock market is drifting higher following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies NEW YORK -- The U.S. stock market is ticking higher Wednesday as strong profit reports from SpaceX , Capital One Financial and other big companies help offset updates from Netflix and AT & T that investors found disappointing. The S & P 500 rose 0.2% and is on track for a third straight modest gain . The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 47 points, or 0.1%, as of 10 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.7% higher. SpaceX helped lead the way and climbed 11.2% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company. Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results late Wednesday, climbed 3.8% and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S & P 500. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 4%, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 6.5%. Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation , higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. It helped offset a drop for Netflix, which fell 2.7% even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT & T fell 4.4% even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled. After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. NFL suspends 2nd Bills player for spitting, though Sam Franklin denies allegation and plans appeal EU unveils a new Arctic push as global warming and security threats reshape the region LeBron James talks smack with Knicks fans, drops 14 points in victorious 76ers debut CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. On Tuesday, it careened between a loss of 6% and a gain of 5%, for example. On Wednesday, it fell 1.4% after erasing an early gain of nearly 4%. Other AI-linked stocks were more solid, though. Nvidia's gain of 1.8% was the strongest force lifting the S & P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 12%. Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields in the bond market, which helps dictate how expensive loans are for the U.S. government, companies and regular Americans . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.09% from 5.12% late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher. Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big swings this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.6% to $108.14 after crossing above $111 earlier in the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between $97 and $112 in October. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3% for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength. AP Business Writers Michelle Chapman and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report. events.title: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company’s acquisition
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Last month, advertising company Infillion acquired location-data platform Foursquare, a once popular social network, at an undisclosed value. Now, in a new blog post , Foursquare co-founder and former CEO Dennis Crowley said that investors didn’t see any returns from the sale. Crowley referenced a post by an angel investor , inferred that neither preferred nor common stockholders got any value out of the deal, and said he was disappointed by the outcome. “I was heartbroken by this ending. So many people put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare — the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth … nothing?” he said in the post. Crowley said that the company did well after it started focusing on enterprise business and had consecutive years with over $100 million in revenue. In 2019, the company raised capital from a private equity firm and in 2021 brought in the banker who led the raise as CEO. Crowley blamed the final outcome on that transition, saying that the management of the company wasn’t able to preserve or create new value. Foursquare, which had raised over $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, eventually shut down its app in 2024 . Several people reacted to Crowley’s post and said that Foursquare was very useful to them in discovering new places in their cities and also gave ideas for new apps . events.title: Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
events.summary: Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle. As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men. The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.” Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.” The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution. Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated. Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels. Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy , which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire , TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring. “It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.” While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health. “Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality. The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos , but Tasso devices have a solid track record .) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone. Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor.

events.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy. Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips. The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models. If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky. Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin. In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand , that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush. In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church. In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days. In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance." Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants. In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa. For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative. Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts. Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining. What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating. His Berlin keynote offers another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet. The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company.

events.title: House prices across capitals post steepest quarterly decline ever
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts House values drop in all capital cities for first time in 15 years, Domain says Australia's most valuable homes are falling the most in value. ( ABC News: Charlie Mclean ) House prices have fallen across every capital city for the first time in 15 years, Domain reports. Data shows Australia's most expensive homes have recorded the biggest drops this year, while lower-value homes have remained largely stable. Experts say rising interest rates and lower market confidence are driving the downturn. House prices have fallen 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record, according to new data from Domain. Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record. The real estate platform's data showed the sharpest decline was in Perth, where prices dropped 7.4 per cent. Combined capital city house prices fell to $1,226,566. Domain said markets that started the year in very different positions "are now moving in the same direction". Houses and units dropped in price for a second consecutive month. ( ABC News: Steve Keen ) Australia's biggest property markets, Sydney and Melbourne, recorded their largest quarterly house price drop in four years, falling 4.7 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively. Unit prices also fell 3.5 per cent, marking the second consecutive quarter both property types declined. It marked a clear shift in the housing cycle, according to Nicola Powell, Domain's chief residential economist. Nicola Powell says conditions have shifted to be more favourable for buyers. ( Supplied ) "What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Dr Powell said. "The balance of power has shifted towards buyers. "Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate, and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations." The cumulative impact of rising rates, lower affordability, and cost-of-living pressures has reduced demand, according to Gerard Burg of data firm Cotality. "It's been a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said. Gerard Burg says the fall in prices has been driven by lower demand. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) Australia's most valuable homes falling the most While all major markets across the country have joined the downturn, prices have not been dropping equally within cities. Australia's most valuable homes are dropping the most, while lower value homes were relatively stable in three months to September, according to property data firm Cotality. Calls for rent cap to stop WA's spiralling rental market Things to consider before renting out a room or part of your home One place in Australia abolished stamp duty and boosted economic activity Tribunal quashes council's over-55s caravan park plans In Sydney, the most valuable quartile of homes dropped more than twice as much as the least valuable quartile. Nationwide, lower-value homes have seen a much slower price drop, Cotality said. Prices grew in Darwin's lowest value quartile. The sharper downturn in more expensive properties reflects fewer buyers and higher borrowing costs, according to property economist Cameron Kusher. "They've typically seen larger increases in values over recent years and when you see that market slowdown, there's overall fewer buyers for those properties," he said. Cameron Kusher says fewer buyers and higher interest rates are pushing down the prices of more expensive properties. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) However, he said the ultra-top end of the market had remained largely stable. Mr Burg agreed, saying lower-priced homes remained affordable to more buyers. "The median house really appears kind of out of reach of the median income household across much of the country," he said. Prices were falling before federal budget The federal budget was a factor, but not the only factor, in house price falls, according to Mr Kusher. House prices peaked last year and had already begun to drop before the changes to investment taxes in May's federal budget, Mr Kusher and Mr Burg both noted. Mr Burg said prices were already falling in many capital cities, and three consecutive interest rate hikes had dampened market confidence. The real estate industry says new laws targeting agents underquoting a house price are well-intentioned but poorly designed. Auction activity, a common gauge of market confidence, has roughly halved from last year, with 1,423 auctions across capital cities last week, according to Cotality. "Confidence has really evaporated. Affordability is very stretched and borrowing capacity is reduced dramatically," Mr Kusher said.

events.title: E-scooter hospitalisations more than triple since 2019
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts E-scooter and e-bike hospitalisations on the rise in Australia, report finds Topic: Transport Accidents and Incidents The report found boys aged between 12 and 15 had the largest increase in hospitalisations due to e-scooter falls. ( ABC News: Marcus Stinson ) A report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) has found e-scooter hospitalisations have more than tripled since 2019. There were 4,089 hospitalisations involving e-scooter in the 2024-25 compared to 1,291 in 2019-20. Two-thirds of those hospitalised in 2024-25 were male with largest increase in young boys aged between 12 and 15. Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW). The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25. Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall. It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified. The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the past decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable. New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said. AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices. "Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said. E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research. When Barnaby Joyce was deputy prime minister and transport minister in 2021, his assistant minister Kevin Hogan made a quiet, but hugely significant change to the Road Vehicle Standards Act. Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth. "Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said. Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns. Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices. "It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said. "But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide." Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation. People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence. Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision. New laws for e-mobility devices in effect from today: what you need to know Laws for e-bike and e-scooter riders come into effect from July 1: we've unpacked the changes for you Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations. It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public. "So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said. Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people. "Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40. "That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode.

events.title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
events.summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another editor from the project has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

events.title: Keppel, SGX and Thakral CEOs win SIAS outstanding CEO award
events.summary: (From left) Thakral Corporation CEO Inderbethal “Bethal” Singh Thakral, Keppel CEO Mr Loh Chin Hua, and SGX Group CEO Loh Boon Chye. SINGAPORE – Three chief executive officers won the Investors’ Choice Outstanding CEO Award given out by the Securities Investors Association (Singapore), or SIAS , on Oct 21. They were recognised for excellence in corporate governance, sustainability, transparency and shareholder communications. The three CEOs tell The Straits Times how they increased the shareholder value of their companies and the top traits a CEO should have. Keppel CEO: Bring the shareholders and staff along on the transformation journey Keppel CEO Loh Chin Hua faced a challenge about a decade ago, when the company was trying to transform from a conglomerate with distinctly separate businesses to an asset-light global asset manager and operator. His goal: To communicate the multi-year transformation journey clearly to shareholders to ensure they were on board. Loh recalled that at the time, there was very little synergy among the various businesses, which were listed separately and run vertically. “The market wasn’t according us the valuation that we thought we should have,” he said. Keppel privatised some listed entities and changed its business model from building projects to owning and operating specialised assets. This has significantly reduced its balance sheet and enabled Keppel to return capital to shareholders while growing its assets under management. Loh said: “We set milestones because this multi-year transformation can be quite daunting for the market to absorb. It is important that we communicate to the market what are the milestones along the way, so that they can follow and track how we are progressing on our transformation.” He added that “communication is key” for a listed company. “In the old days, you might say, ‘Well, we are Keppel. Trust us. We know what we are doing.’ I think nowadays, even if the market does trust us, they also want to see tangible results,” Loh said. He noted that the transformation was a fundamental rework of the business structure and its processes, not “just a narrative”. Keppel has also set and met its goals around aspects like monetisation of non-core assets and growth of funds under management. Loh also emphasised the importance of ensuring that staff were invested in the transformation. Keppel uses engagement surveys to check that staff understand where it is headed, especially as it moves towards integrating artificial intelligence to become an “AI native” firm. Loh said: “I wouldn’t say that we started off by thinking about share performance. “You start off by developing a strategy that will strengthen the company and allow it to be better valued, better appreciated by the market. Bring your board, your management and your people along this journey, and the rest takes care of itself.” When asked about the traits a good CEO should have, Loh said Keppel’s core values of being agile, having a “can-do” spirit and trust are vital. Being able to galvanise people is essential, he said. “Most importantly, they feel that they are part of this journey... not because you ask them to, but because they actually feel it, they can see it and they support it.” SGX CEO: Growing the local investing ecosystem and unlocking value Growing the Singapore Exchange (SGX) as a business and developing the local ecosystem around it has been the focus of group CEO Loh Boon Chye in recent years. The progress so far has been gratifying, he said, with initiatives such as Value Unlock introduced to help companies strengthen their investor relations and close valuation gaps, and the push to revitalise the local equities market. “In the last two years in particular, it was very gratifying to see the whole ecosystem coming together to work on our stock market. SGX in many ways can’t do it alone,” he said. “Importantly, this is not a one-time effort. This is just the start. Indeed, there’s been good momentum, but we need to sustain it to make this durable and sustainable.” He added that SGX has also been working to broaden its offerings of investment tools in a macro environment that is more fragmented, and that offerings go beyond access into just one market or asset class. “It is now really about portfolio risk management, and our focus to broaden that is not just a one-year effort,” Loh said. Some of his plans include growing the foreign exchange business and commodities business, with SGX’s expansion of its gold segment. But besides growth, the market also needs to ensure transparency and good governance, which is done through clear communication with shareholders. “What we’re talking about is more than disclosure – it’s about firms being able to explain the business model, dynamics, strategy, and then how the company can fit into the environment they’re operating in, allocating capital as efficiently as they can,” he said.

events.title: Companies involved in illegal activities that cause haze may face financial penalties: Chee Hong Tat
events.summary: Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat warned on Oct 21 that listed companies involved in illegal activities that cause transboundary haze may face legal and financial ramifications. Chee Hong Tat warned that listed companies involved in illegal haze-causing activities may face legal and financial penalties, which can also hurt shareholders. SIAS urged investors to avoid firms with poor environmental records, while MAS will help by developing IPO guides to improve investor education and decision-making. Chee said Singapore’s listing market is seeing renewed interest, with 10 new listings by end-August raising about S$1.4 billion, as awards recognised governance, sustainability and transparency. SINGAPORE – The rece nt haze crisis has put the spotlight on corporate governance and accountability, with National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat warning that listed companies involved in illegal activities that cause transboundary haze may face legal and financial penalties. “These consequences, these penalties, do not just affect the company’s directors and management. They also affect the value of investments and interests of shareholders,” he said at the SIAS Investors’ Choice Awards on Oct 21. “Hence, it is very legitimate for SIAS (Securities Investors Association, Singapore) to complement the actions of regulators, SGX and banks to speak out on behalf of investors and to seek answers from the companies concerned.” Chee also said good corporate governance means conducting business responsibly and within the law. “The Government takes this very seriously. Where companies are found to have contravened our laws based on the facts and evidence, we will take the necessary enforcement actions against the errant firms and individuals,” he said. Speaking at the event, SIAS founder, president and chief executive David Gerald said all investors should “think carefully about where they put their money”, urging them to “absolutely avoid companies with poor environmental records”. This applies especially to those linked to the haze, he said, noting that the massive destruction of forests and green spaces causes harm to public health. “Investors who fund such companies, even indirectly, share some responsibility for these outcomes.” He said SIAS will continue to raise awareness among investors about environmental, social and governance risks, and encourage them to check a company’s sustainability practices before investing. “By choosing responsible companies, retail investors can protect their own returns while supporting a cleaner, healthier region,” he said. Chee, who is also deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), also announced that MAS will support SIAS in enhancing investor education through the development of initial public offering (IPO) guides. These guides will distil key information from public offer documents when a company wants to list and help investors identify the issues that are most relevant to them, while highlighting matters that they should consider. Chee said: “They will not recommend whether an IPO is a good or bad investment. They will complement, not replace, investors’ own assessment of the risks and the research available to them. The objective is to help investors ask the right questions and make more informed decisions.” The Singapore Exchange (SGX) saw 10 new listings in 2026 by the end of August, which raised about $1.4 billion. Chee Hong Tat, National Development Minister and deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said MAS will support SIAS in enhancing investor education through the development of initial public offering guides. Chee noted that there has been renewed interest from a broader range of companies considering Singapore as a listing venue, from real estate investment trusts and real assets to firms in growth sectors such as technology, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing. He said: “The external global environment has become more challenging, but Singapore’s fundamentals remain sound. We know markets will go through cycles – what matters is that we stay focused on rebuilding broader and deeper capabilities over the long term.” He added that turning near-term momentum into lasting investor confidence requires well-governed companies that earn trust, well-informed investors, and strong bridges between the companies and investors. “As more companies consider Singapore as a listing venue, our IPO ecosystem must inspire confidence among both issuers and investors,” Chee said. This is where the IPO guides and increased research coverage of listed companies come in. MAS has supported SIAS over the years by collaborating in investor education, promoting good corporate governance and raising awareness of investment scams, and this partnership is set to deepen as the market evolves, he added.

events.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
events.summary: President Donald Trump's offer to pay out $5,000 checks if Republicans win belongs to a long political tradition of cash for votes. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win. President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “ DOGE dividend ” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues , and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans. But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view . For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races . I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote. Why vote buying rarely works The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia. By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants . Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s. But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes. If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence. Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent . As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “ Against the Machine .” The importance of competition There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops. First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights. This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “ Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos .” In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets : Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision. Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret. It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment. Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it. Bringing it home Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely. Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate . There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism. The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.” At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vot

events.title: The permitting bill enters a critical stretch
events.summary: Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown. Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time. Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews. Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law. Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank. He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill. Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it. State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders. What's next: The effort goes beyond signatures for some of the former officials, according to letter organizer Arnab Datta of the Institute for Progress, a nonpartisan think tank. "Some folks are engaging beyond the letter itself with stakeholders across the board, and some have made themselves available for members briefings or conversations," he tells me via email. Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job. The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others. Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers." That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs. What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in. But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions. The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess. events.title: eBay to lay off 9% of workforce in push to simplify operations, internal memo shows
events.summary: EBay has set itself apart from rivals by pushing into authenticated luxury goods, collectibles and refurbished products, which draw enthusiasts willing to pay more for valuable items. eBay will cut about 9% of its staff to simplify operations and move money to faster-growing areas, CEO Jamie Iannone said in a memo reviewed by Reuters. eBay is focusing on authenticated luxury goods, collectibles and refurbished products, which have helped its shares rise nearly 40% in 2026, far above the S&P 500. The company also gained from its US$1.4 billion Depop deal and rejected Ryan Cohen’s US$56 billion bid as “neither credible nor attractive”. EBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce as the online marketplace looks to simplify operations and shift resources to its fastest-growing areas, its chief executive officer Jamie Iannone told staff in a memo that was reviewed by Reuters. A spokesperson for eBay confirmed the layoffs to Reuters on Oct 21. The company also let go about 6% of its workforce, or 800 employees, in February as part of efforts to streamline operations. That has helped its shares rise nearly 40% in 2026, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500’s around 12% gain. “Our strategy is working,” Iannone said in the memo, adding that “continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest”. He said affected staff would be informed in the coming days. The company has this year also benefited from its US$1.4 billion (S$1.79 billion) deal for ​fashion resale platform Depop, which expanded its reach among younger consumers ​and strengthened its position in the growing re-commerce market. That helped eBay forecast third-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates when it last posted results, in August. The company is slated to report latest earnings next week. Those efforts have also caught the eye of GameStop chief executive officer Ryan Cohen, who made an unsolicited US$56 billion bid for the much larger eBay in May. EBay had rejected the offer , saying that it was “neither credible nor attractive”. REUTERS

events.title: Ghana eyes mineral export ban to boost domestic processing
events.summary: Ghana plans to ban exports of raw mineral ores by 2030 to boost domestic processing, its president said, reinforcing a broader push by Africa’s resource-rich countries to capture more value from their minerals. “Investors must understand the processing obligations associated with access to our resources,” President John Dramani Mahama said at a mining conference in Accra. The country is Africa’s largest gold producer and also mines manganese, bauxite, and diamonds. The global race for minerals used in clean energy and advanced technologies has intensified competition between China, the US, and Europe for African supplies. Ghana’s proposed restrictions would put it alongside countries such as DR Congo, which restricts exports of copper and cobalt concentrates. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: JPMorgan closes in on Nigeria merchant banking license
events.summary: JPMorgan is on track to secure a merchant banking license in Nigeria after making a $38 million statutory deposit to the country’s central bank, Bloomberg reported. If successful, the New York-based lender, which has been bullish about Nigeria’s prospects , would add considerable heft to the investment banking sector as the country seeks to attract more foreign capital. The move to acquire a Nigeria license is part of the bank’s Africa expansion, including the appointment of an investment banking lead for sub-Saharan Africa this year, and opening offices in Nairobi and Abidjan. It comes as Nigeria’s securities regulator this week unveiled a 10-year plan to grow the country’s capital markets, including a target to raise annual diaspora investment to $10 billion, from $4 billion. It also comes on the heels of the Dangote refinery’s IPO that is aiming to raise at least $1.6 billion by the time it closes. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Today in the UK, I saw how the Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust is using Copilot to cut down on administrative work and make better use of its data, and ultimately provide a better experience for medical personnel and patients. [Read more]
events.summary: Today in the UK, I saw how the Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust is using Copilot to cut down on administrative work and make better use of its data, and ultimately provide a better experience for medical personnel and patients. It's an early example of what's possible as NHS England expands Copilot to as many as 500,000 clinicians and support staff across the country. Read more: https://lnkd.in/gj8h5e4Z The time a crew spends on paperwork is time taken off patients, so cutting admin quietly adds capacity without hiring anyone. What stands out in the Yorkshire example is how much patient-facing care depends on work done well before an ambulance arrives. It would be interesting to see whether Copilot reduces the need to re-enter or reconcile information across handoffs, not just the minutes spent drafting. That’s where an administrative gain could become a measurable operational one. At our recent GrandResolve roundtable, participants said sharing specific success stories is what makes AI adoption believable, and this article delivers. I especially liked the datapoint on Tom Smith , a dyslexic operations manager at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, who uses Copilot to structure drafts and summarize reports, which helps "level the playing field." Congratulations to the Yorkshire Ambulance Service team. This is what leadership in AI looks like. Others in this thread ask where the saved time goes. Your team answers it with a metric, not a minute count. Per Microsoft’s write-up, the trust uses Copilot to organize its data on conveyance to emergency departments, targets 50%, and reports a move from 60% to 56%. That is the standard for every leader rolling out AI: name the operational number it must move before you scale. Copilot stays on administrative work, humans review the output, and accountability stays where it belongs. Well done, and thank you, Satya, for sharing it. 🔎 I don’t want to be pessimistic, and I’m not generally a pessimistic person. If the goal is simply to reduce administrative work and give healthcare professionals more time and attention for their patients, that’s great. But the pessimistic side of me wonders: will AI only assist healthcare professionals and free up their time, or will it also be trained to do their jobs and eventually replace them? Again, I really didn’t want to say this, but I think it’s a fair question. #RACinform view: Rollout optics ≠ runtime reality. Current signals are pilot‑stage and curated; not enough operational data exists to demonstrate sustained impact across NHS workflows. A more honest framing for frontier deployments is a closing caveat: “Early days — we are monitoring real‑world effects.” This preserves integrity, avoids premature claims, and keeps the focus on runtime evidence rather than executive narratives. It would be interesting to know the KPI improvements related to staff/patient experience before vs. after copilot adoption Satya Nadella great to see Microsoft and the NHS England advancing AI adoption in healthcare. While this is a great start LLMs alone are challenged to solve systems-level healthcare problems. Consider EMS as an example. Ambulance dispatch, patient acuity, and anticipated arrivals are early signals in a much larger operational digital twin. Those signals should inform downstream decisions around ED capacity, patient arrival, admission, physician initial assessment (PIA), bed availability, and ultimately emergency department length of stay (EDLOS). Optimizing one workflow does not necessarily optimize the system. Reducing administrative burden is valuable, but the transformational opportunity lies in connecting data, predicting downstream bottlenecks, and orchestrating decisions across the entire patient journey. I see the same challenge across healthcare supply chains, where fragmented systems and disconnected decisions directly affect clinical capacity, operational efficiency, and patient throughput. The next frontier of healthcare AI isn’t simply making individual tasks faster. It’s making the entire health system work smarter, as one integrated ecosystem. The figure that stood out for me is not the 43 minutes a day. It is Yorkshire's conveyance to ED moving from 60% to 56%. That is an outcome metric, not a productivity one, and it is the kind of evidence that justifies scale. From the architecture side, going from 30,000 to 505,000 users is where the real work starts. Two things I would put in the blueprint early: 1. Enforce the admin-only boundary in the design, not only in policy. Once Copilot summarises operational reports, the line between administrative and clinical drifts quickly. Sensitivity labels, DLP and scoped data sources should hold that line, reviewed against the clinical safety case. 2. Fix the data plumbing before the prompts. Copilot can only "join the dots" Samantha Robinson describes if the underlying data is integrated and correctly permissioned. At half a million users, oversharing in SharePoint and Teams becomes the main risk surface. Trust at this scale is an engineering property as much as a cultural one. Curious how NHS England will track outcomes like conveyance alongside time saved as the rollout grows. events.title: UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher
events.summary: Inflation in the U.K. has risen to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to drive up fuel prices LONDON -- Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month. The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That's the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month. The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England's target rate of 2%. Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August. Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz , which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies. Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living. Students and teachers march through Greek capital to protest cost of living UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change Burkina Faso's parliament unanimously votes to reinstate the death penalty Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on Nov. 5. Last month, rate-setters held the bank's main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon. “With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW. Most economists expect an increase in the bank's main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank , have raised rates recently. Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. events.title: Apple iPhone Duo hands-on: Your productivity will hinge on this
events.summary: Apple , this had better be good; you made us wait more than seven years for this to unfold. At long last, the company has introduced the iPhone Duo , its first entry into the foldable device category, and first major hardware release under new boss John Ternus. And, on a personal note, I've never seen my peers this hyped for a device. The National gave the device a spin and ran through its features. Here are our initial thoughts. The lowdown The passport-sized iPhone Duo, when folded, gives you a 13.7cm (5.4-inch) display. Open it up and that digital real estate stretches to 19.3cm (7.6 inches). And it's now Apple's thinnest smartphone, at only 5.2mm when open. The power and camera control buttons remain in their usual slots on the right while it's closed or open in landscape mode. But from here, things get shaken up quite a bit. The volume buttons are now on top, and switching to portrait mode while unfolded brings them to the left for more familiar control. Meanwhile, the USB-C charging port, while still at the bottom when folded, switches to the left side when unfolded, which is a little odd as we're used to that on the right. But there are two notable omissions: there is no Action Button, which is customisable and (probably) most commonly used as the silent toggle No Face ID Face ID – repeat, no Face ID. Instead, a Touch ID, nestled on the power button, makes its return. Skipping the Action Button and Face ID will need some getting used to, particularly the latter, but Apple says key stuff like transactions and verifying your identity will still be seamless – you'll just need your fingers instead of your eyes. Also, battery percentage and carrier details won't be readily visible on the homescreens. Instead, you have to swipe down from the top-right, like the iPhone X. The latest, smaller version of Dynamic Island is also present, but now it now appears on the top right. As for the crease, it is virtually invisible. Apple hasn't released a figure for fold-unfold durability, though the Duo has ceramic shield protection for scratchproofing and is rated IP68 for dust and waterproofing. There are four cameras – the main 48MP Dual Fusion system, the 12MP Centre Stage camera on the cover and the under-display camera on the inner display. You can choose from two colours, night sky and star white, with the former our winner. (It would've been better if there was a defining option like lavender or our all-time favourite, cosmic orange.) By now we know that the Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599, and there are extended shipping times due to overwhelming demand. First steps The iPhone Duo has a clean feel: opening and closing feels reliable, and the sturdy hinge ensures it will stay in place without any wobble or movement. Multitasking is a key feature that allows you to do more with fewer swipes and taps. For example, you can have your email on one side and photos on the other, and you can just drag an image as an attachment. Let the Duo sit L-shaped and you'll be able to do some easy stuff. If you're in the camera app or a streaming service like Netflix, controls will be on screen below for easier navigation. The camera also has a new feature that automatically takes pictures without having to control it; trigger the function, let the main cameras face you and it will track subjects and take pictures from time to time, which you will know when the torch briefly lights up. It also acts as a good teleprompter, which creators and on-camera people will find useful. Apple says apps have been and are being optimised to work with the Duo, and a sign that an app has been updated is when you see controls on the right side. It's also optimised for popular apps such as WhatsApp, Instagram and Slack, to make work, play and creation easier. While we don't have the full list, updates for popular apps are expected to be rolled out on Friday, when the device finally becomes available in stores. While we haven't fully tested it, Apple guarantees battery life on a par with the iPhone 18 Pro, meaning it should, according to our own tests , make it through more than a day and a half. There are two batteries in the Duo, although according to Apple, they work as one, discharge as one and do all things together. The Duo is compatible with the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil. At this point, it is unclear if and when other models of the company's stylus will follow the same path. Initial verdict We're still not sure how much of the iPhone Duo's bigger display we'll be using, considering it has specific purposes and the front screen is big enough to perform most of our tasks. We're foreseeing we'll be using the front display for work and communication, and the bigger one for entertainment and gaming. If the overwhelming orders are any indication, Apple's iPhone Duo is poised to do well. The device feels refined, but its biggest draw may be its seamless integration into Apple's ecosystem. That's a compelling selling point for those who usually find foldables cumbersome or complicated, if they're willing to splash the cash.

events.title: Carriers reroute Riyadh flights to airport four hours' drive away
events.summary: Saudi airlines are turning to Al Qassim, about a four-hour drive from Riyadh, as an alternative to the capital while its airport remains closed following a deadly Houthi attack almost two weeks ago. The kingdom’s main flag carrier, Saudia, is offering tickets to Riyadh via Al Qassim, with a bus connection to the Saudi capital. Riyadh Air, Public Investment Fund’s startup airline, is also giving passengers booked on flights to Riyadh the option to fly to Al Qassim. Riyadh airport is now open to traffic with prior permission, but passenger flights have yet to resume and most airlines have canceled services until anywhere from next week to next year. Local airlines have moved planes parked at Riyadh airport to other locations while the airport remains a Houthi target, suggesting that travel to the capital is not expected to resume soon. — Matthew Martin

events.title: SpaceX and Tesla mega-merger under discussion
events.summary: The News Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, have begun exploring a merger that would create a $3.5 trillion corporate giant spanning key sectors of cutting-edge technology. Musk argued that combining the companies would allow them to deepen cooperation on chip design, robotics, software, and other technologies ; both firms’ share prices rose following the announcement. Liz’s view The outlines of MegaMusk Inc. are starting to emerge, where special committees of SpaceX and Tesla directors will now have to bless the merger. Combining the two would bring the tech and infrastructure parts of Musk’s empire together (the Wall Street pitch) and a hyperconcentrated bet on the billionaire’s inventions, politics, and personality (the actual pitch). Musk already rolled up X, xAI, and SpaceX, whose June IPO paved the way for the Tesla deal. Many of Musk’s projects already bleed into each other — the new Roadster has SpaceX thrusters — and Musk’s employees often work interchangeably across his companies, so there’s some business and governance sense in formalizing what’s already happening. But it’s clear Musk is again using Tesla’s shareholders — and its massive retail investor base — to fund his other exploits, just as he did in 2016 when Tesla bailed out his cash-strapped solar company, SolarCity, and, more recently, when he reallocated Tesla talent and GPUs to xAI. While Musk says he’ll recuse himself from the decision, his companies’ boards don’t have a history of pushing back. Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm told Semafor last year she was skeptical of Tesla investing in xAI; four months later, it invested $2 billion . And a combo would further strengthen Musk’s control over Tesla: Super-voting shares give him roughly 84% of the vote at SpaceX, compared to 20% at Tesla, where every share has equal voting weight. Notable The SpaceX-Tesla tie-up has its own strong logic, one early SpaceX investor told Bloomberg: “Combined, it would be the only company owning the full physical-AI stack … No competitor has an analog .”

events.title: Mecca draws Indonesian sovereign wealth fund investment
events.summary: Opening up real estate ownership in Mecca and Medina to foreign investors could help deliver a boost to investment into Saudi Arabia, after Indonesia’s sovereign fund Danantara completed a 2 billion riyal ($533 million) deal to purchase a hotel and development plots. That agreement is the first time a foreign state has acquired property in Mecca, one of the holiest sites in Islam, and opens the door for further sales to Muslim-majority states, Faisal Shaker, chief executive of Thakher Development, owner of the development sold to Danantara, told Semafor. The company is the master developer behind Thakher Mecca , less than a mile from the Grand Mosque in the city. Sales of another Mecca development called Mathabah will also be launched next year, Shaker said. As part of its plan for sales to foreign investors next year “transactions we aspire to close will not be less than the deal we just announced,” Shaker said. “We are in discussion with multiple stakeholders and different parties from different parts of the world.” Investment into the two cities is “driven by faith and not by cycles,” Shaker said. Saudi Arabia opened Mecca and Medina real estate to Muslims abroad and selected foreign institutions in January. Saudis are still the majority buyers, but Gulf investors are also pouring money into the two cities, Shaker said. Danantara is also considering investing in Medina , Asharq Bloomberg reported. A key part of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s strategy to grow non-oil income is more than doubling religious visitors to the kingdom to 50 million by 2030 from about 20 million last year.

events.title: Hungarian police arrest Orbán-era central bank governor on suspicion of fraud and abuse
events.summary: Hungarian police have taken former Central Bank governor György Matolcsy into custody BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungarian police arrested the country's former Central Bank governor on Wednesday, a significant step in the new government’s pursuit of suspected financial abuses during the rein of Viktor Orbán , whose government has been accused of widespread corruption. Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote in a post on Facebook that the former governor, György Matolcsy, who had also served as finance minister, was in custody, without providing further details. Since taking office earlier this year, Magyar’s government has prioritized investigating suspected financial abuses committed by Orbán-era officials. The arrest followed a statement from Hungary's Central Prosecutor's Office earlier in the day, saying it was “carrying out coordinated investigative actions" in several locations in connection with a Central Bank-related investigation into criminal misappropriation of funds. It did not mention Matolcsy by name but said more details about the case would come later. Matolcsy led Hungary’s central bank from 2013 to 2025, after serving as Orbán’s minister of economy from 2010 to 2013. He was long one of Orbán’s closest economic allies, and has denied any wrongdoing. Matolcsy's lawyer, Pál Bátki, told Hungarian news outlet Telex that the former governor was detained on suspicion of economic fraud that caused significant financial damage and using a forged private document. Couple charged in fatal shooting of 17-year-old on her way to zoo Some changes are coming for Medicare as open enrollment begins Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Much of Matolcsy's tenure as head of the central bank was mired in accusations of corruption related to the bank's establishment of foundations that it endowed with hundreds of billions of forints — equivalent to hundreds of millions of dollars — in public funds. A criminal complaint was filed last month on suspicion of embezzlement, negligence, fraud, and abuse of office while Matolcsy was governor. The complaint came after the central bank audited past real estate investments that it found to have been purchased for inflated prices, causing significant financial damage to the bank. It was unclear whether Matolcsy's detention was related to the real estate purchases or the endowments to the bank's foundations. In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Magyar said it was clear that “certain members of the previous government as well as oligarchs, businessmen and family members connected to them committed serious crimes, typically corruption crimes, both with national funding and EU funding.” His administration in July launched the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which holds investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue cases of misused public funds.
