events.title: Could you soon make your own moonshine? SCOTUS takes up 160-year-old ban
events.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear a challenge to the Reconstruction-era ban on distilling alcohol in private homes. Why it matters: Americans can legally brew beer or make wine at home, but making whiskey, vodka or other spirits can land them in federal prison. The Supreme Court could change that. Driving the booze: SCOTUS will review Department of Justice v. McNutt, an April ruling by the conservative 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that found the nearly 160-year-old home-distilling ban unconstitutional and an overreach of Congress' taxing power. Distilling in your home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 fine or both. The 6th Circuit reached the opposite conclusion in a separate April ruling for Ream v. Department of the Treasury, arguing Congress can restrict distilling at home to protect federal alcohol tax collections. What they're saying: Advocates argue that Congress overstepped their powers by banning distilling in the home through a measure meant to prohibit fraud from commercial distillers, per the Associated Press . The government says Congress acted within its authority as the restriction was intended to stop producers from evading federal excise taxes, per AP. Lifting the ban, the government argues, could undermine Congress' authority to enforce federal tax laws. Friction point: Both appeals courts agreed Congress' taxing power alone doesn't authorize the ban. They split over whether it is a permissible way to collect liquor taxes under the Constitution's Necessary and Proper Clause. Reality check: You didn't hear this from us, but the practice of distilling hooch and moonshine still happens in the U.S. despite the federal prohibition . Some states, like West Virginia, allow some home distilling. But, much like marijuana, those state laws don't override federal law. Advocates hope the Supreme Court will strike down the federal ban and its associated criminal penalty. Why distilling drinks at home is banned Flashback: Congress banned distilling spirits in homes and connected properties in 1868, during the Reconstruction, as part of a crackdown on widespread tax evasion. The restrictions also cover certain premises where beer or wine is made. Yes, but: Federal law allows Americans to brew beer and make wine at home, but not distill spirits. Distilling spirits requires a process that gives people a more concentrated drink and can involve fire hazards and dangerous contamination risks. What happens if SCOTUS overturns the ban? What's next: Even if SCOTUS strikes down the ban, this doesn't mean people can start distilling automatically. Federal alcohol-production rules could limit what people could do at home. The government currently requires permits, registration and tax compliance for the production of distilled spirits. States could also impose their own bans, which would limit what people can make in their homes. The bottom line: SCOTUS could make it easier for Americans to produce their own liquor, but overturning the ban wouldn't necessarily mean anyone could legally set up a still in their backyard … yet.

events.title: Supreme Court will review Reconstruction-era ban on distilling spirits in homes
events.summary: People who want the right to distill spirits in their private homes are celebrating the Supreme Court's decision to hear their case WASHINGTON -- WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to consider whether Congress had the constitutional authority to impose a ban on distilling spirits in private homes more than 150 years ago. Plaintiffs challenging the prohibition on home distilling claim the 1868 law is an antiquated relic of Reconstruction-era politics. They argue that Congress overstepped its taxation powers when it enacted the home distilling ban as part of a tax reform measure designed to curb fraud by commercial distillers. Government attorneys counter that Congress properly restricted where spirits can be distilled to prevent producers from evading federal excise taxes. They warn that lifting the ban would violate Supreme Court precedent and erode congressional powers. Federal law makes home distilling a crime punishable by a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Separate challenges to the law divided two federal circuit courts, which issued conflicting decisions in April, only 11 days apart. A three-judge panel from the Sixth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the federal ban in a case brought by John Ream, a brewpub owner from Newark, Ohio, who wants to distill whisky at home for his personal consumption. A Fifth Circuit panel ruled in favor of different plaintiffs — members of the Texas-based Hobby Distillers Association — and concluded that statutory prohibitions on in-home distilling are outside the scope of Congress’ taxing power under the Constitution. The Supreme Court agreed to review the Fifth Circuit decision, which was the Justice Department’s preference. Plaintiffs’ attorney Robert Alt said they are “thrilled” that the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case. “Our country’s founders would be rolling over in their graves to learn that a pastime in which even George Washington partook, which is as American as apple pie and certainly a lot older, has quite absurdly been turned into a federal crime,” Alt said in a statement. Attorneys for the plaintiffs in both cases argue that Congress could ban a broad array of activities inside private homes — including cooking, gardening and remote work — under the government’s interpretation of the 19th century law. Couple charged in fatal shooting of 17-year-old on her way to zoo Some changes are coming for Medicare as open enrollment begins Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say “The importance of this case and the questions it presents could hardly be overstated,” the plaintiffs' lawyers wrote . “It presents fundamental questions of the extent of federal power and the powers reserved to the states and the people.” Justice Department attorneys said the government’s regulation and taxation on the production of distilled spirits is as old as Congress itself. They noted that Congress outlawed home distilling to prevent those producers from evading taxes or government inspections. “And because the location restrictions were enacted only after lengthy experience with tax evasion, upholding those restrictions would not open the door to hypothetical laws restricting other conduct lacking that history,” they wrote . The government says Ream asked the Supreme Court to resolve an “additional question” of whether location restrictions on home distilling exceed the scope of Congress’s power to regulate interstate commerce. But the government urged the high court to avoid that question, saying it wasn’t part of Ream’s case or the government’s current arguments in either case. events.title: Saudi Arabia postpones FII conference in Riyadh after Houthi attacks
events.summary: Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference after a surge in Houthi attacks on the kingdom. The annual gathering was scheduled to take place from October 26 to 29 in Riyadh. FII chief executive Princess Dr Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said in a statement the 10th edition of the conference "will now take place in 2027", and that the new dates would be announced "very soon". Ms Al Saud said the decision to postpone the gathering "comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates". "Because this is our landmark 10th edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves," she said in a statement. "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best." A message from the CEO of FII Institute #FII10 The Power of Legacy. pic.twitter.com/11Xvf1f5RN — FII Institute (@FII_Institute1) October 19, 2026 The decision to postpone the event follows a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group, including strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. The attacks have disrupted air travel and raised security concerns among international executives and investors. One source told The National their company had remained committed to attending the event despite the attacks on the airport and characterised their mood as "calm and level-headed". They also said they appreciate that safety is a higher priority. The 10th edition of FII was expected to bring together senior government officials, global financiers and corporate leaders, including BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink and JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, to discuss investment opportunities and economic growth. Launched in 2017, FII has become a vital platform for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to promote Vision 2030, the kingdom’s economic diversification programme aimed at reducing reliance on oil and attracting foreign capital. The postponement adds to a growing list of international events affected by the conflict. Saudi Arabia and the EU have postponed a planned summit, while several sporting and cultural events have also been delayed or cancelled amid security concerns, according to a Reuters report. On Monday, Saudi Arabia also announced the cancellation of two more events – Intersec Saudi Arabia and Saudi Retail Forum, according to organisers of both events. Intersec Saudi Arabia 2026, which was due to take place from November 16-18 will now be held in October 2027, organiser Messe Frankfurt Saudi Arabia said on Monday. The Saudi Retail Forum, which was originally scheduled to take place on November 19, has officially been postponed to March 2027. “The decision follows close monitoring of recent developments in Saudi Arabia and was taken in co-ordination with the venue, the local government partners, and the event’s local and international stakeholders,” Messe Frankfurt Saudi Arabia said. It added that the postponement prioritises the safety and security of exhibitors, visitors, partners, suppliers and staff, while “aiming to preserve the international scale and high-calibre attendance”.

events.title: Saudi postpones FII in person after Wall Street lobbying
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia has canceled in-person attendance at its flagship investment conference in Riyadh after Wall Street executives privately relayed safety concerns to organizers, including the boss of the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund, people familiar with the matter said. Organizers of the Future Investment Initiative, due to take place next week, have dropped plans for a gathering of global and regional chief executives, and are telling delegates the event is postponed until 2027, the people said, confirming a Semafor story that a decision to postpone would be made today. The conference, which has become informally known as ‘Davos in the Desert,’ is Saudi Arabia’s highest profile event, attended by some of the biggest names in global finance and business. Next week’s edition had been set to host JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink. Big banks and private equity firms had been privately relaying safety concerns about attending FII to Yasir Al-Rumayyan, Semafor reported earlier, according to people familiar with the matter. Know More Multiple signals suggested FII could be postponed: Rooms at the Ritz Carlton in Riyadh, which is usually blocked for the event, have been available for public booking in the past 24 hours. Other scheduled events such as an exhibition tennis tournament, a charity event linked to the crown prince, and Riyadh Fashion Week have all been postponed after the Houthis escalated attacks on the kingdom. Delaying the conference is not surprising as the airport appears to still be closed, the main business district has instructed tenants to work from home until further notice, and schools have also shifted to home learning. The kingdom, and its neighbors like the UAE and Qatar, have pitched themselves as not just sources of capital, but as a safe home for trillions in financial assets, data centers, and new industries. Speculation has swirled in recent weeks over whether Saudi Arabia would go forward with the event, given high-profile attacks on the Riyadh airport. Organizers have held discussions around allowing overseas executives to participate virtually , Reuters reported last week, and The Wall Street Journal said that some executives had already canceled meetings . The US, along with most other Western governments, recommends against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia. That has knock-on effects on travel insurance costs and advice from internal security and risk teams. Still, Saudi Arabia has viewed attendance at the event, and general support for the Gulf during turbulent times, as a loyalty test for global business leaders. Those who show up in tough times are rewarded, while fair-weather friends are often excluded from lucrative deals . Notable Repeated attacks on Saudi Arabian civilian facilities have dented confidence in the kingdom’s ability to remain relatively immune to the US-Iran war, Semafor reported.

events.title: Exclusive: Secret pay-for-play text rocks Trump White House
events.summary: Top Trump adviser Ric Grenell allegedly outlined a stunning pay-for-influence offer to a Turkish billionaire last year: access to "POTUS," "VIP events" and administration officials, according to a text message, reviewed by Axios, that the White House counsel is investigating. "Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you'll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS," the May 3, 2025, text says. Grenell has called the accusations "lies" and denied sending the text message. Why it matters: Administration officials say the text is a key piece of evidence in the White House's investigation — ordered by President Trump — into whether Grenell abused the president's trust and misappropriated a potential multimillion-dollar donation to the Kennedy Center, which Grenell led at the time. Grenell also served in another Trump-appointed capacity: as special envoy to Venezuela, where Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon also had contracts. "We need to make you the 'American face' down in V," Grenell allegedly wrote in the same 2025 text message to Mildon, whose attorneys sent the text, at least one financial document and other correspondence to the White House counsel's office, according to sources familiar with the investigation. Mildon is married to another Trump adviser: former U.S. attorney for New Jersey Alina Habba, who stormed into the Oval Office on Oct. 9 and accused Grenell of hoodwinking her husband into making a Kennedy Center donation that never arrived, Axios first reported . Zoom in: At the heart of the alleged scheme is a financial transaction involving a private Houston-based defense company's software and the Democratic Republic of Congo, Habba and Mildon's attorneys have told the White House. Mildon alleges that at Grenell's direction, Mildon wired $17.6 million to Texas Armament & Technology. He says the money was to be split in roughly two parts: one for the Congo deal and nearly $6 million for the Kennedy Center. To back up his claims, Mildon provided the 2025 text that discussed the Kennedy Center donation and Congo "software." In the text to Mildon, the sender also says, "There is an e-mail that was sent to you, can you please take a look at it for me ?" That email also was furnished to the White House, as was a May 29, 2025, financial record s howing $17.6 million was wired to the company, known by its initials TXAT, sources said. It would be 17 months before Mildon learned that the Kennedy Center never received the money that he thought was included in the wire he sent at Grenell's direction, Habba told the president. The intrigue : Here's where the story gets mysterious and murky. It's unclear what the Congo contract was for, how it related to the Kennedy Center or what the financial specifics were. The text doesn't mention any financial numbers, either for TXAT or the Kennedy Center. But a source familiar with the situation said that other correspondence furnished to the White House does have financial specifics. The financial transaction sent to TXAT didn't appear to come from Mildon's bank account, as Habba initially indicated to Trump. Instead, the $17.6 million was wired to TXAT from Congo's "Ministère des Finances" in Kinshasa, the capital city, where Mildon has business and access to finances, a White House official said. A spokesman for Mildon would not comment. Spokespeople for TXAT and Congo's government couldn't be reached. "We're trying to find out whose money this is," the official said . Complicating the matter further: Habba's numbers kept changing after she first alerted Trump to the alleged theft of the Kennedy Center money. At first she said the Kennedy Center contribution was for $17 million. Then she said it was about $6 million after talking to Mildon. The exact figure seems to be $5.6 million. The other side: Grenell, who declined to comment for this article, previously told Axios that the claims against him are "absurd." "I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all," he said. "Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations." When told of the text message's exact wording, Grenell hotly denied he sent it because "center" was spelled in British English as "centre," a source briefed on his thinking said. Grenell's allies also have questioned everything from Mildon's background as a businessman to his associates , his age (he's 29 but some records indicate he's 25) and his $10 million wedding last month to Habba, 42, whom he began dating last year. Friction point: As the New York Times examined Mildon's activities in Venezuela, he had a falling out with Grenell, with whom he had been friendly since 2024. Mildon met Habba in 2025 at the Kennedy Center. The Times previously reported aspects of the text message concerning Venezuela and the money from Congo . Inside the room: On Oct. 9, when Habba arrived at the White House, she was "pretty animated," said one administration official, and exclaimed at one point, "Ric stole the money!" The problem, however, was that Habba "didn't have all her stuff in order. She went in there half-cocked without all the facts yelling about Grenell stealing. And the facts keep changing," the source said. "That doesn't mean Ric is out of the woods. This looks really shady." After Habba leveled her accusations, Trump called White House Counsel Will Scharf into Oval Office and asked him to look into her claims, sources said. Trump and Scharf then phoned Grenell, who denied everything and said he would have instantly alerted everyone to the idea of a $17 million contribution. "There's no way this is true. This is crazy," Grenell told Trump at one point, according to a source briefed on the discussion. Behind the scenes: Scharf grew skeptical of Habba's claims early last week because she and Mildon's attorneys were initially slow to furnish any records to help his inquiry, said a source. They submitted the documents on Friday. Scharf is still gathering evidence and plans to verify the digital footprint of the 2025 text, the source said, noting that a printout of the message has the same image of Grenell that appears on his smartphone contact card display. Kennedy Center insiders also have contacted the White House and said they frequently saw Mildon at exclusive events at the facility, indicating he was a big donor. That includes appearances in the vice president's box, next to the president's, a source said. "Here's where Alina might be telling the truth: Mildon did get access. So why did he get access? Was he doing business in Congo with Ric? Why so much access if the contribution was never paid?" one of the administration officials asked. "There's a lot of questions. And POTUS wants answers."

events.title: Supreme Court won't revive accused 9/11 mastermind's plea deal
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied on Monday a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind behind the 9/11 terror attacks, to reinstate plea agreements that would have spared him and two co-defendants the death penalty. Why it matters: The denial keeps the death penalty on the table for the accused 9/11 plotters as they move closer to their June 2028 military trial date, when the government hopes to finally secure convictions more than 25 years after one of America's deadliest terrorist attacks. Driving the news : The Supreme Court released an order list Monday identifying the cases it intends to hear and denying those it won't, like the petition in Khalid Shaikh Mohammad, et al. v. United States. The order doesn't explain why the appeal was rejected. Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from the decision. He served as associate counsel to President George W. Bush, where he reportedly assisted with legal and policy discussions following 9/11. Catch up quick: The government and the three men entered into plea agreements in 2024 that would have spared them the death penalty. The decision was met with outrage and pushback from some 9/11 victims' families. Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin withdrew the agreements days later, declaring that "responsibility for such a decision should rest with me." Mohammed and his co-defendants, Walid bin 'Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, appealed that decision. While a military court initially sided with the defendants, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit sided with Austin, prompting their final appeal to the Supreme Court . Zoom out: Mohammed and his co-defendants were first arraigned in 2008 for their alleged roles in the attacks involving four hijacked planes that struck the Twin Towers in New York City and the Pentagon, with a fourth crashing in Pennsylvania. Mohammed and his fellow defendants have been held at the U.S. military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006. Prosecutors had sought a January 2027 trial date, but a judge determined that timeline would leave too little time to resolve outstanding pretrial issues. What we're watching: The new tentative trial date is for June 5, 2028. Go deeper: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to stand trial in 2028 over 9/11 attacks

events.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
events.summary: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “ Rey ,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization. The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap . Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts. According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States. Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out). On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records . Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal. A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach. That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files. SHINYWIRE KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “ shinywire[.]com .” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates. A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website. The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands. events.title: Zambia makes up with Gulf investor in major copper mine
events.summary: Zambia’s state miner and Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) say they have patched up their financing dispute over Mopani Copper Mines, the development of which is a cornerstone of the southern African country’s economic growth plan. In a letter in September , Zambia’s ZCCM-IH accused the Emirati company of failing to provide equity funding and taking on unapproved debt. The latest statement skirted the issue, describing new joint-exploration projects and saying they “remain aligned on the long-term development” of the mine, but left funding questions open. The truce followed a meeting in Abu Dhabi between Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema and IRH’s CEO on the day the letter became public. IRH paid $620 million in 2024 for a 51% stake in Mopani as part of a deal worth more than $1 billion. Neither side can afford a fight: Zambia, Africa’s second-largest copper producer, needs Gulf capital for its bid to more than triple its output to 3 million tons a year, and IRH aims to lift Mopani’s production from 66,369 tons in 2025 to 300,000 tons by 2029. — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Telecoms group urges cuts to spectrum cost in Africa
events.summary: GSMA, the global telecoms industry body, has urged African governments to cut the cost of radio frequency spectrum, arguing the expense is holding back investment in faster mobile networks. Reforms could add more than $120 billion to the African economy by 2035, expand 4G and 5G coverage, and raise productivity, it estimated. The GSMA said spectrum charges as a portion of annual revenue are significantly higher than the global average for African operators — Botswana, Eswatini, Mozambique, and Zambia were named among the pricier countries. The push for cheaper deals, contained in a report from GSMA’s research wing, comes as more than $10 billion worth of licenses will need to be renewed within the next decade, just as many African governments are struggling to raise revenue and contain debt. In several markets, spectrum auctions have become significant sources of state revenue , creating tensions between governments’ fiscal goals and operators’ calls to use them as a connectivity tool. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: African inventors in spotlight ahead of top engineering prize
events.summary: The continent’s inventors are in the spotlight as Johannesburg prepares to host the final of the Royal Academy of Engineering’s Africa prize . Previous participants have been given a boost in their quest to create life-changing tools. Atish Shah, who took part five years ago, told Semafor his Dar es Salaam-based company Roverlabs is now developing a bionic hand which uses electromyography technology to transform electrical impulses in muscle tissue into movement for amputees. The firm uses 3D printing to manufacture customized assistive devices for people living with disabilities, including insoles, helmets, dentures, and braces. Next month, it is set to begin a home imaging service to ensure people living in Tanzania’s rural areas have access to X-ray and ultrasound technology. — Leah Quinn

events.title: Burundi signs $1.4B power deal with US-backed company
events.summary: Burundi signed a $1.4 billion electricity deal with US-backed Anzana Electric Group, which Washington says will strengthen American supply chains and support mining in the East African country. The country has deposits of nickel, gold, and rare earths. But Burundi, like many resource-rich African nations, has struggled to develop large-scale mining due to power shortages, poor roads and the lack of a direct rail link to export markets. Only one in five Burundians had access to electricity in 2024, according to the World Bank. The 25-year agreement, signed through Anzana’s local subsidiary Weza Power, aims to connect more than 1.2 million households and businesses. It follows a US-backed agreement in March giving New York-listed mining company Lifezone Metals 14 months of exclusive access to assess Burundi’s Musongati nickel deposit, a metal used in stainless steel and some electric vehicle batteries. Washington is pursuing mineral partnerships across Africa to challenge China’s dominance of global supply chains. Last month, US officials also pledged to help Kenya to develop its own mineral processing industry . — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
events.summary: Agility Robotics , the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5 . It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined. From ATRIAS to Digit My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals. We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS —short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait. With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones , and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie . Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year. Agility Robotics Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash. Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1 , which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers. Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins . Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills. In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company , we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO . In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine. Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. events.title: The fallout from Trump's Russia energy moves
events.summary: President Trump's moves to avoid new penalties on Russian energy sent shockwaves through Washington, sparking diplomatic tensions and political turmoil. Why it matters: Trump's push to lower energy prices ahead of the midterms could provide Russia an economic lifeline and is exposing divisions within his own party. Oil, gas and petroleum product exports help finance Russia's war on Ukraine. Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month. That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans. Here's what's on our radar: A new rationale. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in CNN and ABC appearances yesterday, called the diesel deal a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine. It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week." Ukrainian drone strikes have lowered Russia's refining capacity. Trump, in a Truth Social post yesterday, also cast his recent decisions as a way to get a peace deal with Russia. A new clock. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Saturday that Trump wants to take 60 days to review implementing the Graham Act in order to gauge its impact on the global and U.S. economies. A deteriorating relationship. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has sharply and publicly criticized both the diesel deal and Trump's decision to waive, for now, the Graham Act penalties. Trump's post, meanwhile, bashed Zelensky for hitting Russian refineries, "knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." Republican rifts. Many GOP lawmakers and candidates, to varying degrees, have joined Democrats in criticizing Trump's Friday night sanctions waivers and the diesel deal days earlier. Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision not to implement, for now, the bipartisan law named after her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). She's running for a full term after being appointed to replace her brother. Former Rep. Mike Rogers — the GOP candidate in Michigan's tight Senate race — also expressed concern with the decision but avoided directly criticizing Trump on CNN yesterday. Other Republicans were far harsher, including retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who called Friday night's move "beyond irresponsible." Lame duck rumblings. "A growing chorus of House Republicans is warning President Trump that they're ready to block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration gets tougher on Russia," The Hill reports. What we're watching: With the midterms just weeks away, more Republicans are openly breaking with Trump.

events.title: Manchin to campaign with Collins in Maine
events.summary: The News Former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., is traveling to Maine this week to campaign with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, according to details shared first with Semafor. The moderate West Virginian said his visit is motivated by the attacks on Collins for voting too often in support of President Donald Trump. Manchin will hit Maine on Wednesday with Collins and visit Androscoggin County, a fairly evenly divided part of the state. Collins is looking to emphasize her bipartisan credentials down the stretch as her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, leans on his progressive allies and campaigns as a blunt check on Trump. In an interview on Sunday, Manchin said he “can’t remember” a bipartisan effort Collins wasn’t involved in and that he wants to make sure the people of Maine understand how her style of legislating benefits the state. Know More From Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on down, Democrats are attacking Collins for voting for Trump’s nominees and his legislation, though she opposed the tax cuts law and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s confirmation. Collins also helped tank Obamacare repeal in 2017, but Jackson has argued her opposition to Trump is often not decisive. Democrats cite statistics showing Collins votes with Trump 90% or more of the time, but Manchin called those numbers “bullsh*t” because they include mostly nominee votes. He said his trip is dedicated to “debunking” the idea that she’s been an enabler for Trump. “She is not a Trump senator,” he said. Manchin specifically mentioned the Electoral Count Act, a law intended to prevent another Jan. 6-style attempt to block an election result, which Collins sponsored. He also worked closely with Collins on the bipartisan infrastructure law. “In the Senate, Joe and I worked across the aisle to tackle some of our nation’s toughest challenges. Together, we built bipartisan coalitions to end government shutdowns, secure critical COVID-19 relief, and pass the bipartisan infrastructure law,” Collins said. “We need more people in the Senate, not fewer, who are willing to put partisanship aside, listen to one another, and deliver results.” Now that their debates are over, Maine’s Senate race is entering its final stage. And Manchin’s visit will contrast sharply with some of Jackson’s high-profile progressive surrogates like Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Bernie Sanders of Vermont; Jackson will hold a town hall with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., on Thursday.

events.title: Fuel subsidy becomes Nigerian election battleground
events.summary: The News The leading contenders in Nigeria’s presidential election face a defining question: should the fuel subsidy be restored to ease the burden of rising energy costs? President Bola Tinubu, who is seeking a second term in January, has repeatedly defended his decision to scrap a years-long subsidy program in 2023 to avoid wasteful spending and invest in infrastructure development. But his government’s introduction of a short-term petrol price discount this month to counter rising costs driven by the Iran war has reignited the debate as to whether a subsidy would make a more lasting return. Tinubu’s main rivals say they plan to restore some form of consumer support if elected and have accused the president of panicking in the face of pressure to account for his decision, with polls opening in less than 100 days. SBM Intelligence, a Lagos-based advisory firm, found in a survey published in September that more than two-thirds of voters want the government to reinstate a fuel subsidy of some kind. Insecurity, which has worsened around the country, is also set to figure as a major point of contention. The revived subsidy debate is shaping just about every conversation concerning the coming vote in Africa’s biggest democracy. Tinubu and his 17 challengers are hitting the campaign trail to sway voters whose collective purchasing power has weakened sharply in the last three years, in large part due to the five-fold rise in fuel prices in that period which has driven inflation and spawned a cost-of-living crisis . Its resurgence reflects Nigeria’s history as the continent’s top oil producer and exporter that has consistently failed to convert its energy riches into broad-based prosperity. For years, the vast majority of the crude oil produced in the country was exported because none of the government’s domestic refineries were fully functional. Imported refined products were then subsidized by payments from the state-oil company NNPC, enabling a multibillion-dollar largesse that grew into an increasingly opaque and corrupt scheme, according to government fact-finders and international observers. It was also costly: The program’s $10 billion in 2022 exceeded the combined budget for healthcare and education. Tinubu has largely not faced widespread protests or strong political opposition since ending the subsidy. He has told Nigerians that his policy approach is shifting from offering “ emergency treatment ” — ostensibly to fix the faulty foundations of the economy he inherited — to enabling shared prosperity. But in Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, he faces familiar challengers who are eager to make the coming election a referendum on the impact of energy costs. “Bola made life expensive. I will work to make life affordable again,” Atiku said in a campaign video last week. Obi, the other heavyweight in the race, pledged to judge his leadership by metrics that would show Nigerians “eating better, living better, and escaping poverty.” Know More The sharp rise in energy costs that followed Tinubu’s subsidy removal led several businesses to shutter or reconsider operations in Nigeria. But while many questioned the absence of safety net measures to cushion the impact of Tinubu’s so-called shock therapy , the International Monetary Fund praised the subsidy removal, as did several economists. An IMF official last week cautioned Nigeria to avoid the temptation of reinstating a subsidy for political reasons. The Dangote refinery in Lagos, which started supplying fuel in Nigeria two years ago, provides about 70% of Nigeria’s domestic fuel needs. But the country still imports refined fuels. Both Dangote — which buys more than a third of its crude from international suppliers — and fuel importers are vulnerable to global oil price shocks. The potential for further escalation in the Iran war, underscored by recent Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, raises the question of how long Nigeria is prepared to extend the price cap that is initially planned to be in place for 30-days. “I think it’s highly likely that this gets extended, at least through the elections into Q1,” said Ikemesit Effiong, a partner at SBM. BMI, a subsidiary of Fitch Group, expects the price cap to amount to up to 0.4% of Nigeria’s gross domestic product by the second quarter of next year. Alexander’s view Nigeria’s subsidy debates are divisive because the program — once seen by many Nigerians as the only benefit they got from the state — has swallowed historically mammoth sums and is inextricably associated with corruption and state capture by a cabal of favored oil traders. Many analysts say Nigeria’s fuel subsidy burdened public finances and encouraged adverse behaviors like fuel smuggling. Together with changes that allowed the naira currency to float freely by market forces, Tinubu’s subsidy removal helped to improve Nigeria’s fiscal stability and strengthen reserves. But trialling a short-term fuel price cap points to a government reckoning with the pain it has inflicted. “The removal of the fuel subsidy has been economically necessary, but socially painful,” Jervin Nadioo, an analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, told me. He believes Tinubu is “well positioned to secure re-election” but growing public frustration over living costs suggests that an improved economic picture has not translated into sufficient relief for households. Stop-gaps and sweeteners may sway some voters towards Tinubu in January. But it is more likely that the difficulties of the last three years have already hardened views about the candidates. Room for Disagreement The battle for political advantage ahead of elections should not obscure a reasonable expectation that governments can intervene to soften the pain of citizens, said Vahyala Kwaga, country head for Nigeria at policy research group BudgIT. “Anything that can alleviate the hardship that the masses suffered from the day it was announced that the subsidy is gone is certainly welcome,” Kwaga said. Ultimately, though, his concern is with transparency and accountability: “Who is going to be held responsible if the subsidy doesn’t work?” Notable Nigeria’s savings from the fuel subsidy removal have largely been absorbed by higher ‌debt-servicing costs and increased government spending, finance minister Taiwo Oyedele said in July.

events.title: The AI bet is running straight into a capital crunch
events.summary: The Scene A capital crunch is coming to the AI buildout that’s already plagued by shortages of chips, power and materials. “Soon, there will be shortages of capital” and lenders are starting to demand real returns, Tan Su Shan, who runs Southeast Asia’s largest bank said at a Semafor World Economy Global Leaders Dinner in Bangkok. “When the party will end, I don’t know,” the CEO of DBS Group said at the event, held on the sidelines of the World Bank and IMF annual meetings. But “there will come a point where people need to question the returns.” Her bet: If you’re anywhere on the AI supply chain, you might be okay for, say, the next two years, but probably not longer than that. Global investors are already showing “jittery nerves,” Tan said, following a chip selloff across global markets sparked by the Broadcom CEO Hock Tan’s comparison of AI investors to casino gamblers. A lot of investors have “no clue what they are investing in,” he said at DBS’s tech conference last week. But the market reaction isn’t necessarily bad, Tan argued. Unlike during the global financial crisis in 2008, she said, investors can see the weakness coming and that’s starting to play out with more discerning buyers demanding risk-adjusted returns. “They’re bringing up this ROI question, the capex question. The market is speaking, and I don’t think it’s a bad thing,” she said. Q&A Shelly Banjo: The CEOs of Broadcom and Intel sounded the financial alarm on AI, likening investors to casino gamblers. Do you share that concern? Tan Su Shan: There’s shortages in memory. There’s shortages in chips. There’s shortages in power. And soon there will be shortages in capital. So if you’re anywhere around that supply chain, the next two years you’re going to be okay. But what will then happen is that the users of AI will start demanding returns. Now those returns, the ROI, may or may not materialize. Hock [[Tan]] said, “Well, some people are just investing like it’s a casino. They don’t really know what the returns are, but they’re just punting away.” I can’t remember his exact words, but, sort of, it’s a casino. People don’t know what they’re doing. It’s like mom gave you some money to go play video games, and you’re playing video games and wasting the money, and I think Elon Musk, latched on to that, he said, “No crying in the casino.” It really spooked the markets. Why do you think it had such an outsize impact? There was quite a lot of reaction. It does speak to the jittery nerves in the market. But the fact that we’re all talking about it is actually not a bad thing. Unlike previous crises where they just came upon us quite suddenly in one fell swoop, people are now bringing up this ROI question, the capex question. The bond market has spoken, right? I’m demanding more returns for the kind of risk that we’re taking, both on the AI front and the US fiscal deficit. So I think the market’s speaking and it’s not a bad thing. It’s not like there isn’t a lot of money in the world, though. So where do these capital fears come from? The US capital markets have convinced the whole world to invest in their growth companies. No matter how much money you’re losing, it’s okay. In the bond market, no matter how much you’re spending, it’s okay. The incredible genius of the US is its ability to hoover up investments from everyone — from sovereign wealth funds, to private individuals, to retail, down to the youngest investor. The kids are now in Robinhood buying SpaceX. But with this massive hoovering of dollars into this concentrated bucket, there will come a point where people need to question the returns. When the party will end, I don’t know. The private credit market is also adjusting, which is not a bad thing. So I’m hopeful that we could see an equilibrium. How are you thinking about the projects that are locking in this long-term debt at higher rates, and how do you think about that risk for your bank and the customers that you’re serving? The market is adjusting and a lot of the hyperscalers are tapping the market before their credit ratings get downgraded. But they’re moving from being massive cash generators to becoming massive cash guzzlers, and that in itself will be a massive pivot. You’re sitting right in the center of all these geopolitical fault lines, with business in Taiwan, mainland China, and across Asia. How do you strike a balance? This is a great time for middle powers. There’s two big powers, and then there’s everybody else. And all these middle powers, everyone has this ability to stay open, stay world-based, and continue to transact with each other. And frankly, the better connected we are, the safer it will be for everyone. Why? Because AI unleashed with no guardrails and no sharing of best practices and no sharing of cyber know-how means no one’s going to win. This is something that the world needs to take seriously. You’re channeling your inner Mark Carney here. That speech was outstanding. We all need to work better together. This is not a time to start being selfish. DBS was early on using AI with your wealth advisers. Are you at a point where your massive army of wealth advisers are now taking orders from the robots? And if so, can’t your customers just build their own? They probably are, and that’s fine. And at some point in time, it may be our agents talking to customers’ agents. But the key is you want to be there for when their agent’s looking for stuff, you want to be so embedded in their entire journey. Because it should be trusted more than something out on the internet, grounded in policies and governance. And there should be guardrails around what we can and cannot do. Where someone is looking and evaluating your agent. Someone who’s making sure that agents are not accessing data they shouldn’t be accessing, that they’re not doing stuff they shouldn’t be doing, and that you’re evaluating, ‘are they doing what we want them to do?’ Because if they’re not, sayonara, kill the agent.

events.title: The future of medicine may depend on African DNA
events.summary: Medicine is moving toward a future in which a person’s DNA can help to predict disease risk, guide personalized treatment and inform therapies for genetic disorders. But as precision medicine and genetic therapies become more mainstream, the science behind these advances has a major gap: they do not work equally well for everyone. Despite Africa’s central place in human origins and its extraordinary genetic diversity, people of African ancestry remain underrepresented in the genomic datasets used to understand disease, estimate health risks, and develop treatments. Closing that gap is going to require more than just collecting more samples. It will take sustained investment in African scientists, research institutions, biobanks, and bioinformatics capacity. We propose an initial $100 million investment over 10 years to build a coordinated, African-led genomics initiative, with African governments, international funders and life sciences companies sharing responsibility for its success. It will be worth the investment. We already know that studying genetic variation in African ancestry populations has helped reveal a biological mechanism that has benefited patients worldwide. Recent studies of a protein called PCSK9 shows what researchers can gain by studying this diversity. In 2005, researchers identified naturally occurring variants in PCSK9, which is produced in the liver, among African American participants. These variants were associated with lower cholesterol. Follow-up studies linked these genetic variants to reduced coronary heart disease risk. These findings helped establish PCSK9 as a drug target and contributed to the development of PCSK9 inhibitors, a new class of cholesterol-lowering medicines now used around the world. This story matters because the discovery began with human genetic variation that might otherwise have received less attention. A genetic difference can point to a biological pathway, and that pathway can become the basis for a treatment. There may be many more such discoveries waiting in populations that genomic research has overlooked. The effects of underrepresentation are already visible in genetic risk prediction. Tools developed mainly with European-ancestry data can be less accurate when applied to people whose genetic backgrounds differ from the original study populations. As genomic medicine enters routine care, these gaps could influence how reliably we estimate disease risk or interpret a person’s genetic results Closing the gap will need sustained investment into the continent’s ecosystem as we’ve already suggested. Samples and data should not simply leave the continent while expertise and benefits accumulate elsewhere. African-led programs will need long-term support while communities must also have a meaningful say in how their data are used and share in the benefits. Our $100 million proposal is a starting ambition, not a full estimate of what the continent will need. African governments and the African Union can help coordinate national commitments and regional collaboration. International research funders and philanthropies should provide sustained support. Pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies should contribute through equitable partnerships that recognize the value of African-led discovery. This work should strengthen African health systems, too. Research can support local expertise and diagnostic capacity while helping identify treatments relevant to the continent’s health priorities. The scientific gains, however, could reach far beyond Africa. Ultimately, when research reflects more of humanity, we have a better chance of understanding disease and developing medicines that work for more people beyond Africa. The world may be overlooking its next important medical discovery. Investing in African genomics is a practical way to look for it.

events.title: To prep for sale of Ronaldo’s Saudi team, PIF pays off $213 million debt
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund is tapping its portfolio companies to pay off 800 million riyals ($213 million) of debt held by the soccer club Al Nassr — where star Portuguese striker Cristiano Ronaldo plays — according to people familiar with the matter. Public Investment Fund (PIF) is orchestrating corporate sponsorship deals to strengthen the Saudi Pro League club’s balance sheet, which would help facilitate a sale to investors led by AC Milan owner RedBird Capital, these people said. One person close to the fund described RedBird’s interest as “early” and cautioned that a deal might not be reached. RedBird has held at least two meetings with PIF about taking a 70% stake in the team, the people said. RedBird and its partners would pay about 1 billion riyals ($267 million) for the stake, with Ronaldo himself expected to hold a 20% share. Other investors could include the privately held, Riyadh-based media, sports, and entertainment firm Saudi Media Company (SMC). Final terms have not been agreed upon and could still change, they said. RedBird and PIF declined to comment. Al Nassr and Ronaldo’s representatives didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Asharq Bloomberg previously reported that RedBird was leading a consortium in talks to buy a stake in the club. Know More Acquiring Al Nassr would help Gerry Cardinale’s RedBird strengthen ties with Ronaldo, one of the world’s most marketable athletes, whose investment firm, CR7, holds a 25% stake in UD Almeria, a club in Spain’s second division backed by SMC. RedBird, which bought AC Milan in 2022 and manages roughly $21 billion, has built a reputation as a major media and sports broker, most recently financing high-profile media mergers involving Skydance, Paramount, and Warner Bros. Discovery. Buying Al Nassr would put RedBird at the center of Saudi Arabia’s multi-billion-dollar sports expansion, which had been on a tear before the government began cutting back on spending. The kingdom has used sports deals and hosted competitions to promote itself and encourage more active lifestyles at home. But after pouring billions of dollars into the effort, it now needs foreign investors to help turn around loss-making soccer clubs and the breakaway LIV Golf tournament. Saudi Arabia spent around $900 million in 2023 buying up soccer’s biggest players like Ronaldo, Neymar Jr., and Karim Benzema in order to raise the profile of the kingdom’s league internationally. The government transferred ownership of several soccer clubs to PIF and other state-controlled companies to prepare the teams for privatization. The first fruit of that effort came this year when PIF sold a 70% stake in Riyadh-based club Al Hilal in August to Kingdom Holding, the investment company of billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal — a deal that valued the club at about 1.4 billion riyals. If finalized, people close to Al Nassr’s new owners say being part of a wider consortium would allow the team to cut costs and tap media and marketing partnerships with other RedBird and SMC portfolio companies. They also want to boost the club’s profile in the US. Notable Despite lofty expectations, Saudi league insiders say success means standards comparable to Dutch clubs rather than Europe’s elite. They hope stronger domestic competition will help develop Saudi talent ahead of the 2034 World Cup , Camilla Wright writes in a column for Semafor.

events.title: China's economy accelerates on robust exports as domestic weakness persists
events.summary: China says its economy grew 4.5% for the July-September quarter from a year ago HONG KONG -- China said Monday its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for the year as trading partners seek to balance their trade deficits with the country. Economic growth accelerated from the 4.3% year-on-year rate recorded in the April-June quarter, the slowest expansion in more than three years. Its economy expanded 4.6% in the first three quarters. For the whole year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5% , down from last year’s 5% expansion. Earlier this month, the International Monetary Fund trimmed its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5%, the lower end of Beijing’s goal. “Domestic demand was weak, while trade grew strongly,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics. Exports will likely stay strong but global trade barriers remain a risk, he said. China’s domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market. The headline official growth figure is becoming “an increasingly poor indicator of how the broader economy is performing,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board. That’s because it masks “widening disparities across industries, regions, and households,” Zenglein said. Beijing faces difficult trade-offs and managing domestic imbalances may prove more challenging than dealing with external pressures, he added. On Monday, Mao Shengyong, deputy head of China’s National Bureau of Statistics, cautioned of the economic challenges ahead. “The international environment is complex and volatile, the problem of insufficient domestic demand remains relatively prominent and the foundation for a stable, improving economy still needs consolidation,” he told a news conference. With exports being one of the few bright spots, China is on track to surpass last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus globally, after logging a 36% growth in exports last month and already a $938 billion surplus between January and September. Elevated U.S. tariffs have hit some U.S.-China bilateral trade and forced China to look elsewhere, including Southeast Asia, Latin America and Europe. High-tech exports such as semiconductors and autos , including hybrid and electric vehicles, are among areas driving its export growth this year. As China pursues self-sufficiency to help shield itself from Western export controls and trade uncertainties, it has built up massive domestic manufacturing capacities across industries such as solar and EVs, which are heavily subsidized by the government. But output was scaled up rapidly at a time of weakened domestic consumption, so many of these goods are shipped to overseas markets at competitive prices. An export-reliant growth model that’s highly tech-driven has shown limited job creation and broad income gains while risks of artificial intelligence-driven labor displacements continue to grow, said Ecaterina Bigos, senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Couple charged in fatal shooting of 17-year-old on her way to zoo Some changes are coming for Medicare as open enrollment begins Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Many trade partners fear their domestic industries and economies face growing threats from lower-cost Chinese manufactured imports. “It is untenable and unsustainable for the world’s second largest economy to rely on foreign demand to prop up its own growth,” said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University. Through its persistent and large trade surpluses, China “has become a drag on world growth rather than an engine that pulls the rest of the world along,” Prasad said. The European Union is among those impatient to reduce its trade imbalance with China. The 27-nation bloc runs a trade deficit with China of more than $1.1 billion a day. For the first nine months of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were up 16%. EU countries are eyeing more curbs on China after the EU reached an agreement with China this month to roughly halve the number of Chinese hybrid vehicle imports over the next few years. China can work with other countries on disputes and it wants to keep its market access, said Gary Ng, a senior economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis. With a deal with the EU on hybrid cars, for example, China can likely still sell more made-by-China products in the longer run while avoiding a broad tariff hike. Even with agreements made between China and the EU, “trade imbalances will be difficult to resolve quickly,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at Dutch bank ING. Policymakers say an undervalued yuan, China’s currency, against the dollar and the euro has contributed to China’s growing trade surplus, even though China’s central bank has dismissed the claims.

events.title: French protests raise fears of spillover effect
events.summary: A weekend of violent cost-of-living protests in France risks intensifying crises elsewhere in Europe, analysts warned. Though largely peaceful, in some areas they degenerated into riots and mass looting in which cars were set alight, with police arresting more than 2,000 people. France is already grappling with a worsening debt problem and the prospect of far-right and far-left parties dominating 2027 presidential elections. Now, it is at the center of a Europe-wide migration clash; regional leaders last week reportedly engaged in “heated” and “ugly” exchanges . Protests also took place in Belgium, Italy, and Portugal , while Commerzbank’s chief economist warned continental giant Germany “is becoming increasingly similar to France, even if many German politicians do not want to acknowledge it.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: Brazil presidential candidates at loggerheads in the first debate
events.summary: Brazil’s presidential candidates traded barbs in the first debate ahead of Sunday’s runoff, with polls showing a technical tie. Incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had avoided debating challenger Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of a former president jailed for staging a coup — but the rightist’s first-round victory put the president on the back foot. Though the pair are neck-and-neck, Brazil’s political system has already shifted to the right: Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party is now the biggest in both chambers of Congress and has won several governorships. A Bolsonaro win would also confirm Latin America’s broader rightward turn, giving the Trump administration another key ally as it vies to outmuscle China across the region. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: China’s third quarter GDP beats forecasts, though worries abound
events.summary: China’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter thanks to the country’s powerful export machine, with domestic consumption still lagging and the authorities showing little interest in fiscal stimulus. The latest figures put the world’s second-biggest economy on track for the government’s 4.5-5% GDP growth target for 2026, but cemented the growing gulf between iffy domestic demand and surging sales abroad: “ It’s too competitive and there’s no profit ,” one motorbike parts executive told Reuters of the Chinese market. Though broadly upbeat, the data will likely amplify calls abroad for Beijing to do more to stoke consumption, with growing political frustration — particularly in the West — over what critics say is China’s overcapacity hollowing out industries in other countries. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Bob Woodward reveals "dream source" in memoir, "Secrets," out next month
events.summary: Bob Woodward — in an eye-opening excerpt from his forthcoming memoir, "Secrets," that's previewed in the new issue of The New Yorker — reveals that one of his best friends, the late Richard Darman, was also one of his best sources during the Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations. "Darman was willing, even eager at times, to talk about the most sensitive intelligence matters, including N.S.A. intercepts and covert C.I.A. operations," Woodward writes in his book , out Nov. 15. "He was always careful not to talk about matters that would harm national security, I believed, but he would go right up to the edge — a reporter's dream source." Why it matters: Woodward, 83 — who followed the blockbuster Watergate reporting of his youth with a shelf of revelatory books about American presidents — gives a searingly honest account of the collapse of his friendship with Darman after a Post series that was damaging to Bush. Woodward details a disappointment in his Washington Post career and, in the case of a story where he was the responsible editor, a "moral failing." The New Yorker calls the Darman excerpt "A Dangerous Friendship," revealing the danger of "getting too close to a source." Woodward and Darman never reconciled, although "Secrets" describes their deathbed encounter. Woodward writes in his New Yorker debut that he and Darman, who controlled the paper flow to Reagan as staff secretary and was budget director for Bush 41, "had countless long lunches together — Saturday or Sunday — at the Madison Hotel, across the street from the Post , discussing government, journalism, and ourselves": "I felt like I was getting a master class in how government really operated. Plus, many scoops. In later years, Darman would drive out on weekends to our country house near Annapolis, Maryland, to spend large parts of the day with me and my wife, the journalist Elsa Walsh, who was particularly fond of him. Some people found him arrogant, but I loved his comfortable confidence as a friend and a source. It was part of what made him so extraordinary and valuable. He knew how to turn on the charm, and he did for both Elsa and me." Behind the scenes: "From critical national-security information to the colorful office tales he shared, Darman provided me with a gold mine of information," Woodward recalls. "I interviewed him in at least fifty-eight meetings or phone conversations. I have boxes filled with hundreds of pages of notes on our discussions. After our most important conversations, as is my practice, I typed a memo of one to six pages, laying out in detail what he'd said." Detailing Darman's " hatchet man " role, Woodward reveals that the "hardest of Darman's targets to dislodge was the First Lady, Nancy Reagan. While Darman poured scorn on her in private, describing her to me as a 'mean bitch,' he could not find a way to drive a stake into her heart." After a hard-won legislative victory, Darman told Woodward, Reagan said: "Whew! Ever feel like you shit a pineapple?" Keep reading ... Get "Secrets."
